titleEn: Is it truly right for politics to exploit regional
contentEn:
Considering the political characteristics of the Grand National Party, which is Korea's conservative party, its fundamental principle is the protection or growth of the vested interests' maximum benefits. This time, candidate Oh Se-hoon became the mayor of Seoul after winning only 5 districts centered around Gangnam out of 22 electoral districts. How can we interpret this?
'Are there many haves, and do they all live in Gangnam?'
If you ask them if this is wrong,
'Why should the haves share with the have-nots? Wouldn't that be communism?'
'Isn't politics about representing one's own interests?'
They might answer like this. And the answer to that is, yes, that's correct. It is very natural for humans to support someone who represents their interests, and that is politics.
And if you take from the haves through effort and give it to the have-nots, that is indeed communism.
I will acknowledge these two points for now. However, the problem lies in the fact that it's the Mayor of Seoul, not a district head. The Mayor of Seoul should be a person for Seoul, just as the President should be a person for the nation. Therefore, one must recognize that problems are likely to arise if regional self-interest is involved.

Looking at the policy direction of the late President Park Chung-hee, whom conservatives never cease to admire, it was about concentrating water on promising trees, so that those trees would make the pasture green. It was certainly an effective policy for barren land. And its effect was that large trees created shade and improved the soil, allowing small trees and grass to grow. It was about creating a prosperous nation rather than everyone living in a wasteland.
However, as the population shifted from growth to decline, and industry from secondary to tertiary sectors. As Korea's economy overcame the IMF crisis to become a powerful foreign currency reserve holder, and society shifted from 7-day, all-night work to a 5-day work week, choosing quality over quantity, the necessary policies changed. These large trees, which made the nation prosperous in its early days, are now absorbing the nutrients of smaller trees, leading them to wither and die. And such relative poverty is growing, and with policies tailored to large trees being overused, small trees face a situation where they easily die. A prime example is the healthcare insurance policy they are trying to change. It doesn't matter to the large trees whether it changes or not; if it changes, it's even better. But the safety net for small trees is being changed to standards for larger trees. They abandon the weak for the sake of all. This is truly a scenario one would expect only in the worst situations or in battle. It might have truly been that way during President Park's era. But I question whether our society today lacks such leeway.

On the contrary, the social conflict costs resulting from this are gradually increasing, nullifying the effects of development. People who should be proud of our city due to development are building walls, saying 'only our district, that other district is another country.' This is a deeply unfortunate situation for everyone. Far from our wish for unification, this land is divided even in neighboring towns, with lines drawn between 'communists' and 'conservatives'.
And some political forces accelerate and stimulate this, targeting vested interest areas with large populations to achieve their goals. It's a great pity. What I heard from a friend who majored in architecture and civil engineering about Cheonggyecheon is that the money to maintain all of Seoul's streams was poured into Cheonggyecheon. This achieved political effects, but if the same money had been distributed throughout Seoul, the invisible quality of life for all of Seoul would have improved more. However, if that had happened, President Lee Myung-bak might not have existed. Perhaps our public is merely like the monkeys in the 'Jo-sam-mo-sa' (giving three in the morning and four in the evening) fable.
Those blinded by power exploit this and, to obscure the truth, do not choose better decisions even when they exist. If someone chooses such a path, they are immediately held accountable and brought down.
The same logic applies to joint-stock companies. Clearly speaking, this is a drawback of the backward majority rule system adopted by the democracy humanity created. The public is not always wise. No matter how smart and capable a candidate is, the public has neither the time nor the means to evaluate them.
If we want a better democracy, we should consider this more at a systemic level. Beyond votes that are simply split between Party #1 and Party #2. No matter how principled a person joins Party #1, they ultimately cannot change Party #1. Party #2 is not much different either. This is probably because these systemic problems exist within the parties themselves, and politicians are a breed more entangled in vested interests than the public.

How can we develop a system to identify principled and truthful politicians? It's questionable how figures like a party's Dangjin representative from a car racing background, Gwangmyeong representative from a gangster background, and a certain assembly member who became a star by plagiarizing someone else's book and then resorted to phone threats, can become influential figures in a party. Doesn't that imply they have already lost their self-purification ability?

Before, I conscientiously researched each and every candidate. However, after experiencing the drawbacks of this majority rule, this time I ultimately chose the lesser of two evils. I know that's the nature of politics, but I'm not sure how to fix the system.

**Leading those who oppose you is also leadership. That was my advice from the very beginning of this government's inauguration**
**([http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70025465539](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70025465539))**
**and it remains valid. And Democratic Party. We didn't support you because you're pretty.**

What about a method like giving negative weighting to population by region or age group?

titleEn: [Blog DJ] Songs That Hit Differently After Turning
contentEn:
**Naver Music Player is a discontinued service.**

I forgot how to count my age since I was in my twenties,
and now, before I knew it, I'm thirty-two and have become the father of a new life.
 

 
The age of thirty always sounded like an old man's age, but I still dream, love, and nothing has changed.
Kim C's song "Irony" was something I happened to hear, and its lyrics stuck in my heart and wouldn't leave, so I searched for a long time to find out what the song was. For me, who has no interest in the entertainment industry, even finding something like this is a chore.
 
The young father in my memory was a dependable figure at thirty-four, but I still feel like a shallow-rooted reed.
Isn't that why we're human? Perhaps our fathers felt the same way.
 
Recently, something bad happened to my father, and it saddens me to see his shoulders look unusually small.
And what can I do when I'm still too insecure to be my father's cane or a strong support for my child?
 
Still, I must live with a smile. Because I am a child's father, and a son.
Perhaps it's not us who grow, but time itself that makes us grow?

titleEn: [Samsung Blog's Essential Post] Writing Skills and
contentEn:
A huge 'holy ground' has emerged with 18 trackbacks and 923 comments.
This is a post titled [Misconceptions and Truths about Galaxy A](http://www.samsungblogs.com/67)([http://www.samsungblogs.com/67](http://www.samsungblogs.com/67)) written by a Samsung Electronics employee.

First, as a blogger who also comes from a developer background, I agree with some points, but it really makes me realize how cautious developers need to be with their posts. To be precise, the article was written not just by 'a developer,' but by 'a Samsung Electronics Galaxy developer.' This means it cannot be generalized to all developers, and I feel the perspective is very narrow.
Let's briefly break it down one by one.

1. App-related
- "There's a typo in the middle, 'web' instead of 'app'."
- "Apple is at the level of a child in the App business, which started from the 1st generation."
: In fact, Apple introduced the App Store as an eco-standard model, and it's a model that has been proven with products already 2 years old. And unlike Samsung Electronics, it's a major S/W company that built everything from OS to applications in the PC market, with a history going back to 8-bit. Since you're an employee... Apple was already making S/W when you were in kindergarten. When comparing CISC and RISC architectures, Apple was always compared side-by-side with IBM. If you're a developer, it's stranger not to know this. If you want to criticize, it should be based on objective information about the subject.

*** 2010-05-24 Addendum: I misunderstood the above phrase. Looking at the original text, it meant that Google is just starting compared to Apple's App business, which began with the 1st generation, and I interpreted it in reverse.**

- App compatibility issues
: It's surprising to say that app compatibility will be perfect while doing embedded development. Nothing is perfect until you run it. It's natural for Android to fall short in compatibility compared to Apple, which has fewer device models. Of course, most will be compatible, but making such a bold claim only creates an excuse for failure. It's as foolish as a junior developer saying, 'My program has no bugs.'

2. Internal Memory Issue
- All Android developers point out the internal memory issue. Go to a user community. Inconvenience is inconvenience, and memory or storage limitations are stressful for developers. The illusion that apps will always be small is sufficiently debunked by Bill Gates' 640KB prophecy.

3. Useless UI
- You certainly brought up a point that can happen business-wise. There are cases where software specs are limited due to the interests of related companies. However, saying 'I could only make the software that much for the other party' is... I don't know why you're getting paid. A developer's skill is determined by software quality. If Samsung can't make good UI, are only UI companies benefiting? Didn't you consider that Apple and LG would benefit? It's not useless UI, it's useless talk.

4. Company that only emphasizes hardware specs
- Yes. That's how the marketing team and advertisements appear. KT's iPhone ads promoted video editing, copy-paste, etc. Why can't Samsung do that? LG seems to be advertising augmented reality (Scansearch) recently. There's no room for excuses.

5. Attitude towards criticism
- Many people say it's a test product... : If the evaluation is bad, such speculation can arise, and it's rather an excuse. If you say 'I did my best, but the performance is bad,' you'd be subject to disciplinary action. We should work with the attitude that a lack of competitiveness is always due to our own shortcomings, not because the competitor is good.

6. Finally
Many developers don't pay much attention outside their own field and don't know much about competing companies. That doesn't look good. To explain their position, they need to do so with a more objective perspective. Also, an attitude of acknowledging rights and wrongs is important. It's somewhat puzzling why such an article appeared on Samsung's official blog. I know that many developers and practitioners often hear unfair criticism from the media and the public misled by incorrect information. However, to speak out about it, I believe a more impartial perspective and a lot of thought are needed.
(That's why I... don't talk about my work.)
And to talk about developers, you can't have a proper conversation without empathizing with the user's perspective.
(In fact, I've written similar stories before.
[The Gap Between Users and Developers http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70045294046](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70045294046) )

It's truly difficult to become a developer who writes well, but it's also a way to package your achievements and make them look better. I, too, am not particularly eloquent. It's what developers are worst at, but I'm realizing its importance.

* And a concern: It seems like the employee is still quite new, and I hope they don't face difficulties because of this incident. Internet comments are indeed merciless. (The internet is scary, after all..)

titleEn: Legend of Dragonia: Part 2, Chapter
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

Melchizedek reached the deepest part of the prison without any hindrance. The last cell he arrived at seemed quite large, and inside, a prisoner who looked like Gaius was sleeping on a makeshift bed, his hands bound and his appearance disheveled. Melchizedek opened the cell door with the key he had taken. Despite the loud clank, the prisoner was snoring, seemingly in a deep sleep. Melchizedek went inside and checked his face. It was definitely Gaius.
"What a carefree face. Wake up, Gaius!"
Seeing him sleeping so peacefully, Melchizedek's anger flared, and he kicked him. Gaius screamed at Melchizedek's sudden kick and tumbled off the makeshift bed.
"Oh, what is this! Even if I'm a prisoner, isn't this too much!"
Gaius, who had fallen off the bed, grumbled in a voice still heavy with sleep. Then, recognizing the man standing before him, his eyes widened.
"You. You are..."
"How do you do, Gaius? I came all the way here myself because I have something to say to you."
Melchizedek raised the corner of his mouth and saluted with one hand. But Gaius replied as if uninterested.
"Hmph. I have nothing to say to you. I know I'm scheduled to be transferred to the Kingdom of Ceres anyway. Given that, don't you think it's unreasonable to expect me to tell you anything? You also know that if you don't send me back unharmed, this negotiation will be void, right?"
Gaius acted confidently, relying on his backing.
"Oh, was that so? My apologies then."
Melchizedek scratched his head, speaking as if he hadn't known, then kicked Gaius hard once more.
"What is this! Don't you know that the lives of noble children depend on me!"
Gaius seemed surprised by his actions, yet couldn't contain his anger and shouted.
"Oh dear. I've already taken off my uniform, so I didn't realize you were such a precious person. What I came for isn't the lives of young masters whose faces I don't even know."
This time, Melchizedek punched Gaius in the face.
"What I came to settle with you are the lives of my subordinates."
Melchizedek relentlessly beat Gaius, and Gaius, flustered by Melchizedek's sudden rampage, crawled into a corner of the cell to avoid the blows. Soon, as if his kicked stomach hurt, he vomited what was inside him.
"Ugh! I can't believe it. Even so, you, who were so calm, because of such a trivial matter... Ugh."
Seeing this, Melchizedek stopped attacking him and looked down at Gaius.
"How disgusting..."
However, Gaius, who had been vomiting for a while, suddenly started chuckling.
"Has this fellow gone mad from being hit too much?"
Melchizedek let out a hollow laugh at Gaius's laughter, and Gaius, instead of answering, stood up and burst into louder laughter that echoed through the prison.
"Hahaha. Oh, how funny. I'm perfectly sane. Perhaps thanks to a few blows from you, I've now grasped the situation. It's because of your woman. Aysia, I mean. Hahaha.."
At Gaius's words, Melchizedek's relaxed expression instantly changed.
"Don't speak so carelessly. I don't want to hear that name from you."
"Then you've chosen a dead end too. You intend to kill me, don't you? In that case, once you're done with me, there'll be no problem going to the Kingdom of Ceres, right? But isn't it funny that Melchizedek, who tormented us so much, would make such a choice for a mere woman? Hahaha."
"I don't find it funny at all. More than anything, I don't want to see your disgusting laugh anymore."
At Melchizedek's reply, the handcuffs Gaius was wearing clanked ominously and fell to the ground. Then he pulled out a hidden dagger.
"You hid that well."
"I prepared it just in case. I dislike variables. If I just get out of here alive, Laodicea won't care about trivial things like your life. And as soon as I return to the Kingdom of Ceres, I'll make sure Laodicea pays the price for you, or for Prince Dagmon's son."
Gaius lunged at Melchizedek with his dagger. Melchizedek also drew the sword he had taken from a soldier at his waist.
"As you said, I have no intention of letting you live. And I don't care about Laodicea or Ceres. I just want Aysia and Benjamin to be safe."
Melchizedek aimed for Gaius's chest and thrust his dagger, and Gaius parried the blade, sparks flying with a sharp metallic sound. Melchizedek, with his longsword, seemed to have an advantage, but it was difficult to utilize that in the narrow cell, and it even became a hindrance. Moreover, Gaius's skill with a dagger was top-notch even within Laodicea. Melchizedek tried to keep his distance, but Gaius wouldn't allow it.
"You're quite good yourself. You should have trained your subordinates that well too. Then they might have avoided being caught by our intelligence unit and losing their lives."
Melchizedek eventually pushed Gaius out of the cell into the wider area, creating distance between them. From now on, Melchizedek had a significant advantage. Realizing this, Gaius, unlike before, kept his distance when Melchizedek advanced, then suddenly charged again with a loud shout. As Melchizedek took a defensive stance and flinched, Gaius, who had sand in his hand, scattered it towards Melchizedek's face. Melchizedek, complacent in his advantageous position, closed his eyes at Gaius's sudden action, and Gaius didn't miss the opportunity. Gaius's dagger thrust towards Melchizedek's heart. Melchizedek couldn't see, but he instinctively dodged.
"Ugh..."
Melchizedek let out a low groan. Unfortunately, Gaius's blade inflicted a deep wound on Melchizedek's shoulder.
"Lucky you. You avoided a fatal wound. But you won't be able to fight with such heavy bleeding, will you?"
Melchizedek needed to press the wound to stop the bleeding, but he had no such luxury with an enemy before him. The arm on his wounded shoulder felt like it was burning and had no strength, making it difficult to even lift, and the flowing blood was soaking his trousers. Melchizedek aimed his dagger and took an attacking stance towards Gaius again, but perhaps due to the bleeding, severe dizziness overwhelmed him. From the prison entrance, a loud crash echoed, along with a metallic tearing sound as if a barred gate had fallen to the floor.
"It seems the soldiers of Laodicea have arrived. It's all over."
As Gaius sneered, Melchizedek let out a shout and thrust again. But Gaius easily dodged and then grabbed Melchizedek's wound.
"Aargh!"
Melchizedek screamed in pain, but Gaius smirked and mocked him.
"Don't push yourself. I won't kill you. Wouldn't it be more stylish for you to be hanged by the country you served, rather than me killing you? Melchizedek, give up. You can't defeat me."
"Drop your weapons! Melchizedek! Gaius! What is all this commotion!"
General Mithraim's booming voice echoed through the cell.
"This young man is desperately trying to kill me, so how can I drop my weapon? First, guarantee my safety."
Soldiers surrounded Melchizedek and Gaius, pointing their spears and swords.
"Melchizedek! Drop your weapon! Or I will kill you right now!"
"Ugh!"
As Mithraim's command came down once more, Melchizedek reluctantly knelt and placed his longsword on the floor. Seeing Mithraim, Melchizedek thought that everything was over.
"Serves you right!"
Only then did Gaius also put his dagger on the floor and sneer at Melchizedek.
Melchizedek, kneeling, brought his hand to his boot. He felt the hilt of the dagger that had stabbed Aysia. And he saw Gaius's disgusting laugh. Perhaps due to the bleeding, a slight dizziness came over him, and the whispers of the surrounding soldiers and the threat of their spears and swords felt like

titleEn: The Legend of Dragonia Part 2, Chapter 2, Episode 6 - Atonement (2)
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

Melchizedek's gaze was fixed on the dark ceiling as he lay down. He had spent most of the night awake. His wedding was planned to be held grandly at the city church this morning. However, the reason he stayed up all night was not due to happiness about his marriage. It was because he had received information about Caesar's whereabouts from the deputy commander yesterday. Caesar was imprisoned in the castle of Yegonia in the Michael Ende region, under strict guard by the Knights, and was scheduled to be handed over to the Ceres nation in three days.

He had told Deputy Commander Gallap to wait for the escort time, but Melchizedek had other plans. No matter how elite the intelligence unit, even if composed of acquaintances, an operation to attack the Mithraim heavy cavalry unit would have no chance of success.

Melchizedek, who had spent the time awake, realized that the awaited moment had come and rose, opening the window wide. The cold, fresh air rushed in, invigorating his mind. Outside, a thick night fog blurred the streetlights, and darkness still prevailed. Dawn would break in about an hour. It was enough time to ride to Yegonia Castle.

Melchizedek took out his military uniform. It was well-pressed, looking as good as new. It was Aysia's work. He put on his uniform and gathered his weapons. Melchizedek drew his dagger from its sheath and stared intently at the blade for a moment. The sharp blade had taken many lives and saved him from the brink of death. However, the last time that blade had pierced a human body was Aysia's beloved body. Melchizedek spoke to the dagger as if talking to a friend.

"This is the last time I'll use you. Now, it's our turn to atone, isn't it?"

Melchizedek hid the dagger by inserting it into a pre-made empty space in his boot. In the other boot, an iron rod of the same thickness was embedded in the identical position, so there was no difference in weight or appearance, making it impossible to tell that a dagger was hidden.

Melchizedek tiptoed to Aysia's room, careful not to wake Aysia or Benjamin. Aysia was sleeping, holding Benjamin tightly. The blanket had slipped down, perhaps kicked off by Benjamin. Melchizedek carefully covered Aysia and Benjamin, then kissed both their foreheads. His beautiful bride was smiling peacefully, as if having a happy dream. Seeing them, Melchizedek felt a lump in his throat.

"I'm sorry. I can't help it. It'll be over soon."
Melchizedek left Aysia's house and mounted his horse.

"Giddy up!"
Melchizedek urged his horse forward, cutting through the cold morning air with vigor, but his heart remained with Aysia. Aysia, unaware of anything, was dreaming happily with Melchizedek, while Melchizedek galloped at full speed towards Yegonia Castle to fulfill his final mission.

When Melchizedek arrived at Mithraim Castle, it was still early dawn, and the castle gates were closed. Guards stationed in front of the small side gate, built into the large main gate, stopped him as he urgently rode up.
"Halt your horse!" one guard shouted.
Melchizedek dismounted and pulled out his old military ID.
"I am Melchizedek, a commander belonging to the Central Intelligence Unit. I have ridden here urgently to interrogate the prisoner Caesar. Guide me to meet the prisoner Caesar immediately."
Melchizedek demanded firmly. However, the guard replied with a displeased expression.
"We have not received any communication about someone from the intelligence unit coming..."
"This is a matter of utmost urgency, so a formal interrogation request will be notified as soon as day breaks. This is a direct order from the Imperial Palace. Here is Prince Dagmon's token."
Melchizedek unbuckled the sword at his waist and presented it. The sword was a token of friendship Dagmon had given him long ago, signifying the Imperial Palace's trust, but it could not be used as official authentication. However, ordinary soldiers would not know the details, and the Imperial mark on it was enough to persuade them.
The guard who received the sword was surprised and exchanged a few words with a senior soldier, who then rushed over and saluted.
"I apologize for the disrespect. I will guide you to the prison immediately and send another soldier to report to General Mithraim."

Mithraim was forced to wake from his deep sleep by the urgent call from the soldier.
"Damn it! What's going on at this hour!"
When Mithraim roared, the reporting soldier replied in a subdued voice.
"The Imperial Palace has sent someone to interrogate the prisoner Caesar."
"From the Imperial Palace at this hour? Don't those bastards sleep? So, who is it?"
"They say it's Melchizedek, the intelligence unit commander sent by Prince Dagmon."
"Melchizedek from the intelligence unit? Isn't there some mistake? How long has it been since he left the military..."
"I checked his military ID and confirmed the Imperial authentication of the Prince on his sword."
"What? The Prince's authentication on his sword? Then it seems to be him? Wait. Did you say the prisoner he wants to meet is Caesar?"
Only then did Mithraim recall the incident between Caesar and Melchizedek several years ago.
"Damn it! Get all soldiers ready for battle and do not allow him into the prison."
The soldier's face turned pale as he replied.
"Since the Imperial Palace said it was an urgent matter, he has already been sent to the prison."
"Idiots! You did as you pleased! Bring me my sword! I must go to the prison myself."
Mithraim's face contorted as he yelled, and the soldier hastily grabbed his sword.

At that time, Melchizedek was heading to the prison with the soldiers.
Following the single corridor of the castle, they entered the underground, where heavy iron bars blocked their way.
"This castle's prison is well-guarded. At least there's no worry of escape."
As Melchizedek admired the thick iron bars, the soldier replied with an amused expression.
"As you can see, you have to pass through two sets of these iron bars on a single path to enter the prison. Moreover, even without the iron bars, elite soldiers are on guard everywhere. Furthermore, this castle is a supply line for frontline troops and a training ground for heavy infantry. There are more than enough soldiers. Attempting an escape here would be suicidal."
"That makes sense, now that you mention it."
Melchizedek gave an awkward laugh.
"Still, Caesar was an enemy intelligence chief, so we must be careful."
"He is confined in the innermost cell of the prison. You have nothing to worry about. Warden, open the door!"
One of the soldiers guiding him called out to the warden, who opened the iron bar gate from the inside. As Melchizedek and the accompanying soldiers entered, the iron bar gate closed again, locking with a click.
"I am the warden in charge here. I apologize, but you must leave your weapons here from this point."
The warden requested disarmament, and Melchizedek unbuckled Dagmon's sword from his waist and handed it to the warden. At that moment, Melchizedek glanced at the bunch of keys hanging from the warden's waist.
"Let's go."
The warden placed his sword in a box and accompanied him. After walking for quite some time, the prison became visible beyond the second iron bar gate. On the other side, about a dozen cave-like cells, barred with iron, lined both sides of the corridor. At the end, a large, burly guard, twice the size of an ordinary person, wearing a military cap that didn't quite fit, was dozing, leaning on an axe.
"There he is again, dozing off. We entrusted him with something important because he's strong."
The warden accompanying Dagmon grumbled towards the dozing guard inside and opened the second iron bar gate.
Melchizedek was the first to enter. Just as the warden removed the key from the door and was about to secure his bunch of keys, Melchizedek snatched the keys and closed the iron bar gate from the inside. It happened so quickly that the warden was easily dispossessed of the keys, and the iron bar gate locked between the soldiers and Melchizedek. Startled by the loud clang of the closing door, the guard dozing at the end of the prison woke up with a start.
"All clear on duty!"
The burly guard, just waking up, was trying to comprehend the situation with a bewildered expression.
"What are you doing? Open it at once!"
The accompanying soldier shouted, gripping the bars.
"I apologize, but I don't want to be disturbed while interrogating the prisoner."
"Even so, this is problematic. We will arrange for a secret interrogation, so please return the keys and open this door."
The warden replied in a flustered voice.
"I'm sorry, but I cannot do that."
Only after hearing Melchizedek's reply did the warden realize something was wrong.
"General Mithraim would never allow such an act! Guard! Teach our guest some manners."
The warden shouted in anger.
Only then, snapping to attention at his superior's command, the burly guard rose, shouted loudly, and aimed his axe at Melchizedek.
"Well, at least I only have to deal with one of them, I suppose?"
Melchizedek muttered to himself, a faint smile on his face.
As the guard brought down his axe with a force that seemed to want to cleave his head, Melchizedek dodged inside the axe's arc and grabbed the arm holding the axe. Simultaneously, the guard's massive body flew into the air and was immediately slammed onto the hard stone floor. Melchizedek gave him no quarter, pressing down on the guard's thick neck until he passed out.
"Phew~ I've bought myself some time."
Melchizedek crouched down, pulled out the fallen soldier's sword and secured it, then wiped his sweat and stood up. It was a replacement for his sword left outside. The warden, who had witnessed the scene from outside the iron bars, shouted, his face red.
"You scoundrel! Who are you? Are you really from the Imperial Palace?"
However, Melchizedek ignored his shouts and walked further into the prison, beginning to search for Caesar's cell.
"I must inform the General quickly."
The accompanying soldier also sensed that things were going awry and urgently tried to call for help from outside. However, they were again blocked by the opposite iron bars and realized they were trapped between the two sets of bars. Beyond the iron bars,

The soldiers and the chief jailer shouted at the top of their lungs for a long time, but because it was a long, one-way corridor, no sentries were stationed on the other side.
"Damn it!"
Just as the soldiers were about to give up as time passed, the sound of many footsteps approached.
"That fellow from the Imperial Palace attacked our allies and trespassed into the prison. Quickly report this to the General!"
The chief jailer shouted towards the approaching group. But what came back was a scolding like a thunderous command.
"Idiots! How on earth could all of you, with that many people, not stop just one fellow?"
"Gah~! General!"
The soldiers trapped behind the iron bars were terrified at the sight of the general, who was furious to the core.
"Open the door at once!"
General Misraim roared, brandishing his great sword.
"I apologize. The key was taken by that fellow. It seems you'll have to call a locksmith."
As the chief jailer, watching the general's expression, replied in a meek voice, Misraim was flabbergasted.
"What? The key was taken? You're really something else. You all better prepare yourselves. Forget the locksmith, if you really don't want to be cut by my sword, step back!"
Misraim shouted with annoyance.

"It really doesn't suit you. You look like a different person, too neat."
Aysia said, frowning.
"Yeah. This is a bit much, isn't it?"
Melchizedek stood in front of the mirror in a pristine white suit, and the tailor, holding a tape measure, looked at a loss.
"I told you this suit really wasn't it."
"That suit makes anyone who wears it look like a noble; it's our most expensive and best-selling item. It's strange, but it just doesn't suit you, sir."
"Give me that one."
"That one? I don't think that one is quite right."
The tailor frowned, and even to Aysia, the suit Melchizedek pointed to looked a bit dark and old-fashioned.
"Choose something more understated."
"Just give it to me for now. Let me try it on."
Reluctantly, the owner brought over a suit made of neat, slightly coarse gray fabric, and Melchizedek put it on.
"Well, that's strange. You didn't look good in any of the obviously stylish suits, but this obviously old-fashioned one suits you surprisingly well. You might be the only person who could pull off that suit."
At Aysia's compliment, Melchizedek seemed pleased and let out a hearty laugh.
"Haha. Is my life so cheap that even clothes recognize it? Anyway, I'll take this one."
The tailor had thought he finally had a wealthy customer, but he couldn't bring himself to charge a high price for that suit, and his displeasure was clearly visible on his face.
"Then you should try on a dress, shouldn't you? How about that one?"
Melchizedek pointed to a dress hanging in the corner of the shop.
"Why is such a beautiful-looking dress hanging in the corner?"
A beautiful dress was hanging in an inconspicuous corner. But Aysia's first concern was the price.
"That looks too expensive."
"You have a good eye. That dress was ordered by royalty."
The tailor's face lit up as he pointed to the dress.
"It doesn't matter how much it costs, bring it out. My bride is worth wearing it."
"I don't want anything too expensive."
"I promised I'd treat you like a princess. Even if you spend money however you want after we're married, listen to me now."
Reluctantly, Aysia took the splendid dress and went into the changing room.
"It must be wonderful to have such a beautiful bride."
The tailor, pleased at the prospect of selling an expensive dress, smiled and complimented Aysia's beauty, and Melchizedek grinned, agreeing.
"Isn't she? She's the most beautiful girl in the world."
As Melchizedek lingered at the changing room entrance, Aysia exclaimed in surprise.
"Don't look!"
"Alright, alright."
But Melchizedek was impatient to see Aysia in her white dress as soon as possible. Soon, Aysia came out wearing the dress.
When Aysia emerged in the dress, Melchizedek and the tailor simply stared at her in silence. Aysia's face turned red, and she pouted.
"I told you I wouldn't wear anything this expensive and flashy."
Just as Aysia was about to go back into the changing room, Melchizedek spoke.
"It's fine. Let's take that one."
The tailor also said with an expression of admiration.
"Although I made this dress, it looks several times more beautiful on you, young lady. A beautiful imperial princess wore it before, but there's no comparison. It seems you are the true owner of this dress. I won't charge you; please just help promote my tailor shop. If people see you, they'll flock to our store like clouds."
Aysia's appearance was, indeed, truly beautiful. The snow-white dress accentuated Aysia's slender waist and her modest but shapely bust, and the elaborate lace decorations didn't feel flashy on Aysia at all. Looking at her, no one would have thought she was a mother with a child; instead, she looked like a shy, beautiful maiden in the prime of her beauty.
"Are you really giving it to me for free?"
Aysia asked back, smiling brightly at the mention of "free."
"Of course. It's my gift to a beautiful bride."
However, Melchizedek, surprisingly, refused the tailor's offer.
"That won't do. For free? No, that won't do."
"What do you mean?"
Aysia asked, puzzled.
"I can't accept such a beautiful dress for free. And I want to buy it for you; if it's free, it loses its meaning."
At his words, the tailor burst out laughing and said.
"The groom is also a wonderful man. In that case, a discount should be fine, right? Both of you, please choose some shoes too. Those are truly my gift."
Melchizedek, without much thought, chose a simple pair again, and Aysia, delighted by his words, began trying on pretty shoes.
"You must be very happy to marry such a beautiful bride."
Seeing Aysia, the tailor smiled and said to Melchizedek.
"Yes. She is a very precious person to me."
Then the tailor spoke as if something had just occurred to him.
"I've only seen such a beautiful woman once before. It was during a traveling troupe's performance, and it was like seeing an angel. I thought I'd never see such a beautiful woman again."
Melchizedek easily guessed that the woman he was talking about was Aysia.
"You are a lucky man. You mustn't make a lady like that cry."
"Of course. You're right. I will definitely make her happy."
Melchizedek replied with a vow. Just then, the jingle of a bell was heard from somewhere. It was the bell hung at the tailor shop's entrance. A man entered, looked around, then spotted Melchizedek and approached him. He was Deputy Commander Galap. Melchizedek was about to greet him with a bright expression but stopped. His expression was dark. Melchizedek began to feel uneasy, wondering what he had come to say.
"Commander, there's something urgent I need to tell you."
Melchizedek sighed and asked back with an expression of resignation.
"Hmph~ I was worried you'd bring up something like that, and sure enough. So, what bad news have you brought?"
Then the deputy commander replied hesitantly, with a very troubled expression.
"Gaisa seems to be getting released."
Melchizedek was so surprised he almost shouted. But not wanting to show his agitation to Aysia, he lowered his voice and asked again.
"What do you mean? Releasing the enemy's intelligence chief? And wasn't he in your hands?"
"I apologize. While I was away, the military police took custody of him. He was apparently designated for the upcoming prisoner exchange. They needed a high-profile prisoner to secure the release of high-ranking officials' children captured by the enemy, and Gaisa was caught in that."
"Do you think that makes sense? Do you even know how many lives were sacrificed because of Gaisa alone?"
Melchizedek burst out in anger, and the deputy commander said, biting his lip.
"I'm sorry. If I had known this would happen, I would have eliminated him right away. I thought we could extract information from him..."
"It's not your fault. You just carried out your mission... Anyway, the problem is that if he's alive, Aysia and Benjamin are also in danger."
Seeing Melchizedek's dark expression, the deputy commander lowered his head.
"I apologize. Now that he's with the military police, there's nothing I can do. At the very least, I will control information about your sister-in-law within Laodicea Castle. And I will seize the moment he is out of the military police's hands and attempt an assassination."
At that, Melchizedek shook his head vigorously.

titleEn: Don't Pretend Not to Be Hurt, Cactus
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=6256282

#### [Cactus Child](http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=6256282)

Written by Heo Hye-yoon
Tearsponge 2010.04.01
**Rating**

##### Memorable Passage

Crying

Enduring alone.

“To ask for help..

is cheating.”

When did I first get to know Heo Hye-yoon of Tearsponge? It was around 2004, a time when I was fiercely in love and in pain. I came across a breathtaking illustration.

{{IMG:2}}
**[ Cactus Child : Source : **[**http://www.cyworld.com/nunmulsponge**](http://www.cyworld.com/nunmulsponge)** ]**

A child holding a cactus, bleeding red, yet shedding tears. My gaze was fixed on this drawing and text because I felt this image was a reflection of myself.

**A. Experience of Unrequited Love**
This "Cactus Child" is a sad love story about a child who loves despite the pain and not knowing what to do, and a cactus that inherently only knows how to inflict wounds. However, to me, in this drawing, both the cactus and the child were other versions of myself within me. My love, like thorns, only knew how to hurt the one I loved, and because that thorny love was also a part of myself, I had no choice but to embrace it, which is why the drawing resonated so deeply with me.
This is a thoroughly personal thought and a subjective interpretation, but I don't believe this story is about the love between two people. I believe it is purely unrequited love, in other words, the love story of one person.
This book is divided into 4 sections:

1) Losing Myself in Love
2) The Wounds of Clumsiness
3) The Fear of Being Hurt
4) Enduring Alone

If we look closely at the contents of these sections, the object of love is not visible. As you turn the pages, the beloved's actions towards the protagonist are characterized by complete indifference, and they fail to acknowledge the pain of that love. This broadly aligns not only with the beloved but also with oneself and the outside world, that is, the gaze of society.

**B. A Child Who is Clumsy but Desires Love More Than Anyone**
The protagonist of this book is a child. A child who desires affection from someone but is clumsy because they don't know what kind of affection they want, and who only knows how to inflict wounds rather than how to love. However, given that the essence of love is not solely consideration, this portrayal is a story that anyone might have experienced at least once.
It is said that when people are in love, they speak in baby talk and exhibit infantile behavior, wanting to be protected by their partner. However, if a child does not receive love, they become stressed and resort to self-harm or become distorted. Considering these two points, it is a common and painful experience for all who have experienced unrequited love. Yet, the reason we cannot hate this foolish child is perhaps because its actions stem not from selfishness, but from foolishness and love.

**C. Overall Review**
It was "Cactus Child" by Tearsponge, a story that anyone hurting from love can empathize with. Her smiling face, yet somehow sad-looking :), told so many stories. Now, I hope that the Cactus Child, like a line from the book, breaks free from its cage and stops its somewhat painful love.

titleEn: After the App Store, the Web Store is Next
contentEn:
Not long ago, Amalok-nim of [Sambakza](http://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%82%BC%EB%B0%95%EC%9E%90_(%EA%B7%B8%EB%A3%B5)), famous for 'Tteotda Geunyeo' (She's Here), sent me an email. The content was that he was looking for a content distribution platform. It would mainly be for comics and animation, but it seems that an integrated ecosystem like an app store for these areas doesn't currently exist in Korea. Therefore, I couldn't give a good answer. This is an article based on my thoughts on the matter. Currently, the ecosystem is too focused on S/W developers, and because of that, it seems to be missing out on the larger market from a content perspective.

**1. Conditions a Future Content Distribution Ecosystem Must Meet**
Recently, content distribution platforms for S/W content like app stores and e-books like iBooks have been expanding, and they are emerging as very large markets.
**1) Scale**
And the principle of scale is necessary for the requirements of such platforms. A platform that doesn't guarantee a certain level of consumers is inevitably burdensome for content producers to jump into. This is the biggest reason why app stores exerted more powerful influence than WIPI, which was limited to Korea.
**2) Content Producer's Share and Power**
In the case of distribution for older media, distributors not only took a large portion of the profits but also engaged in exclusive contracts that prevented distribution elsewhere, and even biased content review. These actions ultimately distorted the content market.
**3) Community**
A community among those who consume and produce content will be very important in the future. This is because future content will not only be interactive, but word-of-mouth through SNS and similar channels is also a key strategy for content promotion on the internet.
**4) Distributor Participation**
Of course, the above points might sound like they completely exclude current distributors, but the power of current distributors, or hubs, is still necessary. A hub that distributes a collection of verified content across many content types is needed. It's not just about distribution through these distributors; individuals can also distribute, or teams of like-minded individuals can emerge as new distributors, creating a more dynamic form of content distribution group where participation and withdrawal from distribution groups are free. Current team blogs and some blog news outlets are prime examples of this.
**5) Lightweight Authoring Tools**
Having to develop an app for novel, comic, and even animation production is a huge burden. Lightweight authoring tools can increase distribution speed and expand the volume of content. Apple criticized Flash, but Apple does not provide an animation authoring tool as good as Flash. This can actually be seen as deceiving content creators. **If vector and keyframe-based Flash animation is replaced by HTML5-based bitmap streaming, the latter is actually much heavier.**

**2. Absent Content Distribution Platforms**
To my knowledge, there is currently no platform that meets all the content distribution platform conditions mentioned above. They either lack scale, restrict distributor participation, make direct participation difficult for content producers, or have no community at all.
**1) What are the problems with current app stores?**
- Current app stores are lacking in terms of distributor participation and lightweight authoring tools. If you want to distribute comics or novels but have to develop an app, that's a problem. Distributor participation is mostly thoroughly excluded. They don't like models where other paid content is sold within a single app.
In other words, opportunities still exist. **(Of course, innovation is needed here as well, and the domestic content distribution market also faces even bigger hurdles than Apple.)**

**3. Increasingly Diverse and Complex Platforms, So the Alternative is Still the Web**
From a producer's perspective, a simple and massive market is ideal. However, with the emergence of various platforms like Android and Bada, in addition to app stores, producers are actually put in a difficult position. Yet, there is one platform allowed on all platforms: the web.
For the reasons above, the need for web stores is growing. While blog advertising models are good, ultimately, a paid content model is necessary. Of course, this doesn't mean going strictly paid. Like app stores, it's a system where content producers can freely choose between free and paid models and take a share, depending on their model. And a platform-agnostic system. A payment module would naturally be needed here. It's fortunate that recently, transactions under 300,000 won no longer require a public authentication certificate. Another advantage of web stores is that they are borderless and can be launched globally simultaneously. There's no need to create high-tech devices like the iPhone, and there are plenty of customers. And lightweight authoring tools, from Flash to Namo WebEditor, are already abundant.

**4. So, who can create this market? An Integrated Web Store**
First, I believe portals have the highest potential. They already handle major content like comics. Now that the viability of comic content has been proven through mobile, its scope is expected to expand to light novels and genre fiction. However, there might be concerns about being dependent on a specific portal. So, would it be difficult to dream of an integrated web store where content registered on Naver also appears on Daum, and vice versa? Of course, each portal would take its own revenue, but content producers would earn revenue from both, and each portal would collect its respective content distribution fees. Starting with individual portals and later creating an integration feature is not actually difficult. This is because the web has no boundaries. However, app stores and Android Market cannot do that.

**5. The Lifespan of App Stores**
Frankly, I see app stores as a model for the next few years. Eventually, something like the web, a single virtual platform, will take its place, and I believe an era will come where content, not machines, is the primary competitive advantage. In that case, the web, where the most content is currently distributed, is highly likely to become the battleground. And still, such a model and store do not yet exist. **I think it would be much better to focus on this market rather than fighting Google and Apple anyway. The problem is that the UCC market has already been ceded to Google, and the fact that YouTube could become such a model is already a concern. Indeed, Google's advantageous position is quite absolute.**

**And now, when content diversity is a competitive advantage, the Korean government, which is creating various regulations, is going in the wrong direction.**

titleEn: The Legend of Dragonia Part 2 Chapter 2 Episode 3 - Persistent Ties
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

"Uncle! Amazing people have come to the city square."
Benjamin burst into the house, flustered.
"Benjamin. You should wipe your shoes before coming in. The floor is dirty."
Aysia chided Benjamin, but the excited Benjamin ignored his mother's words and continued his story.
"Uh-uh. That's not important, the street right now..."
"You rascal! This isn't important?"
Aysia gave Benjamin a playful smack on the head and scolded him.
"Ow, ow... No, that's..."
"The traveling troupe has entered the city of Laodicea these days, haven't they?"
Melchizedek spoke for Benjamin, anticipating what he wanted to say.
"As expected, Uncle knows everything. I wish my father was like you. Mother said my father was a great man, but..."
"Benjamin."
Aysia cut Benjamin off as he brought up Dagmon. Benjamin instantly cowered as if he had said something he shouldn't have.
"It's alright. The child hasn't done anything seriously wrong."
Seeing this, Melchizedek gently admonished Aysia, then smiled faintly and asked Benjamin,
"Benjamin, do you wish I were your father?"
"Uncle is strong and knows a lot, right? And he's kind to Mother."
"Then, shall I be your father from now on?"
"Really? Can you? Then the kids won't tease me anymore about not having a father."
Benjamin's face brightened as he asked.
"Don't play games with the child."
Aysia said to Melchizedek in an angry voice.
"As expected, it's not possible."
Benjamin replied with a hint of disappointment, then, as if remembering something, asked Melchizedek in an excited voice,
"The troupe has big animals, and people who dance and sing, and a mermaid princess, and a clown, and... anyway, all sorts of amazing things. Did you see all of it, Uncle?"
"Of course. I saw it. Your mom probably saw it too, right?"
Melchizedek looked at Aysia as he answered.
"Really? Mom saw it too? When?"
Benjamin asked in a disbelieving tone.
"You really... Don't say useless things to the child."
Aysia recalled her days with the troupe. Memories of splendid and beautiful performances and kind gypsy friends flashed through her mind. Aysia's memories of singing and dancing with them were now faint, but the emotion was unforgettable. However, there was no time to dwell on those old memories, and Benjamin's question brought her back to the reality of Aysia, not the performer Aysia.
"Mom. I want to see that too... Can't you show me?"
Benjamin subtly asked Aysia, but Aysia didn't answer. She wanted her child, who thought his mother's singing was the best, to experience the emotion of a proper performance, and she didn't want to disappoint Benjamin's innocent, expectant face, but it was only a wish. Above all, the troupe's admission fee was a burden for Aysia's circumstances. Benjamin quickly replied in a gloomy voice.
"Right, it must be really expensive... for our situation... No. Mom. I said something unnecessary. It probably won't be fun anyway."
Benjamin, mature for his age, clearly tried to be considerate of his mother, but he couldn't hide his expression and went outside again, looking very disappointed and dispirited. Seeing this, Aysia felt upset too. Melchizedek, unaware of Aysia's feelings, tactlessly asked,
"Why? Is it because old memories are coming back? Aysia, you like the troupe's performances too, don't you? You were never as vibrant as you were when you sang and danced back then."
Aysia sighed deeply and then replied,
"I'm satisfied now. Because I have Benjamin. And Benjamin is right. We don't have the money to go see such a big performance right now."
Aysia changed the atmosphere and began to complain to Melchizedek.
"Speaking of money, it just occurred to me. If you're staying at our house for a whole month, Melchizedek, shouldn't you have some shame? Our finances are already difficult, but you insisted you had nowhere to go, so I even gave you a room. Go out and get a job or something. You just play with Benjamin every day..."
As Aysia grumbled, Melchizedek replied as if he had just remembered.
"Ah. I forgot. Of course, I should pay for meals and lodging."
Melchizedek rummaged through his pocket and pulled out a coin wrapped in a handkerchief.
"It might be a bit short. I'll look for a job starting tomorrow."
"Surely you're not joking with one shekel, are you? It's been a month already. I should get at least fifty shekels. No. Because you're so annoying, I should overcharge and get eighty shekels."
Aysia unwrapped the handkerchief. Aysia, who had expected to find a silver denarius, was surprised to find a gold talent inside and exclaimed,
"You're really a difficult person. How can you give me such a large sum of money? I can't give you change for this much. And if you have this much money, why are you staying at our house? Go get change and bring it back."
Aysia, with an incredulous expression, returned the money.
"What are you talking about? One talent is far too little. What you've done for me, and the smile you've shown me, are worth a hundred talents."
As Melchizedek added a cheesy line, Aysia's face turned red and she replied in embarrassment,
"What... what is it? You're making me uncomfortable."
"And I plan to stay here for a long time, so consider it an advance payment. And do you still have what I gave you?"
"What you gave me?"
"The ring."
"The one the prince gave me?"
"Actually, I was the one who gave it to you."
"What? So you lied? I thought it was from the prince."
"Do you still can't forget Dagmon?"
"Th-that's not it, but..."
Aysia, caught in her true feelings, stammered and lied.
"How can someone whose calling was an actress be so bad at lying? I know Benjamin's father is the prince. I've been his friend since childhood, so I know what he was like when he was young. Benjamin really resembles him back then."
Melchizedek smiled as he looked at Aysia and replied. Aysia's embarrassment grew as her true feelings were exposed and she couldn't find words to refute the story about Benjamin. But Melchizedek's questioning continued.
"Do you have the ring? No?"
When Melchizedek asked again, Aysia, flustered, found the ring in a drawer and took it out.
"I'll give it back."
Aysia returned the ring to Melchizedek.
"Alright. Then it's my turn to do it properly."
"Huh? Do what?"
Melchizedek took the ring and knelt before Aysia.
"Aysia, marry me. This ring isn't expensive, but it's my mother's keepsake. This ring isn't from Prince Dagmon, but from a man named Melchizedek who loves you. I know you can't forget the prince. But I love you just as you are. I will never again yield to the prince."
Melchizedek, still kneeling, held out the ring to Aysia again. Aysia's face turned red at his sudden proposal.
"How can you do this so suddenly? You have to give me time to think. And for Benjamin..."
"Benjamin will grow up as my son from now on, and I will be responsible for his life. Won't you accept? I won't get up until you accept."
Even at that moment, Dagmon's face came to Aysia's mind. But she erased him, thinking he was no longer someone she could reach. More than anything, Benjamin needed a father.
Aysia hesitated for a long time, then took his ring. Melchizedek's face was filled with joy, and he lifted Aysia up, surprising her with his sudden action.
"Kyaa! I'm dizzy!"
"Now I won't let you go."
Melchizedek said, as if making a vow.
"You foolish man. Who gives up the person they love?"
"Let's go see our troupe with Benjamin. We'll eat delicious food and then tell Benjamin our story."
Aysia felt awkward that Melchizedek's tone had suddenly dropped the formal speech, but she preferred it and said nothing.
"Already?"
"Of course. I'll give you a grand wedding like a princess. Quite a few people of status will come."
"That's too much. I can't associate with such people."
"It's alright. Most of my friends are commoners or have similar personalities, so they're completely incompatible with lofty nobles."
"I really want to see you in a beautiful wedding dress."
Melchizedek spun Aysia around while holding her.
"Kyaa! I said I'm dizzy!"
"Hahaha, that's because you're happy."
Melchizedek's face was constantly beaming with smiles.

Melchizedek and Aysia brought Benjamin to the troupe's performance venue. As they entered the giant tent, Benjamin looked around, utterly fascinated.
"Whoa! What's that strange, giant animal?"
Melchizedek was about to answer Benjamin's question, but Aysia answered first.
"That's an elephant. It's called that because its nose is long. Don't let go of Mom's hand by getting distracted."
Aysia's face was very bright as she watched the troupe. Melchizedek smiled slightly at the sight. It took quite some time to find seats because of the crowd. Fortunately, with Melchizedek's effort, they managed to get good seats quite close to the front. The first to appear on stage was a comical clown. People laughed loudly at the clown's physical comedy, and Aysia laughed heartily, forgetting all the hardships of her life.
However, Melchizedek wasn't focused on the performance. All he saw was Aysia smiling brightly. He felt happy that he could make Aysia smile. When the performance ended and they came out, it was already night, and a bustling night market had opened outside the tent. In one corner, there were snacks that children would love and games like arrow throwing, so people were crowded.
"Shall we play a game? It looks like they give toys if you throw well."
Melchizedek

He pulled Benjamin's hand, and Benjamin exclaimed excitedly.
"Wow! First prize is a cool wooden sword made of paulownia wood!"
It was a simple game of throwing arrows into large and small barrels.
"I'll go first. I'm confident in throwing things like this, so watch closely."
Melchizedek thought it would be similar to throwing shurikens and confidently threw the arrow, but it landed far off the mark.
"Huh? This isn't easy at all."
As the confident Melchizedek became flustered, Aysia burst out laughing beside him and then stepped forward.
"Let me try. I'm good at this."
This time, Aysia threw the arrow. And just like magic, it went straight into the smallest barrel. Benjamin clapped his hands in delight and was able to receive the wooden sword. Melchizedek replied awkwardly.
"It must be the difference in experience, I suppose. Can't be helped. I'll buy you cotton candy instead. Wait here."
Melchizedek left Aysia and Benjamin and went to a cotton candy stall a little distance away. Just as he bought three cotton candies and was about to return to Aysia, a man suddenly called out to him.
"Commander Melchizedek!"
It was Deputy Commander Caleb, dressed in plain clothes. Seeing his face, Melchizedek's heart sank. He wondered how he could explain being seen buying cotton candy in a place like this.
"Oh. What brings you here?"
"I'm on a mission. By the way, Commander, what are you doing here with three cotton candies?"
Caleb asked, slyly hitting the nail on the head.
"Ah... this..."
"Let's move somewhere else to talk. There are too many people here."
Interrupting the flustered Melchizedek, Caleb spoke with a serious expression. The two moved away from the crowd to a secluded spot. Only after confirming that no one was around did Caleb cautiously speak.
"Gaisa has appeared in Laodicea."
"What? Gaisa?"
Melchizedek exclaimed in surprise.
"That's quite loud for you, Commander..."
"Ah. My apologies."
"And, he found Aysia."
Melchizedek's heart sank.
"What do you mean?"
"Well, thanks to that, I also learned that you, Commander, are staying at Aysia's house. And her son..."
Only then did Melchizedek realize that Caleb knew everything.
"Does anyone else know about this?"
"For now, only I know. And it seems Gaisa's side is also handling things independently. We and Gaisa are likely the only ones who know that Benjamin is Prince Dagmon's son. That's why I informed you first. As you know, if the existence of Aysia and Benjamin becomes known to both Laodicea and Ceres, you and they will be the most unfortunate."
Only after hearing Caleb's words did Melchizedek breathe a sigh of relief.
"Thank you for your concern, Caleb."
"Gaisa will probably try to secure Aysia and Benjamin. And we plan to seize that opportunity to capture them. I told you because I thought you should know, Commander."
"I see. I'll be careful too."
"My subordinates will always be around, but please take care, Commander. I'll take my leave now."
Just as Caleb was about to turn away, Melchizedek spoke as if he had just remembered something.
"Oh, and also. I'm getting married soon. I'll inform you of the date later."
Caleb, who was about to leave, stopped in surprise and looked back at Melchizedek with a smile, saying.
"Ah, my apologies. I made a mistake. Next time, I'll call her 'sister-in-law.' I'll visit you once everything is safely concluded."
Caleb then disappeared into the darkness. Melchizedek stared into the darkness for a moment, then hurried back to where Aysia was waiting.
"Why are you so late?"
Aysia asked with a pout.
"The line was a bit long, that's all. Here. I picked out the tastiest one for you instead."
Melchizedek handed the cotton candy to Aysia and Benjamin, and Benjamin rejoiced as if it were his birthday. From a distance, Caleb watched them, and their affectionate appearance, as if they had always been a family, filled him with warmth.

* This novel is simultaneously serialized on Munpia ([http://www.munpia.com/](http://www.munpia.com/) >Regular Series > Dragonia Legend).
