titleEn: The Girl Who Gathers Bones of Strange Imagination
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=2923907

#### [The Girl Who Collects Bones](http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=2923907)

By Mick Jackson | Translated by Moon Eun-sil
Saenggakui Namu 2007.05.19
**Rating** 
		
	

 
		
		
		
	First of all, I bought this book because I liked the gloomy illustrations that reminded me of Tim Burton's 'The Melancholy Death of Oyster Boy'. Just as there's a Gothic style in art, I heard this book is also of the Gothic novel genre. Gothic seems to refer to the oppressive and rigid feeling of the Middle Ages. It's said to contain a bit of the grotesque and black humor, but honestly, I didn't find it particularly scary. 
Compared to the truly grotesque horror I felt from Giger, this feeling was more like a fairy tale, I'd say?

{{IMG:2}}

http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=275040

[Giger](http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=275040) 

H.R. Giger | Translated by Ahn Kyu-chul
Art&Books 2003.10.15 .
Although it dealt with themes like bones, undertakers, and murder, rather than horror, it had an alienating feeling, like the fairy tale of Hansel and Gretel burning the witch. That's probably why I compared this novel to a Grimm's fairy tale. And looking at the title, it is indeed a Tale (fairy tale).
It's also brighter than Tim Burton's book I initially thought of.

{{IMG:3}}

http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=88664

[The Melancholy Death of Oyster Boy](http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=88664) 

By Tim Burton | Translated by Yoon Tae-young
Saeteo 1999.12.01 .
If 'Oyster Boy' had a bottled-up, melancholic feeling, this book feels a bit more mundane. It's a strange world, but that world, which suddenly intrudes into reality, doesn't feel unfamiliar at all. This is probably because it's not a perfectly imagined world, but rather the result of imagination built upon the author's experiences. The fear of an unfamiliar real world that children possess. Imagination layered upon that.
Anyway, it remained in my memory as a novel that was a bit blander than I had expected.
That's not to say it's not worth reading, though. The ingenious imagination is good. And I like the illustrations.

titleEn: Stories of Hidden Supporting Characters in Myths, Illustrated:
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=5907805

#### [Myth Like a Painting](http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=5907805)

By Hwang Kyung-shin
Artbooks 2009.03.04
**Rating**

Greek mythology has been widely discussed over time, especially having a profound influence on art. Today, the gods of Greek mythology are less objects of worship and more like stories for media. Greek Mythology Through Pictures, this book tells the stories of hidden figures in Greek mythology that we might not have known well, accompanied by beautiful illustrations. Uniquely, instead of the well-known tales of Theseus, Heracles, or the great Zeus, this book tells the stories from the perspectives of other characters hidden within their narratives.
The Minotaur, killed by Theseus, or Medusa, killed by Heracles – in most books on mythology, they were merely figures placed to create heroes, but this book tells their stories. The Minotaur was not born a half-beast by choice, and like Oh Dae-su, he was trapped in a labyrinth without knowing why. For the naive and beautiful Medusa, not only was the terrible curse of turning her hair into snakes not enough, but the gods also killed her to make Heracles a hero. And to top it off, they even affixed her dead face to a shield – truly a horrific tale. Throughout, it defends the positions of these supporting characters and victims, whom we previously knew as a monster bull and a monster snake.
Furthermore, it reveals that these stories are not merely being re-examined today, but were already embedded in the paintings of famous artists from the past. The image of Medusa in this book, clutching her head in despair, was not the venomous figure we knew; it was a painting where the despair of the cruel curse inflicted upon her was profoundly felt by the viewer. Paintings hold as many, if not more, hidden stories than narratives. I was able to see all of this – the stories and emotions contained within – together.

It is a joyful thing to discover new meanings in stories we already know. The particular charm of Greek mythology, I believe, lies in the fact that what we feel within it is not poetic justice, but rather a sample of contradictory and imperfect human emotions. That is why all the characters are alive. Being alive means having emotions, and that means we can empathize with them.
It was a wonderful book that allowed me to read stories alongside beautiful illustrations.

titleEn: The Last Episode of Queen Seondeok -
contentEn:
I finally watched the last episode of Queen Seondeok yesterday. Since I watch it on IPTV, I always end up watching it a week late. Personally, I liked the final episode of Queen Seondeok more than that of Iris.

I believe the main storyline of Queen Seondeok was actually about Mishil and Bidam. And although, in the end, in a conversation with Misaeng, it was implied that Bidam brought everything upon himself and acted foolishly, I cannot agree with that idea. Throughout Queen Seondeok, the character I felt most affinity for and understood was actually Bidam, and the reason is his human side. In contrast, I feel that even Mishil, Yushin, and Deokman, who act by thoroughly excluding human warmth, are closer to being workaholics. I absolutely cannot agree with the notion that emotions can be completely disregarded for the sake of work, and that this is the force that moves history and the way of heaven.

And in the process of justifying that workaholism, there lies Silla's grand cause of unifying the Three Han states. How many people must have died during the unification of the Three Kingdoms? Was that truly a grand cause? The result of a grand cause that required pushing those beside them into deadly situations was ultimately the loss of territory north of Goguryeo and having to wage war with the Tang Dynasty.

In my opinion, it was just politics. It was called a grand cause, but ultimately it was greed. Was the reason for defeating Mishil truly a grand cause? What if Deokman and Yushin had become Mishil's people and changed Mishil? From the beginning, they established a confrontation between the royal family and the aristocracy, and the reason was precisely because Deokman was a "Seonggol" (sacred bone). "Only Seonggol can be the master of the country..." If you say that, what's the difference from the aristocracy?

A prosperous nation, the unification of the Three Kingdoms – wasn't it just a political franchise? Just as the fallen Gaya became Silla people, if Silla people had become Baekje people or Goguryeo people, what would have changed for the common folk?

Of course, good politics is desirable. But what about the common people and soldiers who died in the process? Bidam, at least, had no falsehoods even when walking a path of blood. He was honest with his heart and dreamed a blue dream in the weak, weak hearts of people. Is the human heart truly so weak? Yes, it is. But isn't achieving a grand cause and having compassion for the people also a matter of the human heart?

Misaeng, who called Bidam pitiful, spent his final scene smiling, saying he had fully utilized his abilities and done everything he wanted. So, what about Deokman, Yushin, and Mishil? They probably weren't much different from Misaeng. However, they lacked one crucial thing: a heart. Wasn't it Deokman, Yushin, and Mishil who were truly pitiful, not Bidam?

I wonder if they regretted their dishonest hearts in their final moments. Bidam, who walked step by step forward and reached out to Deokman until the very end, just to call out "Deokman-ah" one last time, is truly a happy man. Because he was able to reach out. Yushin, who later achieved the unification of the Three Kingdoms, who accomplished that bloody war and grand feat, wouldn't he have regretted it later? Not being able to reach out to the person he loved, and Deokman, who only watched.

As Bidam put it, Yushin won everything and possessed it all, but in reality, Yushin never did anything truly from his heart. I think it was Bidam who showed the meaning of living fiercely and what it means to be human. To possess one person is harder than possessing the whole world, and to be able to give up everything for that. That might be even harder than unifying the Three Kingdoms.

Although Queen Seondeok indeed contained many satirical takes on today's politics and worldly affairs... I cannot agree, even in the real world, that such things take precedence over anything personal.

**That's right. Perhaps I am as selfish as Bidam.**

Perhaps because I've experienced such a difficult love once... I agree that its weight is greater and more valuable than the world, and I believe the value of that seemingly light human heart is not light at all.

titleEn: Semantic: How Smartphones and Smart PCs Truly Become
contentEn:
**1. Are Today's Devices Really Smart?**
{{IMG:1}}
[ Smartphone? Omnia and iPhone ]

I am a developer by profession, and I've been using smartphones for almost 8 years. Today's information terminals, including PCs, have powerful processors and large-capacity memory. I remember when I first learned and memorized the CPU structure of a computer at a computer academy during elementary school. Was it the memory unit, arithmetic logic unit, and control unit? The PC I first encountered then was quite different from the omnipotent computer I had initially imagined. Computers that conversed with users had long appeared in movies and comics, but actual computers were no different from much more complex calculators. Twenty years later, a phone named 'smartphone' recently emerged. It boasts powerful hardware and software, and can connect to the 'sea of the net' anytime. However, one question arose here: Is the phone truly smart? The conclusion is that while it can do a lot more, it's still not smart. Was it Von Neumann who first devised the method of loading data from current storage into memory to run a computer?

http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EC%A1%B4%ED%8F%B0%EB%85%B8%EC%9D%B4%EB%A7%8C&os=185271&ie=utf8

[**John von Neumann**](http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EC%A1%B4%ED%8F%B0%EB%85%B8%EC%9D%B4%EB%A7%8C&os=185271&ie=utf8), Mathematician
Born: 1903.12.28.
Many users actually use this concept without fully understanding it, but they implicitly experience the process, and there hasn't been much development in this area. Software must be purchased separately from hardware, users need to understand which hardware can run specific software, know what software they need, update it annually, and recently, security issues like antivirus software have become much more prominent. To even go to the bank, you need to install certified certificates, secure web software, etc. Users are not concerned with whether they understand the structure of certified certificates or what a keylogger attack is. It's simply a mandatory gateway. What used to be as simple as sliding up a phone and dialing a number from a notebook now requires managing contacts in Google Calendar and installing a "consonant search" app. Let's go back to the distant past. With the first telephones, when you picked up the receiver, an operator would answer. You'd say "Mr. Kim from [district name]," and the connection would be made. Which one would feel smarter to the user? **Today, the term "smart" seems to be confused with "powerful." Simply put, "smart" is a term applied to machines that resemble humans, not to devices where the user has to become smart by finding and using applications.**

**2. Powerful Devices Need to Become Truly Smart**
The more powerful a device is, the more it can do. But conversely, the less smart the user is, the more the device becomes "pearls before swine." A survey showing that 80% of users don't install any apps suggests that many users are still using their devices no differently than feature phones. In fact, it's said that among the features on feature phones, not much was used besides alarms and games. Similarly, many iPhone users tend to perceive it primarily as a gaming device. However, this is not smart. If that's the case, it might be more appropriate to have a phone attached to an NDS or PSP. While there's clearly a demand for such devices, I don't believe this represents the ultimate vision for smartphones as information terminals. **Therefore, what's needed is for the device to become smart instead of the person. Technology where the device understands, prepares, and provides what the user wants – a device that "gets it" – that is the core function missing from the powerful devices we hold in our hands today.**
{{IMG:2}}
[CLAMP Anime Chobits: Humanoid Computer]

**3. Smart Technology, Semantic Search, and the Potential of the Search Bar**

[Source: [http://cafe.naver.com/yyk2398/3951](http://cafe.naver.com/yyk2398/3951)]
Unfortunately, machines don't fully understand their own resources. And users are often poor at articulating what they want. So, what is the "dialogue window" between the user and the device? It's the input/output device. This could be touch, text input, or sometimes a gyroscope. Some of these allow the user to anticipate how the device will respond. For example, if there's a specific icon, touching it will launch the corresponding application. But the problem lies elsewhere. **What if there's no such icon? What if the user knows nothing about the device?** In such cases, the user searches the internet to find the answer and locate the function. If an iPhone user doesn't know how to record a video, they'll type "how to record video on iPhone" into the search bar. The search content will combine the contexts of "iPhone," "video," and "how to record" to search the database and display results from knowledge forums, blogs, etc. After learning this, the user will record a video on their iPhone and realize, "Oh, the icon was here."
**What did the search engine learn during this process? The few words mentioned above.** And if it also knows that this search query came from Safari on an iPhone, what can it infer? "This user doesn't know how to record video on an iPhone." In that case, wouldn't it be possible to display an "execute" button for the iPhone video app at the top of the search results? After a few times of the user learning how to use it, they might even realize that the search bar is more convenient than touching an icon. If personal records accumulate and settings can be customized, simply typing "video" would launch the video recording function. **If this result is combined with Google's voice search, the user would naturally just say "video" to their phone, and it would launch.** Extracting meaning from user queries and matching that meaning with computer resources is what a search engine does. The meaning of these resources can be expressed using RDF or TOPIC MAPs. And once a user accepts a relationship, it becomes repeatedly established through personalized search, like neurons, eventually becoming a fixed (constant) result.
**I believe that the search bar currently holds the greatest potential for "smartness," and it's something only the search bar, which receives the most queries, can do.**

**4. The Need for Semantic Search in WebOS**
Everyone anticipates that devices will eventually operate in a seamless environment. There's also a prediction that the web itself will become the OS in such an environment. In fact, having all resources locally is incredibly inefficient. **Why do I constantly have to install things on my SSD when there's a massive storage like iTunes?** My personal files alone are not enough. Imagine a web OS like Chrome. And it has Google's voice search integrated. And that search bar is the engine controlling all resources of the web OS.
Simply saying, "I want to play a ladder game," could lead the search engine to recommend one of the companies offering ladder games on the web, or even launch and display it directly.
Another common example of semantic search is booking train tickets.
"I want to take a train from Seoul to Busan."
The search engine understands that the user wants to take a train and finds resources within the context of "train ticket booking." **(In actual semantics, the most difficult part is assigning context to web resources. For text, there's usually a way to find a clue, but for images, applications, or videos, the problem becomes extremely difficult.)** It sets the necessary parameters, such as origin and destination, from the relevant resource and asks the user for the missing information (parameters).
"Please tell me your desired departure date, time, and train type."
"This coming weekend, between 12 PM and 2 PM."
"There are seats available on KTX at 12:15 PM and Saemaul-ho at 1 PM."
"Make it KTX."
The scenario above could be text-based, not just voice.
This concept is actually similar to Naver's current Smart Finder, and broadly speaking, Smart Finder can also fall under the concept of semantics. The problem is that it doesn't extract context from search queries like "buy car," "search car," or "find car," but rather matches them to "car Smart Finder," which seems to be just keyword occupation, so strictly speaking, it doesn't seem to be a semantic concept.
{{IMG:3}}
[Disease Smart Finder, seemingly applying an Expert System]

**In any case, what's important is that from the perspective of user needs, rather than technical meaning, this kind of semantic search will be the most crucial element in the future.**

**5. Misconceptions and Illusions about Semantics and Artificial Intelligence**
{{IMG:4}}

[Nate Semantic Search]

Many people recognize the importance of semantic search as shown above, but there seems to be a dominant perception that it's difficult or impossible. This is because many people think of semantics or AI as a machine's ability to learn natural language. What first changed my perspective during AI classes was realizing that the AI we see in comics is different from real AI. The core of AI is to mimic human reasoning to infer conclusions for ambiguous values that don't result in a single answer. Therefore, due to human ambiguity, 100% satisfaction is impossible, and a usable engine emerges in the 90% range. Furthermore, learning is not the only genre of AI; in cases like Expert Systems, a collection of rules is also considered an AI system. Today's Smart Finder, in a way, can also be called AI in that it is a collection of rules similar to an Expert System. This can be implemented with simple if-else statements. Just a few human reasoning processes like grouping, partitioning, and classification can enable character recognition (OCR). **All of these are genres of AI, and machine learning is just one of those fields.** In detail, there are various methods in Machine Learning besides MLP, which is similar to human learning. **RDF, TopicMap, or the Semantic Web Layer are formal guidelines; they cannot be the entirety of semantics (AI) themselves. Therefore, evaluating the performance of AI absolutely depends on human subjectivity or the results of test cases, rather than technology or devices.** Even the Turing Test, which evaluates AI performance, assesses a machine's capabilities based on human questions. Even if it's entirely filled with if-else statements, if a human perceives it as human rather than a machine, it passes as AI. Similarly, it's difficult to judge whether something is semantic or not based on whether it uses RDF or Topic Map. Using these international standards simply means that compatibility can be ensured. Recent discussions regarding Nate's semantic search...

Many people seem to question, "Is that really semantic?" but I don't think it's a very productive question. Even if it's 100% powered by part-time workers, if the concept of Context exists, it's semantic.
Therefore, what's important is how you set your strategy, and there's no reason to be intimidated by technical difficulty. **The reason Cyworld, which wasn't a perfect Web 2.0, succeeded was because it possessed some of those elements even before Web 2.0 emerged.**

**6. The ultimate path for all devices is smart devices**
My initial goal when I first started with computers was also to create the fantastical machines from cartoons. Even looking at today's flashy devices, if you think about why they are inconvenient devices, worse than Knight Rider's KITT which only spoke, you can figure out the reason with a little thought. **They are clueless, stupid, and have no flexibility whatsoever. Multi-processing, fast speed – is that really all there is?** Apple's devices aren't popular because they boast incredible specs. Perhaps it's because they've become just a tiny bit smarter than existing smartphones or feature phones. **Clearly, "smart" does not mean being able to do everything.** Investment in artificial intelligence in Korea doesn't seem to be very high. And experiments or ventures related to it are not very visible from companies either. Nate's recent semantic search was quite a fresh shock. It seems to be one of the reasons why Nate is formidable, as they chose a completely different direction with technology and a future-oriented, head-on approach, rather than Daum's usual strategy of imitation and marketing.
While Daum holds an advantage in mobile thanks to marketing, it's not actually ahead in the number of apps or mobile web content. Windows Mobile isn't even supported at all. It's also a curious point how they will handle things when Android comes out. Furthermore, mobile search must ultimately compete with the resources available on the web. This is why Naver, which currently holds an absolute advantage in web-produced content, and Google, the undisputed king of crawling, are formidable.
{{IMG:5}}
[ To Heart's HMX-12 Mass-produced Humanoid Robot Multi (Maruchi) ]

**7. A time for long-term vision and strategy**

[ Source: [New Version of My "Metaweb" Graph -- The Future of the Net](http://novaspivack.typepad.com/nova_spivacks_weblog/2004/04/new_version_of_.html) ]

What I've felt recently in the S/W industry today is quite bleak. A technology-oriented R&D atmosphere is hard to find in most companies. While IT, especially the S/W industry, is said to be experiencing a whirlwind in the US and Japan, Korea seems to be focusing on H/W and services. At companies, they say they understand the goals, but that such things are for academia. **They say it's difficult to prepare for the distant future when there's not even enough firepower for immediate frontline support. Shareholders, moreover, dislike such things. Most centers referred to as R&D centers in Korea are simply service development centers. Even if preparations are made, projects frequently disappear in Korea due to constant changes in organization and strategy.** **In large companies where such things are possible, it's rare to find someone with a proper IT strategy and technology strategy; they only set business strategies. Technology strategy and IT strategy leaders change frequently. Is this a Korean habit of negating everything from the previous administration depending on the current government?** In such an environment, technology in fields like AI, which require the longest-term vision, is not at a very high level. Indeed... I question whether we can truly play a leading role in such a future environment. Personally, I feel a lot of skepticism, but I still hope for a slightly better environment and results to emerge in Korea.

[Idea] Shake Dialer (A Calling Program
contentEn:
**Title: Shake Dialer**
**Date Conceived: December 16, 2009**
**Author: Forest Story ([http://blog.naver.com/fstory97](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97))**

**Background:** Touch phones like the iPhone are becoming more common, but in weather like this, taking off gloves to make a call is a hassle. So, I conceived this item to figure out how to make accurate calls without taking off gloves, or even while driving.

**Condition:** The phone must have a built-in gyro sensor capable of motion recognition.

**1. Speed Dial Setup Mode**
In the settings, set up speed dials. (Existing speed dials can also be used.)

**2. Speed Dial Selection Mode**
Each time the device is shaken, the speed dial number increases.
{{IMG:1}}
At this time, the device's display provides information about the selected speed dial via voice and screen.

**3. Calling Standby Mode**
** - State where speed dial is selected and stopped -**
** 1) Time Expiration**
If shaking n times (at intervals of at least 1 second) is stopped (exceeding 1 second) and you wait, the n-th speed dial is recognized as selected, and a Timer starts.
When the Timer expires, the selected speed dial is released.

** 2)  Calling**
If shaken one more time, it attempts to Call the corresponding speed dial.

** 3) Cancel**
If shaken twice (a concept similar to double-clicking), the speed dial selection is canceled, and it returns to the speed dial selection mode (initial state).

**4. Calling Mode**
While attempting a Call and the ringtone is playing, shaking more than twice stops the Call.

**5. Conversation Mode**
During a conversation, if you want to end the call, shaking more than twice ends the call.

**6. Tutorial Mode**
Tutorial for the shake gesture Commands
Tutorial for increasing numbers, double shake (selection and cancellation), etc.

*** All processes are reflected simultaneously on screen and via voice. Even while driving, all call operations can be performed simply by shaking the phone and using voice feedback.**

ps. I don't have an iPhone, nor a Mac... and my current smartphone doesn't even have a gyro sensor. Is there anyone who can develop this? Just because I've published it on my blog, you wouldn't take it and develop it without any notification, right? This post prohibits commercial use and modification **(refer to CCL)**.
It would be great if it could be uploaded to the App Store... For capacitive screens, it's even worse because you can't touch them with gloves on, but honestly, even resistive screens are equally annoying to use for calls on cold days. Touch phones are indeed inconvenient...
I considered patenting it, but since methods using gyro sensors seem too easy to circumvent by simply changing the gesture, I'm just releasing it publicly.

titleEn: iPhone: The Next Decade and the Transformation of Korean
contentEn:
**1. The Wireless Internet Market Returns to 8 Years Ago**
As discussed in [**A 10-Year Story of Korean Wireless Internet Revisited Due to iPhone**](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70075401680) ([http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70075401680](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70075401680)), I'd like to briefly talk about what's next. The changes brought by the iPhone currently include a drop in wireless internet prices and the announcement of the prelude to a platform war among Android, Bada, Symbian, and Windows Mobile. In fact, this situation reminds me of the time when I first became seriously interested in wireless internet, about 8 years ago, when SKVM, KTF Brew, and LGT's J2ME competed. Of course, unlike then, the game of scale is different. At that time, the market, divided into three, brought duplicate development issues for CPs, and SKT's influence grew because its market was the largest. The iPhone opened the door to wireless internet while reintroducing these problems. From a CP's perspective, the market has become much wider than just domestic, but other markets are equally tempting. Even if it's troublesome and costly, they will ultimately target both the App Store and Android.

**2. Will a Standard Emerge Again in the Wireless Content Market?**
So, will a standard like WIPI emerge again in the wireless content market?
My answer for the future is "Yes." However, I don't know what that will be. Also, looking at the web market, if we consider why web standards didn't take hold in the past, the competitiveness of Apple's and Samsung's closed OSes is likely to remain effective for some time. The power of standards in the mobile environment has not yet shown completeness in software, and this situation seems likely to continue for a while. Apple's completeness seems to be unmatched even by the recently introduced Droid. This was also why early mobile platforms had high device dependency, not just carrier dependency. Therefore, competition will unfold among Apple, Android, Bada, Symbian, and Windows Mobile, and their respective influence will be judged by market share.

**3. The Wireless Internet Market That Will Emerge After the iPhone**
Looking at the content that has recently appeared with the advent of the iPhone, I personally feel it's a transitional market, and I believe there's potential for improvement and reasons for change in the future. In this process of change, the iPhone's dominance might wane. I'd like to talk about the iPhone's limitations and the future possibilities of the wireless internet market.

** 1) App Directory, Then App Search**
First, let's look at how apps are found. Applications and websites sorted by category are reminiscent of Yahoo's directory search service. This service model creates a high demand for the initial page, and as users increase, page ranking has the effect of distorting software quality. What overturned this method was Google, which focused on search. Content that increases exponentially is highly likely to shift from a directory search method to a search method. Apple will likely strengthen its search capabilities in the future.

** 2) Changes in App Sales Model: From Individual to Mall...**
Second is the issue of the sales model. Currently, Apple exclusively operates all software sales. This significantly increases inspection costs, and while it helps the company grow, if it becomes excessively large, quality will eventually decline, and complaints about not accommodating minorities will erupt. The reason is that Apple exclusively sells wireless content, much like SKT, showing no consideration for existing software sales channels. How will Apple manage adult content, and how will it deal with different software laws and intellectual property rights in each country?
**Reference: Patent Issues in Software Open Market** [http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70071025972](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70071025972)
**- After App Store, Introduction of Mall in Mall**
Ultimately, the answer lies in looking at what came after Auction's market. It was Gmarket. The big difference between Gmarket and Auction is the Mall in Mall model. It's a structure where small malls can set up shop. Using this, companies can be managed, and their software can be, in a sense, delegated. In other words, T-Store could potentially open a store within the App Store. And, I've heard that the Android Market is actually considering such a model.
Also, how will traditional mobile gaming powerhouses like Com2us or Nexon Mobile tackle this market? Or what if Activision, EA, or Blizzard jump into this market? A little imagination shows the answer. The early WIPI market offered a vision to individual developers, but as corporations entered, it quickly became a very difficult market for individuals. However, conversely, S/W quality significantly improved. This greatly increases the need for a Mall in Mall.

** 3) Virtualized OS / Virtual Machine Market to Break Down Barriers Between Devices**
Also, the question arises, "Does it have to be Apple?" Can apps only be created by developing with the SDK provided by Apple? The goal of CPs is not that the App Store is excellent, but rather that the market is large and attractive. However, a drawback is that development for the App Store and Android Market must be done separately. So, what if you want to develop one piece of software and sell it simultaneously on Android and the App Store? This is where the concept of a virtualized OS, a Virtual Machine, comes in. In fact, this solution was already demonstrated with WIPI, and Flash, JAVA, and Silverlight are already using this method. Each software ecosystem would only provide sales solutions to the software, allowing the actual platform to be chosen selectively. While this is not a welcome scenario for Apple, which seeks to monopolize the software distribution environment, it is a possible scenario, and the need for it is growing due to the web. Of course, hardware development must support it to that extent. But at the current pace, I don't think it will even take 5 years.

** 4) The Ultimate Goal: WebOS based on Web Standards**
What is the ultimate form of the virtualized OS mentioned above? It is web standards, backed by a global, actual standard. HTML5 and Chrome OS. It is a very natural prediction to expect Chrome OS to merge with Android. Some even say it's a duplication of investment, but I think Android's strategy is very effective at a point where it hasn't even gone through the scenarios above. If you only have a browser, you can use software directly from a website. That is the concept of WebOS.
**Reference: Imagining Chrome OS in 2018** [http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70074821366](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70074821366)

All these steps will likely not be welcome to Apple. This is because the process is similar to how Windows conquered Apple. Ultimately, it's also similar to the sequence of Apple -> MS -> Google. However, for Apple, which was revived by Jobs' return, this much has been a huge achievement, and there will be more to gain than what they've already gained. (Apple's dominance is unlikely to be broken easily for about the next year.)

** 4. Changes in Infrastructure. KT Chose Potential Over Profit**
The credit for the iPhone's introduction this time goes to consumer demand. There's a lot of talk about domestic companies bowing to overseas pressure, but I have a different opinion. The introduction of the iPhone is entirely to KT's credit, and for KT, it was actually a strategy that accepted losses. The introduction of the iPhone is still uncertain whether it will be a benefit or a poison for KT. While stories about AT&T's performance suggest that coexistence between the iPhone and carriers is possible, those figures only showed increased revenue, completely omitting AT&T's capital investment and network maintenance costs. Simply put, whether 3G or 2G, data communication is still not truly suitable. Although subscriber numbers have increased from SKT to KT, these are new users who occupy several times the network capacity while using iPhones. Therefore, while KT is grateful, it also has to bear the maintenance costs. Furthermore, the reason Apple did not enter Korea was the AS issue, which is still being criticized. To be precise, there was no normal and official sales and distribution network in Korea. Therefore, KT bore all those costs to bring in the iPhone, so it's not a profitable business for KT in any way. Considering the subsidy per device, it's even possible that the deficit could grow as subscribers increase. Forcing a specific company to incur losses solely based on user demand is impossible in a capitalist society. But KT did it. Why? User demand for Apple? I believe KT is looking beyond that.
**- KT's Absolute Mission: Establish Cook&Show, FMC = Netspot (Wifi) + Wibro in the Market!**
First, let's skip the subscriber acquisition strategy for KT's iPhone introduction, as everyone knows about it... KT's ultimate goal is the Cook&Show FMC model. And Wibro. As you know, KT's technological advantage, which holds an absolute lead among the three carriers, is Netspot and Wibro. KT chose the iPhone as an act to expand user usage patterns for these technologies. Of course, the iPhone did not have Wibro installed, nor did it support FMC. However, one thing becomes clear: users are adopting usage patterns that most require FMC through the iPhone. Furthermore, the very reason for Netspot's existence, which had been a white elephant, has been completely transformed.
If this scenario plays out, Netspot, which was criticized for being a waste of money, will suddenly become a golden egg.
The first part of the scenario is the Netspot + 3G combination. That's the iPhone. Then users become aware of Netspot's existence. However, they feel a certain inconvenience here: expensive fees, slow speeds, and disconnections when switching from Netspot to 3G (though you might not notice if you don't use VoIP). This is where Wibro is inserted. That's the Cook&Show phone. And KT gains the capacity to continuously invest in Wibro. While Wibro's base station coverage is not significantly narrower than 3G or LTE, it can be a solution for KT, which has struggled with base station installation costs and nationwide expansion, or for Wibro, which has recently been embroiled in effectiveness controversies like City Phone.
The strategy KT aimed for was to choose the 3GS iPhone as a bridge for what it could do best in a 4G environment. And this point is also a solution that can excellently overcome AT&T's precedent.
For the next two years or so, KT might spend more money than it earns due to the iPhone, but the fact that a mobile carrier took such a gamble is very surprising to me, and I see it as a part of KT's potential to shed its image as a state-owned enterprise.
**Right before the iPhone launch, I was concerned about KT's pricing plans, and KT actually managed to open Netspot to users, which I had thought was impossible.**
[**Reference: http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70070748929**](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70070748929)
I believe that if KT continues to cultivate these possibilities, opportunities will come, and I support such a KT.

** 5. 4G is a Seamless Environment**
What we can do faster than overseas countries where the iPhone was introduced early is this 4G. Korea also possesses quite a lot of core technologies for LTE and Wibro. While Samsung Electronics often gets criticized due to the iPhone's introduction, Samsung Electronics is also a beneficiary of the iPhone. They sold a lot of RAM. What's concerning might be the domestic phone market share, but for LG or Samsung, what they earn from domestic sales is not that significant in their overall revenue. Of course, they wouldn't want it to decrease. Many advertise DMB as a strength of Korean phones. This is true to some extent. Many users want DMB. But thinking in reverse, why did it become a strength? Because the business was done properly at the right time. If terrestrial DMB had been wiped out by satellite DMB in the early days, would that advertisement be effective now?
If the Korean market already had WIPI and 4G activated, and wireless internet was freely available, would KT have gone to such lengths to introduce the iPhone? To each their own imagination.

I'll leave it at that. What else does a seamless internet environment mean? It means a significant increase in web dependency. Therefore, the success of the WebOS I mentioned could come sooner in Korea. A seamless environment holds these various possibilities.
Also, according to some overseas data, what affects wireless internet users the most is not the device, but the pricing plan. Omnia's simple activation strategy to counter the iPhone, isn't it?
**Create a 20,000 won flat-rate wireless internet plan. Then, pre-install a VoIP app and assign a 070 number. And make it so only Omnia users can subscribe. Everyone will subscribe, even if others try to dissuade them.**
 
**You think it's a stretch? It might be possible in the 4G world. And we still have a chance.**
 
{{IMG:1}}
ps. I was wondering why the number of visitors suddenly increased... it appeared in the blog section.
The first part of this appeared on Daum View Best, and even though my insights are lacking, thank you for your interest.

contentEn:
아이폰이 들어온 시점에서야 갑자기 무선 인터넷에 대한 관심이 증폭되어 열광하는 모습이 보입니다. 그러면서 무차별적인 국내 기업의 깎아내리기 또한 보입니다. 이에 대한 반론? 아니 제가 보고 느낀 지난 10년간의 무선인터넷 시장에 대한 진짜 이야기를 해보려고 합니다. 특정 기업을 비난하는 것이 될 수도 있겠다 싶어 그동안 참아왔던 이야기입니다.
제가 처음 무선 인터넷, 최초는 무선 pc통신이었습니다. 그것에 대한 가능성을 본 것은 10년 전 제가 대학교 2학년이었을 때 였습니다. 그 후로 군에 갔다오고, 실제 모바일 개발에 관한 기술을 학습했던것이 3년 정도, 그리고 실제 필드에서 국내 무선인터넷 브라우져와 단말기 mmi개발을 수행했던 2년, 그리고 관심 있어서 살펴본 국내 무선 기술들의 로드맵. 실제 필드에서 보고 느낀 주관적인 시장이야기를 해보려고 합니다. 사실 지금에와서 이 이야기를 하는 것은 무척 착찹합니다. 한때 전세계 최고였던 무선 인터넷 소프트웨어 기술이 빛을 발하지 못하게 된 역사기 때문입니다. 이 이야기에는 시선에 따라 특정 기업이 악으로 비춰질 수도 있습니다. 그러나 이는 전략의 문제 였다고 생각합니다. 우리가 알고 있는 것 만큼 기업이 똑똑하지 않다는 것과 근시안적인 조직간의 이익과 힘을 놓고 벌인

fixed it so that downloads were only possible from that website. LGT and SKT browsers used the same browser, but they couldn't access each other's WAP portals. Why? It was the same browser... but they could access Cyworld WAP or Naver WAP. That's how mobile carriers began to draw a strict line even with the internet.
The government even imposed billions of won in fines on carriers that didn't open their networks, but that wasn't particularly important to them, and for some reason, the media didn't cover it extensively. It's also true that few people knew what wireless internet was.
When developing WIPI, it's uploaded to test phones using a cable. As some of you may know, mobile carriers blocked this cable connection. There was a workaround to unlock it, and some of you might have seen applications or ringtones being uploaded via cable using an application called QPST. Basically, in the RAM space called EFS, there's a directory structure just like on a computer, and if you just copy the class file to that directory, the WIPI application runs. It's like copying an MP3. During my undergraduate years, I advised my professor that we needed to enable cable access for the spread of wireless internet, and the professor said he would try. It was a common opinion in academia. However, it seems that was merely an academic opinion. At that time, I had a dream of creating a mobile phone WIPI GNU group.
However, mobile carriers unified the distribution method: enter a wireless page, click purchase on that page, get charged, and download. This method further strengthened the mobile carriers' power because getting onto the initial page was incredibly difficult, and impossible without a cooperative relationship with the carrier. The registration review was also done by mobile carriers, and the industry rumor was that an application uploaded to KTF could absolutely not be simultaneously uploaded to SKT without significant negotiation power. If that's the case, why was WIPI even created? And on a small phone screen, with expensive wireless communication fees, weren't mobile applications distributed this way an obvious losing game? That's how several years quickly passed.
In the case of overseas markets, since there was no software distribution channel, device manufacturers didn't seem to feel the need to include WIPI, and thus WIPI devolved into a "scary feature not to be pressed" for users.
And at some point, mobile carriers began to put forward WIPI as a defensive shield. "Remove WIPI to lower device prices." That was an absurd statement. Let's be clear. I suspect it was the mobile carriers who feared wireless internet. Unlike other platforms, WIPI is domestic, so it doesn't incur licensing fees. Browser prices don't exceed 1,000 won per unit. Development costs aren't that high either, because device manufacturers also use a common platform. Samsung's Bada platform seems to be built on top of that very platform. The browsers supplied by domestic S and L companies were already fully ported not only to WIPI but also to the underlying OS.
Let's talk briefly about Apple. Did Apple care about something like WIPI? No. My thoughts are different. What Apple worries about is the potential that WIPI holds. It's the same reason they hesitate to include Flash, Silverlight, and Java. WIPI is fundamentally JAVA. Saying its specs are lacking is, of course, a lie. If specs were the problem, why would Flash and Java run on the older Arm11 or Arm9 series phones I developed years ago? Apple, which wants to dominate the software distribution network just like mobile carriers, seems to be commercially hesitant about virtual OS concept solutions appearing on Apple devices. Of course, I believe they will eventually be supported. The trend towards the web is inevitable.
What I wanted to say here is this: WIPI was a platform that could have dreamed everything the iPhone dreamed of. But it wasn't utilized, and now the opportunity is gone. Content Providers (CPs) also turned away from the mobile carriers' tyranny (not copyright fees, but spec limitations, page placement negotiations, political reasons, and carriers unwilling to vitalize the market), and the game has already moved to OpenOS.

** 4. Does Wireless Internet Really Need to Be That Expensive?
** Let's briefly calculate wireless internet fees here. One packet is 512 bytes, which is 4096 bits when converted. Voice uses 8kbps, or 8000 bits per second. The fee would be around 18 won for 80,000 bits. Voice call rates haven't changed much, but wireless internet prices have significantly decreased recently. What was the cost for 1MB of internet usage in the past? Converted to voice call units, it's only 12.8 units. I calculated it to be 230 won. However, a few years ago, when I downloaded a 512KB game, thousands of won were charged for data usage. Don't even get me started on SMS, which is only 80 bytes. MMS varies wildly in size depending on the photo, but it's a flat 100 won. Based on capacity, it really feels like a "rubber band" pricing system.
Furthermore, few people know that when WIPI was launched, there was briefly an unlimited internet plan for 26,000 won per month, which then disappeared. At that time, including the basic fee, it was roughly equivalent to today's i-slim plan. I thoroughly enjoyed it with the first WIPI model, the SD9230. However, it's said that the plan was abolished because some users were spending millions of won using laptops, and even now, SKT excludes tethering (laptops) from fixed data plans.

** 5. Why Are Domestic Mobile Phones So Restricted?
** In phone development, ROM prices are very high and significantly impact the unit cost. Therefore, optimizing and saving memory space is correct, but conversely, some convenience features are restricted by specs politically determined by mobile carriers. In my case, I needed to write long notes frequently, but when a certain company developed a phone, they limited the memo program to 1000 characters. The heap space was 2MB... but the memo's usable space was only 1KB. ㅡㅡ; Such incidents are quite common. Many people tend to lump device manufacturers and mobile carriers together, but their relationship is more complex than you might think. Samsung Electronics and LG Electronics sell phones globally, so their need for good technology is quite high. A certain phone I developed was the first dual DMB phone, but after months of network certification refusal by the carrier, it was eventually released with only terrestrial DMB. While I understand it was an effort to save TU, it was truly bitter to see a PMP with dual DMB released by a subsidiary of that group a few months later. It meant PMPs could have it, but phones couldn't. And when TU faced more severe difficulties recently, dual DMB phones were finally released. That's how I directly experienced the carriers' spec-downs. But the problem isn't the spec-down itself. They fail to realize that by clinging to short-sighted profits, they squandered greater possibilities. At the time, articles highlighting the shortcomings of government-led terrestrial DMB lined up, and advertisements for satellite DMB flooded the market. And the result is as you see. Terrestrial DMB successfully made it to the German World Cup, but that was it. More than anything... it was too late, and now it's in an ambiguous position due to mobile IPTV on all-IP networks.

** 6. Was Korea's Wireless Internet Market Really That Underdeveloped?
** Now, let's briefly talk about the mobile web. When I worked at a certain mobile phone browser development company, I felt that its level was no less than Safari's. Of course, in terms of scale, it's not comparable. It's been three years since I left that company, so a full browser was already completed back then and was scheduled to be supplied to mobile carriers. The company's technical staff worked hard to make Cyworld, which even the current iPhone couldn't handle, work, and a Korean consortium for Mobile OK, led by W3C, also started with domestic portals like Naver. All these stories are more than three years old. And that company actually went public, and users are still using services like OZ. Although today the trend is unifying around WebKit, a global open-source project, I want to emphasize that its level was incredibly fast. At the time, Ajax was a hot topic, and Ajax implementation had already begun, resulting in a browser capable of running Tetris with JavaScript. However, it was useless in Korea because the market was at the level I mentioned earlier. It only began to shine after OZ was introduced.

**** 7. 3-5 Years of Stagnation
** In my view, the Korean wireless internet market remained stagnant for about 3-5 years. During that time, Japan easily surpassed us as an advanced wireless internet nation, and now, with Jin Dae-je having stepped down and the Ministry of Information and Communication disbanded, it seems to be floundering amidst political issues. All that moved forward was the mobile carriers' efforts to establish video calls by prominently featuring 3G. The roadmap for data communication was not forgotten but rather something to be hidden, and the leap to a software distribution platform was a forgotten dream. The fact that some smartphones encroached on the phone's domain meant that, apart from the phone module, wireless capabilities should have been thoroughly blocked to make it seem as if those features didn't exist. While numerous PDAs came with Wi-Fi as standard, smartphone lines, in particular, had Wi-Fi thoroughly removed. With VoIP specs and solutions already available, mobile carriers must have been concerned about the future.
The reason I keep telling this story is not to criticize the iPhone. It's about the complacency of the Korean market during that time, and the hindering factors of Korean wireless internet that continue to this day. If the Korean market remains stuck on the iPhone, that's as far as it goes. The iPhone opened the door to what we dreamed of in the past. However, the iPhone has many shortcomings for moving into the future. It's merely an implementation of the roadmap I envisioned 10 years ago, not an implementation of the roadmap I'm currently thinking of. Perhaps it's also because the iPhone that came to Korea was already more than a year old.

It could be a door.
Also, even if the platform market seems hopeless now, there are still some opportunities. Next, I'll talk about that. I hope past mistakes are not repeated.

Although this is an incomplete article and a brief thought, next time I will discuss the changes brought by the iPhone, its limitations, and the path forward for the domestic wireless software market to overcome them.

P.S. This article was featured on Daum View Best. I'm embarrassed that such a humble piece has garnered so much attention, especially since it's a somewhat sensitive and subjective topic.

titleEn: Legend of Dragonia, Part 2
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

Meanwhile, Aysia was still trapped in the warehouse. After Gaisa, who had tried to violate her, left, she remained terrified for a long time, flinching and trembling at every loud noise from outside. Lights and shadows flickered through the high, small bars, signaling that something big was happening outside.

Melchizedek, having joined forces with Misraim, advanced his troops under the watchful eyes of the Knights. With the well-trained and iron-clad heavy cavalry joining them, the allied forces were unstoppable. The knights, armored in steel, were no match for the bandits, and even the formidable black-clad enemies fell one by one under the combined assault of the Demon Sword Unit and the Knights. Gaisa was flustered by the sudden appearance of the Knights. It was Prince Zacchaeus's arbitrary decision to bring in the heavy cavalry, who should have been on the front lines, but for Gaisa, it was an unexpected enemy force.

The original plan was to annihilate Melchizedek's forces with the bandit groups and troops stationed outside, but with the Knights joining, there was no chance of victory. Gaisa gave an order in a resentful voice.
"Damn it! We're getting out of here. Debora, bring Aysia."

Debora went down to the warehouse to get Aysia. When Debora unlocked the door and entered the warehouse, Aysia was trembling in a dark corner. Aysia felt fear engulf her body at the sound of the door opening. However, recognizing the entering shadow as Debora, she sprang up and ran towards her, calling her name with joy.
"Debora, you're alive! That's a relief. What happened to the others?"
But Debora cruelly pushed Aysia away with force.
"Ack! Why? What's wrong?"
Aysia, who had fallen, finally looked at Debora's expression. Debora was glaring at Aysia with a terrifying look.
"You know better!"
"What do you mean?"
Debora approached Aysia with a resentful expression and stomped on her.
"Ack! It hurts! Debora! What's wrong! Stop it!"
"I don't have much to say to you. I'm just getting revenge on you and Prince Dagmon for him."
Then Debora grabbed Aysia and pulled her up, but Aysia was so exhausted that she had no strength left to resist.
"Don't stumble, walk straight!"
Debora pulled Aysia along, shouting irritably.
"Debora, please don't do this!"
Aysia cried and pleaded, but Debora's response was only cold.
"Just go, don't say anything!"

Debora, dragging Aysia up to the first floor, was a little flustered. The situation was even more unfavorable than before. Fires were breaking out everywhere outside, dyeing the night sky red, and it was already a chaotic scene, with several bodies of bandits and Gaisa's subordinates lying around, indicating a fierce battle had taken place there. Aysia turned her head away from the horrific sight.
"Where should we go? Where is Gaisa?"
Debora bit her lower lip.
"Debora. I was wrong. Let me go. *sob* *sob*"
Aysia, terrified, didn't understand what she had done wrong, but she begged and pleaded with Debora.
"Don't be ridiculous! Your crying won't bring him back to life!"
As Debora shouted irritably, there was a loud crash, and a wall collapsed, followed by a shout.
"We found Aysia!"
A demon swordsman from Laodicea shouted from beyond the broken wall. On the other side of the wall, Knights and intelligence unit soldiers were clearing out Gaisa's remaining forces.

Aysia and Debora, frozen in confusion, not knowing what was happening, were suddenly targeted by a large sword thrown by a knight.
Aysia, startled, fell and narrowly dodged the sword, but Debora, right behind Aysia, didn't even see the sword flying towards her. When Aysia, who had fallen, regained her senses, she screamed at the sight before her. Debora, who had been standing next to her just moments ago, was impaled against the building wall with a large sword through her stomach.
"Ugh... Aaaargh!"
Debora also screamed when she discovered the long sword embedded in her stomach. She continued to scream in pain, pulling the sword out with her own hands. As the sword came out, more red blood gushed out all at once, and Debora collapsed forward. She died with her eyes wide open in terror.
"Kyaaah!"
Aysia continued to scream, watching the terrifying scene. She backed away while sitting, then bumped into something behind her, startling her and making her scream again. It was the corpse of a dead bandit. Next to the corpse was a blood-stained shuriken. Aysia picked up the shuriken, got up, and started running aimlessly, crying. As she ran, she used the shuriken to free her bound hands and then threw the shuriken away. Her hastily freed wrists were cut by the shuriken and bled, but Aysia didn't even feel the pain.
"The woman is escaping! Chase her!"
Behind her, she heard the shouts of Laodicean soldiers. As Aysia, panting, rounded a building wall, there were more Laodicean soldiers. They had just killed two bandits, and one of them was stepping on a dead bandit's corpse to pull out his sword. Aysia stopped when she saw them and made eye contact with the soldier who had drawn his sword.
"Lady Aysia!"
It was Melchizedek. Aysia's legs gave out when she heard his voice. She believed he would save her now. She believed he would take her to Dagmon, whom she loved. She ran to him, grabbed his hand, and pleaded, clinging to him.
"Please, take me to the Prince."

Just then, a loud shout came from the direction Aysia had run from.
"Melchizedek, what are you doing! Are you disobeying Prince Dagmon's order to kill the woman!"
It was the Knight Commander, who had been chasing Aysia, shouting at Melchizedek. Misraim, with a terrifying expression, was approaching, holding a large, blood-stained sword. Aysia instantly let go of Melchizedek's hand, took a step or two back, and looked at him with disbelief. Aysia instinctively knew something was wrong. Melchizedek held his blood-stained sword with trembling hands, his head bowed, unable to meet Aysia's eyes.
"Melchizedek!"
When the Knight Commander shouted again, Aysia left the frozen Melchizedek and started running again. The outer areas of the building were thick with smoke from the fire. Aysia, finding nowhere else to run, held her breath and plunged into the smoke. Through the barely visible smoke, she was lucky enough to escape the bandits' lair through a hole the Laodicean forces had made to enter. But before she could catch her breath, she heard the sounds of soldiers chasing right behind her.

Before she knew it, she was running through the red-light district. In that place, full of dazzling lights and women in revealing clothes, everyone looked at Aysia running with contempt. They seemed to regard her as nothing more than a fleeing prostitute.
As she left the market and entered the residential area, it was late, so people were even scarcer. The wind blew, and then it started to rain. At first, it was just a chilling dampness on her neck, but soon it began to pour. Most of the houses were dark with their lights off, and only the oil lamps on the street illuminated the rainy path. Aysia fell several times but got up and ran again. Her clothes were already covered in mud and torn in many places. She didn't know where to run. All she could think about was meeting Dagmon. Her shoes were already gone, she didn't know where. She ran through the deserted city streets, making splashing sounds. But, despairingly, she could feel the soldiers' footsteps getting closer.

Melchizedek, who was chasing her, felt unspeakably miserable. The rain began to lash his face, and he couldn't distinguish whether it was tears or raindrops. Misraim, running beside him, had a terrifying look on his face, wanting him to complete his mission. He knew well that if he didn't complete the mission, Misraim would cut him down and Aysia down as well. Melchizedek had even thought about cutting Misraim down first. But there was no chance of success. And even if he succeeded and he and Aysia escaped, he couldn't bring himself to have the courage to do so, thinking that his innocent subordinates would be in danger.
The sight of Aysia's back, running in front of him, felt pitiful. The group chasing her, so fragile and pathetic, was like hungry wolves.
He wished he were running now to get closer to the one he loved. But now, he was chasing the one he loved to kill her. Melchizedek would rather have run away. Even if he couldn't be by Aysia's side, if she could escape this situation and survive, he thought he wouldn't mind never seeing her again. But he knew it was an impossible wish.
He saw Aysia fall in front of him. Melchizedek felt so heartbroken at the sight that he wanted to grab her and help her up. But all he could do was hope that Aysia would succeed in escaping. However, Aysia was already very exhausted, so her figure was getting closer and closer. Melchizedek was so afraid that his tightly clenched fists trembled. He had faced countless life-or-death situations and battles, but this was the first time he had experienced such fear.
Rounding the corner of a building, Aysia finally stopped right in front of the canal that cut through the city. Melchizedek and Misraim also stopped running, and the soldiers who came with them quickly blocked her escape route. Aysia was cornered. Behind Aysia, the canal, swollen with rain and muddy, flowed with a terrifying sound. She had nowhere left to escape.
"Melchizedek, obey the Prince's command."
Misraim's deep voice was heard. Melchizedek slowly approached her with faltering steps. Aysia, like a wounded little bird

Her eyes trembled with fear, and her body was covered in wounds, both large and small. Her lips quivered as she asked in a small voice.
"Why..."
Melchizedek approached her, gritting his teeth, and spoke. He had wished hundreds of times that this moment was a dream.
"I'm sorry. It is the Prince's will."
"Lies... It's a lie! He wouldn't do that!"
Aysia was shocked by the fact that Dagmon was the one who had ordered her death.
"Take me to the Prince! I want to see him! H-h-h."
Aysia burst into loud sobs. At this moment, she missed Dagmon more than anyone. She felt that if she could just meet Dagmon, everything would be resolved. At least if he were there, she wouldn't feel this anxious or scared.
"I'm sorry. It is the Prince's command."
Melchizedek replied with a choked voice and drew the dagger from his waist. When Aysia saw the blade, she instead wore a look of resignation. The fact that she could no longer meet Dagmon saddened her more than the fear of death itself. Melchizedek had wished she would at least show anger, but her profoundly sad expression pained him even more.
Melchizedek finally plunged the dagger into Aysia's abdomen. The distinct sensation of it piercing through soft flesh and bone was transmitted to Melchizedek's hand.
"You said you loved me... you'd protect me... but... Dagmon... Dagmon..."
Aysia spoke in a tearful voice, calling Dagmon's name before collapsing into Melchizedek's arms. Melchizedek caught her. Holding Aysia, Melchizedek wished time would stop right then. And he desperately wished the knife that had stabbed her was not in his hand.
Aysia's blood flowed and touched Melchizedek's wrist. When Melchizedek felt the warm blood, he shuddered with revulsion, as if a ghost had enveloped his entire body. As Melchizedek pulled the knife from Aysia's abdomen, she slid and fell into the canal.
The canal, swallowing Aysia with a splash, completely concealed her form.
"You fool. What will you report to the Prince if you don't bring Aysia's body?"
Misraim shouted in anger.
"If we had brought Aysia's body, the Prince would have disliked it even more."
When Melchizedek cut him off, Misraim, assuming there was a reason for his resolute demeanor, did not retort.
"Collect the bodies of our allies and the bandits, and station guards at the bandits' stronghold. The remaining soldiers will return with me to the supply base."
Melchizedek commanded the soldiers and turned back.
After giving that final order, Melchizedek kept his head bowed low throughout the entire journey back with the soldiers. On the way back, Deputy Commander Galap found Melchizedek's appearance strange and approached him to speak.
"Commander! Are you alright? The rain is really..."
Despite being spoken to, he remained silent, his head still bowed. But the quick-witted Deputy Commander soon said nothing further.
The unseasonal night rain poured down in torrents, swallowing all sounds. It was not a pleasant night for the soldiers returning to the encampment, drenched in rain. They had won, but there was no victory song, only a gloomy night remembering their fallen comrades. Perhaps because of the sound of the rain, there was no conversation among them as they marched in formation.
Amidst the soldiers shrouded in gloom, one man was weeping sorrowfully. He was dressed in a commander's uniform, but that was not important. He couldn't even properly utter the confession that had been at the tip of his tongue, and he had sent the woman he loved away with his own hands.
The pouring rain, just as it had hidden the body of a gypsy woman, also concealed the man's weeping.

titleEn: [Gather on the Web!] The Future of Chrome OS
contentEn:
Google has announced Chrome OS, but the market's reaction remains cool.
{{IMG:1}}
The current Chrome OS would certainly fail when compared to Windows 7. However, Microsoft likely considers Chrome OS to be the biggest headache to emerge in the future. And ultimately, Chrome OS, which started on PCs, has the potential to spread to all devices, including mobile. The reason for this is that it is based on the web, which allows for seamless service anywhere, as long as there is a connection.

**1. Standardized Open Eco Chrome OS that does not monopolize service distribution**
Apple's iPhone OS is limited, and the potential of Android that I mentioned earlier is that it is a platform that will be supported by various vendors and does not monopolize distribution through a "mall-in-mall" approach. This idea also applies to Chrome OS. If Android can be the foundation for mobile, with vendors like Samsung, Nokia, and Motorola, then Chrome OS can be the foundation for PCs, netbooks, and MIDs that support the web relatively freely, with vendors in Korea potentially being Naver, Daum, Nate, and Yahoo. This is because Chrome OS fundamentally possesses the MashUp characteristics of Web 2.0.

**1) Why? Because it's open source.**
First, Chrome OS is open source. What does this mean? There's talk that Google's ambitions will fully unfold if Chrome OS logs in with Gmail. In one sense, this is true, but in another, it's not. Unlike Microsoft, which takes everything, Google's Chrome OS will likely aim to be the core of cloud services. What Google wants to create now is not a service, but a platform. The web is characterized by mashups. Couldn't a mashup service of login accounts be applied to Chrome OS? The web already has SSO services like Open ID and i-PIN, which are essentially mashup services for logins. Or, Naver or Daum might open the Chrome OS source and create Naver OS or Daum OS according to Google's rules.

**2) The web has already achieved a sufficient technical level of RIA, threatening desktops.**
As mentioned in a previous post, web tools at the level of Photoshop already exist, and office environments are almost fully developed, including the briefly attempted Naver Office in the past, Microsoft's recently unveiled Web Office, and Google's Office. For storage, Naver in Korea opened the door to virtualized storage with N Drive. Flash games already form a large market, and games are even placed on Naver's main page. Google's attempts to cover 3D in the web environment are also ongoing and will likely be included in the HTML5 specification. The time is fast approaching when web services must be viewed as web applications through RIA technology.

**3) Competitiveness of Web OS within enterprises**
What about enterprises? The web has been the foundation of SaaS and SOA technologies, leading to a gradual movement in this direction. However, there are no standards, experience is still limited, and resources are scarce. In our company, web developers primarily need Eclipse, editors, and an office environment. What kind of results would emerge if Chrome OS were applied here? Or if applied to POS? Chrome OS could likely be the answer in terms of cost savings, control, security, and customization. This explains why Google strongly emphasized security. Of course, being open source, the impact of zero-day attacks cannot be ignored, and it would be difficult to take responsibility for issues arising from customization errors. Let me reiterate, Google's Chrome OS is open source. In other words, it would be possible to implement independent storage rather than Google's cloud storage, and I believe it could solve the security issues that enterprises are wary of.

**2. A day in the future, 2018**
Finally, let me briefly share a future I imagine.
{{IMG:2}}
[ Mimi's Computer Journey / Image source: [http://blog.naver.com/pooh_1030](http://blog.naver.com/pooh_1030) ]

**1) The golden age of Web OS begins.**
Despite the great popularity of Windows 7, Chrome OS has been spreading since 2015, leveraging its price competitiveness. Of course, existing customers still prefer Windows 7, as they can essentially enjoy all the features of Chrome OS. However, the problem lies with hardware manufacturers. They refused to continue installing Microsoft's expensive OS, and Microsoft belatedly announced its own web OS. While it managed to maintain a certain market share, Microsoft's influence declined compared to the past PC environment, and its profitability was severely impacted by the cheap OS.

**2) Desktop Environment**
A domestic user downloaded a customized Chrome OS from a local GNU group and installed it on their PC. A screen appeared asking to set the login vendor. After contemplating between i-PIN and OpenID, they chose i-PIN to use the recently applied internet banking service and domestic portal services. (Currently, domestic portal sites support i-PIN, and i-PIN 2.0 is expected to be released as a platform independent of IE.)
Since they already had an i-PIN, they simply selected it and logged in. Being a customized version, familiar domestic services appeared.
For internet search, they still installed two widgets: Naver and Google. Various Naver casts were created as widgets and placed on the desktop screen. It seems this GNU group receives support from [http://dev.naver.com](http://dev.naver.com/). For local storage search, they set the Google widget in the environment settings. Icons for NateOn web messenger, Naver's N Drive, Daum's map, Microsoft's web office, Naver's photo editor, and Google's YouTube widget were also visible.
Preferring a clean look, they removed all cast widgets and installed a Chrome OS girl theme. Widget icons were also hidden using a widget management web widget like Widget Dock.
All of this is the benefit of cloud and mashup services. Unnecessary services are deleted, and desired services are added to my Chrome OS by clicking "Add Widget" on the website and then arranged on the screen. All these technologies utilize web standards.

[ Current Windows 7 Madobe Nanami Theme ]

ChromeOS-chan wags her tail, asking to play. But this one is a 3D character. This one is also a web service, but it's outside the square frame. HTML5 now supports not just square pages but also 3D.
I plugged a gamepad into the USB port. NCSoft's Aion runs on the web. The internet already supports QoS at gigabit speeds, giving a strong feeling that games can also be enjoyed via streaming. For device management, ChromeOS is also Linux, and Google is supplying stable drivers, taking on the role that Microsoft once played for Windows. Google is also making a profit here.
****
** 3) Mobile Environment**
I turned on my phone. My phone already has the power of a 2009 netbook and is a model with FMC (Fixed Mobile Convergence) applied to WiBro and Wi-Fi, which have expanded nationwide.
{{IMG:3}}
The number is 070, and while KT is the mobile carrier using the transmission network, I'm using LG070 service for internet VoIP. The transmission network and internet phone service are now dualized, and the transmission network charges are paid as a flat rate with a wired/wireless package.
It's equipped with an OS called Android Chrome. It's a version where a lightweight Chrome OS is ported on top of Android. Recently, some people just install and use Chrome OS, but it's inconvenient because some mobile device features cannot be used. Google recently announced that it is abandoning the Android project and will maintain all Android technologies and backward compatibility with a mobile version for Chrome. The first models are said to be released simultaneously by Samsung and LG. I'm eagerly awaiting them.
When I press the ChromeOS button on my phone screen, the desktop switches to a locked state. And I can see the exact same screen I saw on the desktop, on my phone. Of course, some parts are optimized for the phone, so the screen layout is changed. This OS saves separate profiles for each platform. However, one consistent thing is that most functions can be used continuously from the desktop. For example, if I'm writing a document, turn off the PC, and then turn on my phone, that document window is still open on the phone.
Apps? We don't use those these days. Although some special web widgets exist for mobile environments, all of this runs in a web environment. Although they are called 'app stores' due to Apple's past influence, they are, to be precise, 'web stores'. Web stores can be easily found on Naver, Daum, etc., and these companies distribute a certain portion of their profits to Google. (Similar concept to how search revenue is currently shared with Google and AdSense)

**3. Will this really happen?**
What do you think of the scenario I've described? Of course, it might not turn out this way.
Because even today, many companies are revising their strategies, presenting value, and competing. The internet penetration I predicted was 3 years faster due to StarCraft, and the growth of wireless internet and smartphones was 5 years slower due to mobile carriers.
Who knows if MS will release even better services, or if a comet-like company will appear in Korea and catch up with Google? However, while I'm no Zhuge Liang, I imagine such a future might unfold given the current landscape.
Google's ambition for world domination continues unabated. World domination isn't about overt conquest; if you capture the infrastructure and systems, the rest naturally follows. That's why Microsoft once dominated the OS market and ruled the world. Next is... the web.
