titleEn: My Love, My Side: The Movie That
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

http://movie.naver.com/movie/bi/mi/review.nhn?code=51076

#### [Closer to Heaven](http://movie.naver.com/movie/bi/mi/review.nhn?code=51076)

Starring Ha Ji-won, Kim Myung-min
Production 2009 South Korea, 121 min
**Rating**

**1. A movie theater visit with my wife**
The reason I watched Closer to Heaven was actually because of the actor Kim Myung-min. My wife and I (actually, my wife is a fan of Kim Myung-min) were captivated by his acting and the news of his extreme diet. We took advantage of an extra day off after the short Chuseok holiday in 2009 to visit the theater. The theater on a Monday afternoon at 2 PM was less than half full, but the young students behind us and the middle-aged couple next to us were quite noisy.
I already knew the ending of the movie. Lou Gehrig's disease is fatal once contracted. The setting is Busan. And then the actress appeared: Ha Ji-won. Honestly, I started watching without even knowing Ha Ji-won was in this movie, overshadowed by Kim Myung-min's name. It's a fact I would have known if I'd just looked at the poster, but I guess I was too fixated on Kim Myung-min's name. Ha Ji-won was doing a "double-header" in Busan, along with Haeundae?

**2. A movie that begins with death**
The movie begins with death. Baek Jong-woo's (Kim Myung-min) mother's funeral. And Lee Ji-soo (Ha Ji-won), whom he meets as a funeral service employee.
{{IMG:2}}
The movie's ending leads to death, and Lee Ji-soo's profession is also a mortician, so the theme of death dominated the entire film. The final scene was predictable from the very beginning.
'Ji-soo, whose job is a mortician, will eventually send Jong-woo off herself.'
Actually, I've seen a story like this before. It was "The Happy Funeral Director," which made me realize Im Chang-jung was an actor, not just a comedian.

{{IMG:3}}

http://movie.naver.com/movie/bi/mi/basic.nhn?code=27629

[The Happy Funeral Director](http://movie.naver.com/movie/bi/mi/basic.nhn?code=27629)
Director Jang Moon-il Starring Im Chang-jung, Oh Hyun-kyung, Kim Chang-wan, Jung Eun-pyo Released 2000.01.08 Korea, 98 min.
The only difference from that story was the presence of Lou Gehrig's disease and Baek Jong-woo. However, the perspective of this movie is clearly different. Because it's a story about directly fighting a real disease, Lou Gehrig's disease, it's not a particularly happy story, and as the poster suggested, it overtly forced tears.

**2. 2% of Regret**
The movie shows quite a few attempts to force tears in many parts, which might be its regrettable aspect. I wonder if this movie was too ambitious, trying to tell too many stories in its two-hour runtime. It's the story of the people in Baek Jong-woo's hospital ward. Each person's story could have been deep enough to be another movie. What did the girl say to Baek Jong-woo, who couldn't speak, after asking Ha Ji-won to leave? Also, while this movie was entirely about the two of them, the title and song "Closer to Heaven," which sings of the sorrow of the one left behind, felt a bit out of place.

| My Love My.. |
| --- |
| My Love My.. |

The movie had talented actors and good material, but I regret that it didn't try a little less to follow the template of a tearjerker. Rather, it felt like the good old template spoiled the taste of the movie.

**3. Nevertheless, a story worth watching that transcends reality (this world) and unreality (the afterlife)**
I saw a review that said the 19+ scene in the hospital was unnecessary, but I don't think so. That scene isn't just explicit; as a married couple myself, I can empathize with it. Many people today delay marriage registration. The story of Jang Jin-young's husband registering their marriage right before her death became a hot topic precisely because of people's excessive sense of reality today. Recently, Ha Ji-won's attempt to stamp the marriage registration form on Kim Myung-min's final journey was an effort to leave even one more trace of the dying person, and from the perspective that humanity's greatest preparation for death is to leave descendants, it is perfectly understandable.
In fact, there are quite a few unrealistic scenes. Lee Ji-soo is excessively kind. Im Ha-ryong and his wife are also the same. This is probably because it's a movie. If it had been more realistic, the audience might have felt more frustration than sadness. Throughout the runtime, Lee Ji-soo, true to her nickname "moth," burned everything for Baek Jong-woo. I feel both envious and a little complex about it. **Perhaps love is, in fact, something that exists in the realm of the unrealistic, and we all step into that unrealistic realm once or twice in our lives.**
Even in the miserable reality where Baek Jong-woo couldn't even swat a mosquito, he wasn't entirely unhappy because Lee Ji-soo was there. It's difficult to say that this movie has only one attitude towards death. The patient's family asking for euthanasia due to hospital bills and the doctor's dry words about dying because of money are stark realities, and Ha Ji-won also realizes this as she looks at her bankbook.

**4. The story of heaven for the one who stays and the one who leaves, the two at the center**
{{IMG:8}}
However, patients and those who wait for them live in a fantasy of their own, like the curtains drawn around a hospital bed. The belief that they will wake up, the belief that they will get up. And the despair when that belief is betrayed. The movie depicted reality, but it focused more on their story. That belief and fantasy offer hope and an opportunity to discover the inherent human beauty in facing death. This is why countless novels and media still use the theme of incurable diseases with a terminal diagnosis.

I was reminded of the fable where both heaven and hell use spoons longer than their own height. In hell, people try to feed themselves with the long spoon and live in hunger, but in heaven, they feed each other with the long spoon. In that sense, Kim Myung-min successfully carried out his request to Ha Ji-won, asking her to send him to heaven herself. Although I don't think Ha Ji-won is a particularly beautiful actress, her imitation of Fin.K.L in front of Kim Myung-min was cute. It reminded me of my wife sometimes acting cute (I'm absolutely not saying my wife isn't cute!!).

**5. A story for lovers, especially married couples**
{{IMG:9}}
Perhaps lovers or married couples would have exchanged a word or two after watching this movie.
"What would you do if I couldn't even control my bladder and bowels?"
Actually, that's one of my wife's regular lines.
I always reply, "Don't say such unlucky things," but it seems all I can do is hold her hand tightly. If you're in love, it might be normal to feel happy laughter rather than tears after watching this movie.

**This movie is, unfortunately, clearly a "couple-flaunting" movie. Absolutely not recommended for singles!**

titleEn: The Changes and Challenges the iPhone Will Bring
contentEn:
**{{IMG:1}}**

The iPhone, which has tormented us with countless rumors, seems to finally be making its appearance. The market atmosphere seems highly encouraged, and Apple devotees who believe in Steve Jobs appear to be preparing their ammunition. Perhaps the significance of the iPhone, which was merely a smartphone, was that it served as an opportunity to inform the general public what a smartphone is, and it played a leading role in transforming regular phones into smartphones. And, if these usage patterns truly become widespread, what changes will come to us? I've thought about this a bit. Of course, these are just my personal imaginings, so they might be nothing more than that.
****
****
**1. Increased Need for Realistic Data Plans**

This need has existed before, but it will now materialize, and the market will move. Of course, we'll have to wait and see how realistic KT's plans will be.

**2. Increase in Home Wireless APs**
**{{IMG:2}}**
[Image Source: [http://blog.naver.com/csr1214?Redirect=Log&logNo=20020411093](http://blog.naver.com/csr1214?Redirect=Log&logNo=20020411093)]

Home APs, already spreading with services like LG 070 phones, are expected to increase with the addition of iPhone users who desire Wi-Fi. This holds potential for future development into home gateways, accelerating subscriptions to TPS (Triple Play Service) and positively impacting the spread of IPTV.

**3. Increased Need for 4G**
**{{IMG:3}}
**[Image Source: [http://blog.naver.com/gojump0713?Redirect=Log&logNo=140054162664](http://blog.naver.com/gojump0713?Redirect=Log&logNo=140054162664)]

While 3G assumes data transmission, it is not entirely IP-based and has bandwidth limitations. Wi-Fi coverage has clear limits unless KT opens Netspot and sufficiently expands its coverage. While on the move, 3G usage will increase as much as Wi-Fi increases, eventually becoming the driving force for all-IP-based 4G.

**5. Spread of VoIP Internet Phones**
** **
[Image Source: [http://blog.naver.com/cyberibh?Redirect=Log&logNo=100016200413](http://blog.naver.com/cyberibh?Redirect=Log&logNo=100016200413)]

Apple had a negative stance on Google's VoIP application, but this seems to have been strongly influenced by its business model with AT&T. Even without the iPhone, the situation is already quite possible due to mobile platforms from MS and Google. The iPhone's great significance lies in already demonstrating the potential of VoIP in mobile communication, and eventually, a new business model from a competing operator could change the market landscape. In Korea, QPS is not technically true convergence yet, but the convergence of internet phones like 070 and mobile phones holds significant potential.

**4. Increase in Wireless Content**
**{{IMG:4}}**
[Image Source: [http://blog.naver.com/joowon77?Redirect=Log&logNo=68595954](http://blog.naver.com/joowon77?Redirect=Log&logNo=68595954)]

Not only applications like the App Store but also an increase in dual-platform websites like mobile Naver and Daum is expected, leading to an increased demand for mobile web designers, mobile web programmers, and mobile web planners. No one knows if the treatment of IT personnel will improve, but IT still accounts for the majority of re-employment processes. Furthermore, mobile public projects are expected to increase as administration and banking move to mobile platforms.

**5. Increased Need for Mobile Business Models**
**{{IMG:5}}**
[Image Source: [http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?sid1=105&oid=073&aid=0001997979](http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?sid1=105&oid=073&aid=0001997979)]

As websites become dual-platform, costs will increase, and so will the need for business models. Mobile shopping and the advertising market are expected to expand, with the biggest beneficiaries being domestic portals that already possess the largest number of users and content. Among Korea's top three portals, Naver and Daum will maximize the use of their own content, while Nate seems likely to target the market through a strategic alliance with SKT. Google, unfamiliar with localization, will likely have an even lower mobile web market share in Korea than in the PC web market. Even with full browsing support, platforms required while on the move will inevitably have at least minimal differences, and these small differences for domestic companies will be a significant barrier for Google.
However, one possibility for Google exists: the success of the Android Market leading to content localization by voluntary domestic developers. In this case, it differs somewhat from full browsing and will be more application-centric. Google's revenue in Korea will likely come more from mobile platforms like Android than from mobile web.

**6. Did it Have to Be the iPhone? And Our Task**
**** ****
{{IMG:6}}

These environmental changes would have occurred with any mobile device that had such an impact on the market, not just the iPhone. If we consider only the technological drivers that created this environment, devices of similar capability have existed among us for a very long time. However, regardless of its market share in Korea, the iPhone drew the attention of the general public, beyond power users, to technologies like full browsing and convergence with networks other than mobile communication networks. Such technologies were already available in Korea during the 2G era, but due to various environmental factors, they largely remained at the level of voice communication networks.
Many complain about Korea's mobile environment, and perhaps due to underdeveloped pricing plans, data communication usage isn't very high. However, Korea's mobile software technology and wireless infrastructure technology are among the top five in the world. If we can leverage these strengths, we won't need to envy overseas countries that adopted the iPhone earlier. The problem now is not the environment, but our actions and strategies, which can create our sustenance for the next 10 years. If we hesitate, the market will not wait.

**Finally, however, no one knows the future.** The moment I wrote and published this article, it might have influenced someone's strategy, and it's said that public prophecies are less likely to come true. More than anything, the market is far more complex, and what drives it are people with inherent uncertainty. People often make absurd mistakes and display unexpected, great abilities. Nevertheless, I hope the new future will be a slightly better world for us.

titleEn: [Google is Freeloading, I'm Angry
contentEn:
[Naver: "Google is a Freeloader, I'm Angry"](http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&sid1=105&oid=092&aid=0001953384)
 
**1. Is "Freeloading" a complete lie?**
{{IMG:1}}
 
First, COO Lee Jun-ho's statement is not wrong from the perspective of a domestic business operator.
 

 
**This is true not only for Naver, which would suffer the most if its DB were opened, but also for Daum, which has cafes, and SK Comms, which has mini-homepages.** Daum's cafes and Cyworld's mini-homepages are also not exposed in Google searches.
 Furthermore, while some criticize Naver's approach as closed for trying to conduct business through openness and linkage between Naver and other web services, it is fundamentally the same as the open policies of Google, MS, and Apple. **They are all in a silent competition to make their own platforms the standard for the open web. There is a tendency for media outlets, which often view Naver unfavorably, to exaggerate certain words in their reporting.**
 
**2. However, an inappropriate remark**
 However, I agree that Dr. Lee Jun-ho's "freeloading" remark, taken in isolation, was inappropriate. **Such complaints from CPs have always existed since Yahoo's directory search began, but Naver, as a company that also performs web search and directory search, cannot be free from the same criticism. Moreover, domestic web companies have gained a competitive edge at the starting line precisely because of their contributions to the domestic web.**
 Above all, the web is exposed to diverse competitive environments and market trends. Naver, as the dominant domestic player, must also adapt to these trends as a choice for survival. Market trends and competitors are always a threat to businesses.
 
**3. To beat Google, it's not the time to complain about their strategy.**
 While I fully acknowledge the contributions of domestic portal operators to the Korean web and hope for the success of domestic companies, **I don't think it's necessary to say that market trends and competitors' actions are cowardly. After all, it is a company's instinct and strategy to hide its weaknesses and strengthen its advantages.**
 I know that Naver is more technology-oriented than any other domestic company and invests heavily in search, and I understand the immense wall that Google presents, but we can never beat them by complaining about the enemy's strength and strategy.
 **While it might have been a natural complaint for a business operator or an individual, it seems it was a remark that should have been made more carefully in a setting full of reporters looking for something to criticize about portals.**
 
P.S. Overall, it felt like a statement that made Google's wall seem even thicker. If Korean companies continue to fail in their overseas ventures, I wonder what Korean IT companies will remain in 10 years. Research centers are increasingly moving to China and India... If even domestic services are taken over by foreign companies, will only games be left? Users might be happy, but many Korean engineers like me will have nowhere to go. It's already a tough IT landscape, so this is truly disheartening.

titleEn: The Legend of Dragonia Part 2 Chapter
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}
Inside one of the tents in the gypsy village, a woman was weeping bitterly. She had been crying for days, refusing to eat or drink. Aisia, with a worried look, brought her some warm milk and bread and spoke to her.
"Bnina. Stop crying. It's been days."
But her sorrow was so deep that she couldn't stop.
"The living must go on..."
At Aisia's words, Bnina cried out irritably.
"Get out! Leave me alone!"
Aisia didn't know what to do for her. Bnina was also a top dancer, no less skilled than Aisia in the troupe, and had always performed in sync with Aisia. She was plunged into grief because her boyfriend had died a few days ago. He was the young man whose arm had been cut off by Melchizedek after killing a soldier a few days prior. After his death, Bnina had also stopped eating and drinking and had been crying for days. Kind-hearted Aisia felt sorry for her and would visit her whenever she had time, but it wasn't helping much.
Suddenly, as if something had occurred to her, Bnina sprang up and started searching for something.
"Bnina. What's wrong?"
Bnina found and pulled out a gleaming blue knife. Aisia cried out in surprise.
"Bnina!"
"I'm going to kill all those soldiers, and then I'll kill myself! What has this country ever done for me!"
"Bnina! Put the knife down!"
Aisia was also very afraid of the knife, but thinking of Bnina, who might do anything, she carefully tried to reason with her.
"Please... calm down. Even if you do that, he won't come back to life, and you'll only lose your own life."
Aisia, startled, pleaded with her from a slight distance.
"Then... my beloved... he died so unfairly... so unfairly. What do I do?"
Bnina, in her distressed state, surprisingly easily gave in to Aisia's persuasion. She dropped the knife and started crying again, and Aisia's legs instantly gave out.
"He wouldn't want this for you either."
"Get out! I said get out!"
Bnina threw her bedding. Aisia had no choice but to retreat. Just as Aisia was about to leave the tent, she ran into Gaisa in front of it.
"Ah, Aisia. You get prettier every day."
Gaisa smiled slyly and spoke.
"Director, what brings you here?"
"What do you mean? I heard Bnina stopped eating and drinking. Is she alright?"
"No..."
Aisia shook her head, wondering if the director had such a side to him.
"Aisia was Bnina's friend and colleague, wasn't she? When you two danced, it was like watching flowers. It's hard to perform these days. You must be worried too."
"Why don't you go in?"
When the director brought up performances, Aisia felt a sense of contempt for him, wondering if he should be talking about such things at a time like this. Thanks to this, her earlier thought about the director's new side vanished, and she worried that the director might do something inappropriate to Bnina.
Aisia parted ways from the tent, and the director entered Bnina's tent. Seeing this, Aisia felt a little uneasy, but she believed she would feel better once she met Dagmon. With that thought, she somehow felt sorry for Bnina.
Bnina was a little surprised by Gaisa's unexpected visit. She stopped crying for a moment, somewhat flustered by the visit, and said,
"Director, what brings you here..."
"How great your sorrow must be..."
"......I want to die..."
Bnina started by saying she wanted to die. Gaisa hesitated, then spoke.
"Listen carefully to what I'm about to tell you. It concerns the death of your lover... In truth, your lover died in my place."
"What?"
Bnina asked back, startled by his words. Gaisa told her that he was a spy for the Kingdom of Ceres, that the operation a few days ago was to capture him, and that he would retaliate against them.
Gaisa was making various calculations. Sounding out Bnina like this was to see if she was worth using. If Bnina didn't follow his will and seemed likely to reveal his identity to the Kingdom of Laodicea, he planned to kill her and fake it as a suicide. If not, he intended to proceed with his next plan.
Fortunately for Gaisa, Bnina was on the side of her deceased lover. The anger over her lover's death dominated her.
"I wish this country would just perish. It doesn't welcome us gypsies anyway, and everywhere we go, we face scorn... and contempt... This world is truly sickening."
"There's one more thing I need to tell you. It's about Aisia's lover."
Gaisa had found out more about the previous operation. He learned that it was carried out by Melchizedek's direct superior, Dagmon. He intended to use that very point. Gaisa told Bnina everything about it.
"Aisia's boyfriend is this country's prince, and he ordered my beloved's death? I can't believe it."
"Then, Aisia carries a pendant, a symbol of the prince. In fact, Aisia herself is a spy for the Kingdom of Laodicea, infiltrated into our troupe. It was actually she who leaked the information that there was a spy from the Kingdom of Ceres in our troupe."
Gaisa lied. Bnina was Aisia's friend, but also her rival. Gaisa knew well that while they were close, Bnina would become cold towards Aisia when choosing the lead for a play. Moreover, everyone in the troupe knew that Bnina's deceased lover had once courted Aisia and been rejected. Because of this, many people didn't understand why Bnina and Aisia got along so well.
"No matter what... still..."
"Actually, I investigated Aisia. She is a member of Melchizedek's unit, the one that raided our troupe last time. Aisia joined the troupe when we were performing in the Kingdom of Ceres. At that time, Aisia completed her reconnaissance of the Kingdom of Ceres and returned with us to the Kingdom of Laodicea. Because she was part of the troupe, she could gather information about the Kingdom of Ceres without any suspicion.
Even I only found this out recently. I am a Ceres intelligence agent, after all, and to think there was a Laodicean spy in the troupe I manage. Only after information about me leaked did I suspect our troupe members and finally figure it out.
You know Aisia's acting skills, don't you? She can easily present a different image from what we know. That's why she always monopolized the lead roles and became the idol of many men."
Gaisa deliberately provoked Bnina's jealousy. Upon hearing his words, Bnina felt uneasy. Aisia was always ahead of Bnina. No matter how hard she tried, she couldn't catch up to her. She knew better than anyone how desperately the man she loved had once loved Aisia.
Their relationship had begun at a drinking session with him after he had been rejected by Aisia. He was a delicate but purely loving person. She felt sympathy for that side of him, and that feeling had turned into love.
Therefore, although Bnina didn't show it, a not-so-small jealousy towards Aisia always resided in her heart.
"But how can I believe that?"
"She wears a pendant necklace. It has the blue dragon, the emblem of the royal family of Laodicea, engraved on it. She seems to have even charmed the prince with her beauty. And around midnight, she goes to the back forest to meet the prince. If you don't believe it, you can check for yourself. She always carries the pendant on her, but she won't show it to others, so it might be difficult to confirm.
You should be careful of her too. She may seem innocent on the surface, but she's a spy for the Kingdom of Laodicea. If her identity is revealed, she'll probably try to kill you too."
Bnina, despite everything, recalled Aisia's kind face and wondered if someone with such a face could kill. But then she remembered Aisia's face in a past play, playing a woman consumed by revenge after losing her beloved. Aisia at that time was like a devil, and Bnina, her co-star, was so startled by her appearance that she forgot her lines.
"You must not reveal my words to anyone. If you do, your life will be in danger. One or two gypsies dying is nothing in this country. If you cooperate with me to capture Prince Dagmon and Melchizedek, the Kingdom of Ceres will protect you. You can get your revenge, and isn't that good?"
Bnina hesitated for a long time before answering.
"Please give me a little time."
Bnina wanted to confirm the facts with her own eyes first.
"When you've made up your mind, come to my tent."
Gaisa stood up with a sly smile, not missing Bnina biting her lower lip. He had already read Bnina's expression and realized his scheme had worked, and as he left the tent, he had to struggle to stop himself from bursting into laughter.

titleEn: Legend of Dragonia Part 2,
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}
While everyone in the gypsy village was asleep, there was someone secretly writing something in the pitch-black night.
The carrier pigeon tied next to him cooed, and he was writing something with a pen dipped in a chemical. The document he wrote was a secret one that would become visible when exposed to fire. Even when Laodicea's intelligence forces suddenly raided a few days ago, his documents remained safe because of these precautions. He put the written document into a small tube attached to the carrier pigeon's leg, then limped to a nearby forest. And from that forest, he released the pigeon.
'It's dangerous now. It's time to leave this place.'
The man thought as he watched the pigeon disappear into the night sky. One of his eyes, reflected in the moonlight, was covered by a black eyepatch. He was Gaius, the leader of the gypsy troupe. As he was about to return to his tent, he heard some murmuring, hid behind a rock, and drew a knife from his chest. He intended to kill anyone who saw him.
Surprisingly, it was Aysia and a man who appeared before him.
'Tch... Did Aysia have a man?'
Aysia and the young man sat in front of the rock where Gaius was looking down from. Aysia smiled and spoke to the young man.
"Phew... You know how scared I was back then. But these days, I feel safe because you, Royce, are here."
"You feel safe because I'm here?"
"Yes."
"Even though I wasn't there?"
"You promised, didn't you? That you'd protect me no matter where I was."
"Haha. I did, didn't I? I definitely said something so cheesy."
"Somehow, I feel like you'll appear no matter what the situation."
Dagmon was about to refute her words but stopped. Her face, illuminated by the moonlight, looked incredibly clear and mysterious.
"Aysia, do you trust me that much?"
"Yes. I think I can trust you to the very end."
"I trust Aysia too."
"Aw~ There's something I want to hear more than that..."
Aysia said with a disappointed "Pfft~".
"Ah, haha. I can't win against Aysia. I love you... I truly love Aysia so much that I wouldn't trade you for this entire country."
Instead of answering his confession of love, Aysia began to sing a song about love. As her song spread through the forest, Dagmon fell into an astonishing ecstasy. He even wondered if such a voice existed anywhere else in the world.
However, after singing for a bit, she stopped and spoke. Dagmon, on the other hand, felt a pang of regret as her beautiful singing stopped, desperately wanting to hear it again.
"These days, there are no performances, and I'm a bit sad. I really love singing on stage. Of course, it's also nice that the leader, that guy, doesn't leer at me in my stage costume."
"The leader?"
"That one-eyed, limping old man. He's been bothering me since way back. Actually, there are scary rumors about him, so I don't go near him."
Gaius was startled, realizing they were talking about him.
In truth, Gaius had harbored dark intentions towards Aysia for a long time. Of course, it wasn't a feeling like love, but this situation was certainly enough to make him feel jealous. Gaius decided to kill the young man and claim Aysia for himself right then, tightening his grip on the knife.
Anyway, these days, with no performances, Aysia's existence was merely something he desired to possess, nothing more, nothing less.
However, he decided to watch them a little longer. If he was going to have her anyway, he thought the pleasure would be greater if he watched their interaction a bit more before taking her.
Looking at her face illuminated by the moonlight, Dagmon spoke.
"I love Aysia's singing. When you sing, it feels like the air changes."
"Huh?"
"It's like a fragrance. A beautiful scent."
"Not the smell of the forest?"
"Yes. And I wish everyone was like your face. Everyone in this country."
"Everyone in this country?"
"Don't people usually say 'everyone in the world' in such cases?"
Only then did Dagmon realize his slip of the tongue.
"Ah. That's what I meant. I'm usually not very good with words. Haha."
"Royce. You have a much kinder heart than you appear. To think so warmly of everyone in this world."
"Does it come across that way?"
"But you know what? You're the first person who's made me feel this way. I wish you'd only look at me, not everyone else in the world."
At her words, Dagmon looked directly into Aysia's eyes. Her eyes, reflected in the moonlight, were breathtakingly beautiful, so much so that he was afraid to meet them. Dagmon's heart pounded so loudly it felt like the forest would echo, but he looked straight at her and replied.
"You don't have to worry about that. In my eyes, I only see you. And this world is no match for you."
For a moment, Dagmon felt guilty about deceiving Aysia. He considered revealing his identity but then remembered the incident with Melchizedek a few days ago and stopped. He wanted to reveal everything to her now and consider a more serious relationship.
"Aysia. No matter what happens, please trust me."
Dagmon said seriously. Aysia then asked with a puzzled expression.
"What's wrong? It's as if something's going to happen. *Gasp*."
Dagmon kissed Aysia before she could finish her sentence. Aysia's face instantly flushed.
"How embarrassing... What if someone sees us? Suddenly... Where did this come from?"
Gaius's stomach churned at the sight of them. He wanted Aysia before she could be touched by another man. Just as Gaius drew his knife and was about to approach them, Aysia nestled into Dagmon's chest. She saw something sparkling on Dagmon's neck and asked.
"Oh my. Royce. You wear a necklace too? It's pretty."
Dagmon took out the necklace. A pendant hung from the necklace. It was a gold artifact with the emblem of a blue dragon and a crown, a royal item, but fortunately, Aysia, being a gypsy, would not recognize it.
"You didn't get this from another woman, did you?"
"Ah, no. Of course not."
Dagmon replied with a smile.
"This is actually a family heirloom."
Dagmon's answer was both true and false. It was something he had received directly from his father, a pendant that proved he was a prince.
"If you like it that much, I'll give it to Aysia."
Dagmon had no interest in the throne anyway, so he readily placed it around Aysia's neck.
"Is it really okay, even though it's so precious?"
"Yes. To me, Aysia is more precious even if I were given this entire country. But promise me one thing. You must never show it to anyone else."
"Huh? Why?"
Dagmon said this because he was worried someone might recognize the pendant, but he couldn't find a suitable excuse. After a moment of hesitation, Dagmon smiled and made an excuse.
".... Because it's a secret just between the two of us. Understood?"

titleEn: Absurd, Empty Promises for WiBro Netbook Sub
contentEn:
Fundamentally, I believe Wibro, rather than LTE, is the path Korea should take. I also think it's a product that should be actively encouraged and nurtured. Recently, I was tempted by the offer of a free netbook when using Wibro, so I diligently looked into it. However, **huge disappointment!! Such pricing plans can absolutely not activate Wibro.** I assert this. I clearly realized that neither KT nor the government has any interest in Wibro activation.
I didn't even bother looking up SKT, which is famous for its expensive rates. The pricing plans are as follows. Please correct me if I'm wrong. I truly hope I am.

| Plan | Price | Netbook Installment Support |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1G | 10,000 won | None |
| 30G | 19,000 won | None |
| 50G | 27,000 won | 10,000 won/month (up to 36 months) |

**1. The Most Economical and Realistic 1G Plan**
**1G is the optimal condition for smartphone users, commuters on buses, and for me, who wants to blog on the bus. In reality, over 50% of mobile users would fall into this category.** However, there is no subsidy. If Wibro phones come out in the future, I would subscribe to the 1G plan. It's the model most likely to contribute to the initial spread of Wibro. However, there is no netbook installment support. Searching 'Jishikin' (Naver's Q&A), I found countless posts from part-timers claiming they initially intended to get 1G but switched to 50G.
([http://kin.naver.com/detail/detail.php?d1id=1&dir_id=10401&docid=9513838&qb=7JmA7J2067iM66GcIDFnIDMwZw==&enc=utf8](http://kin.naver.com/detail/detail.php?d1id=1&dir_id=10401&docid=9513838&qb=7JmA7J2067iM66GcIDFnIDMwZw==&enc=utf8))
I don't know if they've actually used it, but exceeding 50G wirelessly while using wired internet at home is a waste of money.
It even seems they confuse Bit, a unit of speed measurement, with Byte, a unit of capacity measurement.
Frankly, using a 50G (capacity) wireless plan while utilizing 100Mbps (speed) IPTV or TPS products is an utterly incomprehensible act.

**2. The 30G Plan, Applicable to the Remaining 50%**
**30G is realistic for people who use the web a fair bit. It's sufficient for music and multimedia transfers, and ample for just enjoying web surfing.** Of course, this assumes high-resolution movies are downloaded via wired internet. Most netbook users fall into this category. Netbook installment support is most desperately needed for this plan.

**3. The 50G Plan, Which Nobody Needs**
Why does the 50G plan suddenly jump to 27,000 won for just a 20G difference? Only one type of person needs it: a user who doesn't use wired internet and relies entirely on wireless. I believe such users hardly exist nowadays, as TPS (Triple Play Service) is becoming common.

**4. The Strange Difference Between 30G and 50G**
I explained the difference in user needs between 30G and 50G above. The difference between 27,000 won and 19,000 won creates an 8,000 won gap. For the 90% of users who choose the 50G plan but consistently stay within 30G, looking at the 8,000 won difference in plan cost from the netbook installment support (10,000 won), only a 2,000 won benefit actually occurs. The actual discount is **2,000 * 36 months, totaling 72,000 won**. And that's not a one-time discount, but rather a calculation of discounts spread over 36 months. Furthermore, the netbook model and supply price are set at promotional prices, which differ from the lowest market prices for netbooks. Considering that HP netbooks recently dropped below 400,000 won, it's not very appealing.

**5. Conclusion**
Wibro activation is just talk! Pricing plan games. Isn't it time to stop? Terminal subsidies and government support come out of taxes. Wibro pricing plans should fundamentally be considered as an extension of wired communication network development. If wireless isn't intended to completely replace wired, I hope they'll propose realistic support measures. No user will cut off wired internet and only use expensive wireless internet. What's important are plans under 30GB, and in the current situation where VoIP integration is impossible, competitiveness will emerge from prices below 20,000 won.

While I don't particularly like criticizing, it truly infuriates me to see such obvious tricks being played while pretending to make efforts for technology dissemination. If things continue this way, LTE will win, and Wibro will become a forgotten technology.

titleEn: Web Trends for Mobile Games: HTML5 or Flash?
contentEn:
**1. HTML5 or Plugin?**
It seems there was an event where web plugins (Flash), which had made ActiveX a public enemy, and web standards (HTML5) were discussed as platforms for the next-generation mobile web. However, personally, I can't shake the feeling that it's excessively ahead of the market. In fact, I think this discussion is not very fruitful. This is because mobile browser companies and mobile vendors hold the cards in the current situation, and they have their own plans and actions, and the power of giant corporations like Google and MS cannot be ignored. Rather, the W3C, which experienced a failure with XHTML, is now pushing HTML5, and their own capabilities are the most questionable. Perhaps it's fortunate that Google, MS, and Mozilla don't consider them enemies due to the trend of web standards?

**2. Current Mobile Platforms**
In the case of Adobe Flash, simple plugin mobile games are still running on mobile platforms today. Through Wap or the web, Java or WIPI binaries are downloaded via specific links or events and automatically launched. In that sense, current mobile phone games may look different, but they are not much different from Flash. The difference is whether Flash appears as part of a webpage or not, and the development of this Flash plugin is credited to browser companies, while Java or WIPI are credited to hardware vendors. Flash games rarely communicated with other web controls beyond navigation, so the value of web controls and communication as a game platform was low. Furthermore, most mobile browsers already support Flash, and although users may not know it, Flash was already widely used in phone UIs and wallpapers.
{{IMG:1}}
[Com2uS's WIPI-based MMORPG, Aimo]

Of course, when aiming for the web as a platform, it would be right to exclude existing Java and WIPI, or mobile OS platforms like Android, OSX, and WinMobile. However, within the framework of the mobile game market, game developers will obviously face the same dilemma regarding platforms. Isn't it absurd to discuss the market without including the people who create content?

****
**3. Still, Why the Web as a Game Platform?**
Why insist on running games on the web? This is ultimately because the web's greatest advantage – the ability to serve many users with a single source, anywhere, on any platform – cannot be overlooked. However, for now, I believe this discussion is too premature. Google's approach of improving the environment with two directions, the web OS Chrome and Android, is probably for this very reason.

****
**4. Improvements Needed for the Web to Become a Game Platform**
**1) Local DB**
This is already underway, and some solutions have emerged. There's nothing special about it. However, I'm a little concerned that as the use of local DB in web browsers expands, it will clearly become a more tempting target for attacks than cookies. But our great Google God assures us that such things won't happen. For now, we'll have to wait and see. However, even if it's the Google God, it's as unconvincing as the lie of bug-free software.

**2) Diverse Input Devices**
{{IMG:2}}

Gamepads, even Wii Remotes and augmented reality – the trend in recent games is moving beyond keyboards and mice. Even iPhones have built-in gyro sensors, but Flash doesn't even support them. Games must always show agile movements to users who desire more diverse experiences, and they are, in fact, hardware-dependent. However, improvements to web standards are incredibly slow. Not just slow, but crawling. It's been ages since multimedia spread, and now multimedia tags are officially being included. The reason existing multimedia ran via Flash plugins was precisely this.
Of course, if we give up game genres that require such new input devices, there's nothing more to say. Even with such a compromise, the web, originally a document presentation format, is not very smooth for keyboard and mouse input due to its control-based nature. To assign character attributes to a text box and inherit them, you have to resort to tricks comparable to implementing C++ in C. The web platform has a significant gap compared to existing game platforms.

**3) Dazzling Graphics and Sound**
{{IMG:3}}

[Source] [I tried C9 Open Beta. (Total War™)] (http://cafe.naver.com/praetorians/68620) | Author [Camille] (http://cafe.naver.com/praetorians.cafe?iframe_url=/CafeMemberNetworkView.nhn%3Fm=view%26memberid=camille1300)

Modern games offer truly dazzling graphics and wonderful sound. Behind this are technologies like 3D graphics, hardware acceleration, software double buffering, and sound mixing. For Windows, a special API called DirectX ensures hardware performance and these software technologies. However, the web performs rendering in div units and web object units, which involves downloading HTML from the server, interpreting HTML, and then downloading and arranging web objects again. This process is performed every time a page reloads, and AJAX emerged to improve this speed. AJAX pre-downloads more resources than appear, which can be seen as a concept similar to game loading. And reconstructing the screen via JavaScript is absolutely dependent on browser performance, and its speed is incomparable to technologies like double buffering that directly write to memory, which games require. This is because browsers do not implement it using DirectX.
Of course, Flash supports it to some extent. That's why shooting web games are rare, but there are tons of Flash games on Hangame. In other words, Flash is playing the role of DirectX on the web.

**4. So, Is There No Potential for Web Games?**
{{IMG:4}}

[Source] [Current status of web games...;;] (http://blog.naver.com/gagawa/20086747298)| Author [Maxim Goliath] (http://blog.naver.com/gagawa)

That's not true. The web is already at a decent level for asynchronous game types that the web itself possesses. Board games, turn-based games, and traditional RPGs are already possible. And these games, which might be slightly less flashy, can evolve into various forms of game elements and user participation unique to the web. Even today, board games are still welcomed. If someone says a game failed because its graphics weren't flashy, they would be the person who knows the least about games.

**5. Summary**

| Category | Technology | Governing Body | Platform Dependency | Characteristics | Suitable Game Genres |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OS | Android OSX Windows Mobile | Google, MS, Apple, Mobile Phone Vendors | High | Flashy UI, 3D hardware acceleration, high hardware utilization | MMORPG, FPS |
| Plugin | Flex Silverlight Java Fx | Adobe, SUN, MS | Medium | Fast screen, shooting, action 2D games | Shooting, Real-time Strategy Simulation, RPG |
| Web Standard | Html5 Ajax Javascript | W3C, Private Organizations | Low | Cannot guarantee synchronicity | Board, Turn-based, Puzzle Games |

- The table above is my own creation, so no complaints.

The lower you go, the less sensitive to market trends, and the higher you go, the higher the platform dependency. Looking at the entities, the bottom consists of non-profit organizations like W3C, and the top consists of traditional corporations. The non-profit organizations at the bottom will evolve with a vision to encompass all market functions, while the for-profit organizations at the top will try to make their platforms compatible with all market platforms and dominate the market. **The organizations at the bottom represent horizontal expansion, while those at the top represent vertical expansion.**

*Cloud is a bit different; it's a horizontal expansion model performed by commercial vendors, starting from lower layers like storage and network rather than user applications. Therefore, it should be considered somewhat outside the scope of user experience, so I didn't mention it.

**6. Conclusion**
Ultimately, platforms are just a standard war between business domains. Does a platform truly exist that is suitable for games? Is that really the case? When a platform emerged, suitable games followed, and if they were fun, they poured out regardless of the platform. Was there any platform where Tetris and Go-Stop couldn't be implemented?
Each side is attempting to expand into other areas by leveraging its strengths under the guise of unifying the world. In this situation, wouldn't it be difficult to say which platform is the truth? Many game companies already have their own platforms and are also making efforts to easily port them to any platform.
Rather, I think it's more realistic to consider which users to target at the right time and which game is more suitable for which environment. That's why platform vendors strive to secure many customers.
However, a trend is just a trend; if the content is good, it's possible to sustain an entire platform (e.g., Nintendo). A well-made game will surely succeed no matter what platform it's on.

{{IMG:5}}

**[Source]** [Pokémon Game Collection (2) ([No.1]Lovely Poke Pokémon Drawing)](http://cafe.naver.com/lovelypoke/554) |**Author** [Ash Riolu Flygon](http://cafe.naver.com/lovelypoke.cafe?iframe_url=/CafeMemberNetworkView.nhn%3Fm=view%26memberid=chlwldn10)

 
It's becoming an increasingly gloomy world for developers, even as there's more to learn.

titleEn: What Would Korea's Web Ecosystem Be
contentEn:
We often hear that Naver is a cause for concern and that the Korean web ecosystem has not diversified due to Naver. But is that really true? I've also wondered what it would be like if a company like Naver didn't exist in Korea. Of course, these are just my subjective thoughts, so they're not very credible; please take them as a reference. Comments and trackbacks are always welcome.

** 1. Would the portal-centric environment have improved?
**I don't think so. This is because the second and third-place sites look similar to Naver.
{{IMG:1}}

**[Source]** [Comparison of Portal Main Screens for March 1st: Naver, Daum, Yahoo, Nate, Paran, Google](http://blog.naver.com/rmadyd1000/60063572812)|**Author** [Open Yang](http://blog.naver.com/rmadyd1000)

In fact, Naver, which offers a cast service, has the most outbound links. It's relatively recent that second and third-place sites started advocating for openness, and the second-place player always wants openness, even without Web 2.0, because the site itself wants to lower the cost of user migration as an alternative. Therefore, it's difficult to expect another company to open up if it were to take Naver's place. This business issue is precisely why KTF and LGT relatively desire network openness. Of course, I'm only discussing the business environment, separate from recent trends and Web 2.0 user needs. **If second and third-place players weren't portal-centric, it might be different, but our current situation, where they are, means that in Korea's business environment, it's difficult to survive in a narrow market without being a portal.**

** 2. Which company would have taken the most profit?**
{{IMG:2}}
I'm speaking based on the premise that Daum did not become the second Naver and everything was truly open. **Without a doubt, it would be Google.** What made Naver what it is today is the search advertising market. Even Naver, which is quite good at search, is currently transferring a significant portion of its profits to Google and Overture. **If the web environment were completely open, including Knowledge iN, Naver's search competitiveness would actually be questionable.** Google is a company with vast equipment, world-class talent that cannot even be compared, and financial power to buy Naver several times over. Even search engines created by genius physicists like Wolfram or Microsoft are in an all-out war to catch up with their search.
Google's global search market share is 69%, and as with Naver domestically, web-wide profits are concentrated globally. Even if an excellent search engine like Chotnun existed, breaking even would be no easy feat. In reality, the technology of Chotnun, acquired with enormous money, is not rotting at Naver, as far as I know.
**Ultimately, the current runners-up would have either become Naver, offering exclusive services to Google, or much smaller companies, with Google taking most of the search revenue.** Nate coveted Naver's Knowledge iN database through Empas but, conversely, does not allow Cyworld's data to be searched. This is because it would mean giving up their own advantages. And **this threat is not a safe situation for Naver either.** The desire for openness and trends among users cannot be ignored. Eventually, there might be a day when they open up and compete with Google, but the possibility of opening before gaining competitiveness seems low, and they are making efforts to replace Google and Overture.

** 3. The era of venture and Web 2.0 would have arrived.**
**
**This time, I'll talk about Nate Cyworld, which is in third place. Their success is actually a venture myth. The same goes for Me2day, but the explosive growth in the middle was driven by the power of large corporations, and many companies abroad also succeeded through Google's M&A. **And in a narrow country like Korea, to grow to that size, you have to encroach on other markets.** Cyworld clearly channeled a lot of web consumption time into Cyworld, and when Cyworld hit its limits with acorn sales, what it immediately started was portalization. That's proof that our market has no easy answers. **If you only stay in the domestic service, any wonderful Web 2.0 service, with the current business models, has clear limitations. Going into the global market is definitely the answer, but the web is fundamentally a service and culturally dependent.** **Ultimately, this means the difficulty is even higher, as Korean culture itself has a negligible global influence.** If it were a service targeting global users from the start, it would be possible even now, without Naver. It's hard to find any non-English speaking foreign country encroached upon by Google that has experienced a boom because of it.**

**
**
** 4. Limits to Portal Growth**
{{IMG:3}}**
News has emerged that Google's growth has slowed. The reason is the **saturation of Google's search market share**. With excellent technology and services, it has relentlessly encroached upon the world's web market, and most of its revenue comes from search. YouTube, a representative Google service, is now also being developed to generate profit, and **Naver is similar; its revenue has not diversified in many areas, so it has hit a limit after consuming most of the pie.** Even if Google were to take over the entire domestic search market, it couldn't achieve the same growth as in the past, and the only remaining big opportunity is China. This is why Google values China so highly and where domestic search powerhouses still have a chance to compete. Naver, too, when viewed solely domestically, is bound to follow Google's concerns.
**Therefore, what Google and Naver have chosen is to expand the pie.**
{{IMG:4}}**
Their method of expanding the web pie is simple. First, **increase web usage time through mobile and convergence**. Examples include Google Phone and Android, the 800MHz auction, Naver's acquisition of Me2day, and mobile OK services that domestic portals have participated in since before, and IPTV is also in this domain.
Second, **grow services outside their own to expand the overall web pie.** The revenue structure of search engines like Naver and Google is similar to that of a brokerage firm that earns from stock commissions. **It's more important how much trading occurs through their company than whether they hold all the securities internally.** What they held internally was merely a means to an end. Currently, the **challenge for these two companies is to maintain search market share and expand the size of the web.**
For Naver, this need is even more urgent. The cast service can be understood in the same context. **For Naver, openness has become a necessity, not an option, precisely because of the limitations of this growth model.** Especially for IT companies, future value significantly impacts operations and valuation, so a decreasing growth rate soon brings a shock equivalent to negative growth. Google and Naver currently seem to be at this inflection point and need to break through something.

**
**
** 5. Their Breakthrough
**Personally, I don't want to see Google win. **While users might see Google as a good company, if you ask me if Google is positive for the Korean IT environment, I would answer negatively.** Currently, **Naver is a company that employs many IT professionals to gain competitiveness and significantly raises the average working conditions for developers, which are otherwise poor.** Of course, it's not comparable to financial institutions, public enterprises, or energy companies. (If you get a job there, the working conditions would be much more rigid than Naver, but the compensation is incomparable. It's the number one workplace I recommend to my juniors, and the competition rate proves it.) Other companies complain that Naver attracts good talent, but that means they can't offer comparable compensation. Still, it's not as amazing compensation as you might imagine. It just means that the Korean IT market is unstable and poor.
**Assuming Google took over the Korean web market, it already has enough good talent, so its impact on domestic IT would be limited to that of Microsoft Korea. Furthermore, it would take most of the revenue generated from the web, with little chance of reinvestment in Korean IT.** I'm not much of a patriot, but as a pathetic developer who isn't good at English, I'm not confident I'd be one of the few to get into Google, so that situation doesn't look very rosy to me.
Considering Google as a global competitor, Naver's concerns are understandable. **Ultimately, it's about overseas expansion.** Korea is a country that relies on exports due to its small market. IT cannot be an exception. The need for domestic companies to succeed in overseas expansion is more critical than ever.

Among them, the solution for domestic portals is overseas expansion into Japan and China, where cultures are similar and Google's market share is not high.
{{IMG:5}}
In China's case, even if they don't come in first and only secure a few percent market share, they can gain something greater than the monopoly of the Korean web. Corporate value would naturally rise. In the mobile sector, it's worth competing because local characteristics are stronger than in the search market.
{{IMG:6}}
Then what about Google, which has already dominated the global market? **They chose a strategy of breaking the web's framework itself and permeating from the bottom up. To break the web's framework, they started creating browsers and operating systems, and from the bottom up, they began to create and sell their web platform technology under the name of cloud.** In this market, Naver could eventually become a Google customer. This means that while using Naver services, the platform itself could be Google's.
However, for now, cloud services are a new business, and there are still many security and legal issues to resolve. Companies like Naver, domestic SI firms, and MS are also aggressively jumping in, leveraging their strengths. Therefore, it's difficult to predict Google's monopoly in the platform market yet, but so far, they have shown the most successful performance. Since this market has fewer local characteristics, both opportunities and threats exist simultaneously for us and for them.

**6. Demands for Change in the Korean Web
1) Businesses**
Businesses move on their own to survive. **They will build technological capabilities, weigh user needs and their own competitiveness on a scale, make business decisions, and fight.** If a company truly fails to read user needs, it will be truly frustrating and soon fail, and this will be reflected in its corporate value. Since stock prices reflect many psychological factors, it's safe to say that the weight of user needs is already reflected.
Furthermore, they must secure **competitiveness in the web advertising market** such as search and banner ads, and it also seems **necessary to create new business models that move away from advertising-centric models.** Many services think along the lines of "just gather users first, no matter what," and when asked about their business model, they commonly all talk about advertising. However, considering the slowdown in growth for Google and Naver, and the diminishing influence of traditional media, it's not a new business but, from a broader perspective, a zero-sum game in the advertising market.
**2) Users**
For Korean users, the distribution of high-quality information via the web must increase. There is a need for the distribution of information beyond just IT and society, encompassing culture, creativity, technology, and academia. By actively utilizing links and refraining from abuse, and through awareness of a clean internet and copyright, it must become a stepping stone for software companies to grow. This is the path Korean blogs must take to be properly evaluated.
**3) Nation**
Furthermore, the nation needs vision, strategy, and appropriate investment. If the next-generation web is mobile and cloud, then infrastructure commensurate with that is required, and this is not solved by technology alone, but also involves many necessary aspects like systems, policies, and even pricing plans.

**7. Additional Remarks**
To become a truly strong nation, not just an IT powerhouse in name only, we must become a strong nation in the software industry. However, that path clearly seems long. Business conditions are not good, both internally and externally, and while user needs are world-class, the market structure and perception of software are at rock bottom. Perhaps for these reasons, I hope that at least one Google-like company could exist in Korea. Of course, perhaps Google emerged there because it was already such fertile ground, but who knows? Perhaps fruit can bloom even in barren environments. I look forward to the power of Koreans. For a forest to grow from a single tree, that single tree and its owner must provide the answer.

titleEn: Is 20 billion KRW really a
contentEn:
Wisia Chart posted on Opencast

[[ Title: More Valuable Things for the 20 Billion Won of Public Money Used to Train an Astronaut ]](http://www.wisia.com/chart/15)[This file does not support direct playback. Click to play in a pop-up window.](http://blog.naver.com/EmbedHttpView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=70068176118&hashKey=5c6748e537123193f8bc1b965debc51f) [More Valuable Things for the 20 Billion Won of Public Money Used to Train an Astronaut - Wisia Chart](http://www.wisia.com/chart/15) 
 
How much money did the United States pour into space development? Although the astronomically expensive space development plans competitively pursued during the Cold War era have provided immense opportunities to the US and Russia to this day.

 Due to massive projects like space development, from the F-22 Raptor to Jellopen. Even what are called cutting-edge technologies, and project costs initiated to manage large organizations and immense expenses. Even the ability to manage risky projects with unknown futures. It seems many are unaware that the reason we pay countless costs in IT today and learn advanced processes and technologies from developed countries is precisely because of these investments.

 More valuable things. Of course, there might be more valuable things.
However, **a person who does not dream is dead. Dreams are hard to quantify in terms of value, and sometimes they make people risk their lives. I find it truly bitter that Korean society only compares things based on relative value and monetary value.**

 It's hard to briefly explain what I felt from the anime Planetes. Dreaming isn't that simple. When asked if the lives of Einstein and Newton, who dreamed, and the dozens of astronauts who died without ever reaching space, are lighter than those of starving children, I'm not confident I can answer well.

 However, what is certain is that even when approached solely through economic logic, technological development has value.
Also, although I am in STEM, hoping for results without cost is a fallacy. Does 20 billion won seem like a lot? How much would a single building in Seoul cost? It's less than one apartment complex in Gangnam. How much does it cost to build a single subway station? Do you know how much money was spent, how many people dedicated their time, or even lost their lives to send Armstrong to the moon?

 Korea's first astronaut. Perhaps, as some claim, it was nothing. If you only look at the outcome, that's true. It's certainly possible to go to space at a much lower cost, and it might truly just be a show. However, it's virtually impossible to get the know-how for astronaut training and various technologies for free. And when have Koreans ever looked up at the sky? We need to catch up in a short amount of time. 20 billion won is merely seed money. Do you know how much one Sidewinder missile costs? 

 Trillions of won were invested to acquire LCD and CDMA technologies. Compared to comprehensive space development, such technologies are less difficult and not dangerous. Still, when I think of the people willing to risk their lives to go to space and the children with sparkling eyes looking towards space, Korea's current situation seems truly bleak.

** Living merely to eat is no different from being a pig. No matter how much you dislike society or are dissatisfied with it, if you lose your dreams, what difference is there between the haves and those who fight them, and pigs?** Japan, reduced to ashes by the atomic bomb, dreamed after seeing Astro Boy and has become a developed nation capable of landing artificial satellites. **As long as this kind of thinking is widespread, that is our limit.**
 
 In Korea's case, one might talk about mobile phones, but the technological gap there is not even a few months. Furthermore, there's a tendency to focus on applied technology rather than core technology, which leads to poor profitability and makes it difficult to establish a long-term vision. Is it no longer possible to find a vision for science and technology in Korea after the downfall of Hwang Woo-suk? Even though Naro-ho failed, I was proud of it. 
 A country that had no tanks and was reduced to ashes in the 1950s is now launching rockets into space and trying to enter the full-fledged space race. As the media puts it, the first gate to the sky has opened, and space is just beginning.
 To achieve that (in Princess Mishil's tone...), a bit of a show is necessary.

titleEn: The Legend of Dragonia Part 2 Chapter 1 Episode 1 - Dagmon's Nightmare (1)
contentEn:
I am resuming the serialization to barely keep my promise of returning in August. I took a major exam, but I don't know the results yet, and work has become much busier, so it seems I'll have much less time to focus on writing or creative activities. I've only managed to write a little over twenty chapters for Part 2, as promised, which is only enough for about one mid-length episode. Nevertheless, I'm starting the serialization, as I believe releasing one chapter a week for about 20 weeks will help maintain the Munpia category. I think it's much more refined than Part 1. Especially since I wrote this after actually dating and getting married, I expect it to be better than before, at least.

I extend my gratitude to the approximately thirty people who read Part 1 to completion, the 148 people who haven't removed it from their favorites, and those who have waited for several months.

This novel is simultaneously serialized on [http://www,munpia.com](http://www.munpia.com/).

{{IMG:1}}

On the pitch-dark city streets at night, a lamplighter was walking, lighting the streetlights. As a chilling wind blew, he carefully finished his work, lest the flames extinguish, and slowly disappeared into the darkness to light other lamps.
On the street after he departed, only a mischievous wind lingered, trying to swallow the lights he had lit. Successively, raindrops began to dampen the cold stone pavement of the street, one or two at a time, and

Held by his mother, he stepped outside.
Even on a special day, all they could afford was warm bread from a small restaurant and soup with a little chicken mixed in. However, for the poor, a dish with meat in it was an extraordinary meal. Adele pestered Benjamin for food, and the child tore off a piece of bread for the ferret.
While eating, the child's mother discovered a wound on his wrist.
“What's this now? Did you fight with someone again?”
“No.”
The child shook his head.
Just then, a woman entered the restaurant, holding a child's hand and looking angry.
“Who is it? Is it that brat?”
The woman pointed a finger at Benjamin, who was sitting in front of his mother, and asked the child who came in with her. Soon, the woman approached Benjamin, her face flushing red and then pale.
“Did you hit him?”
The woman's child's face was a mess.
“What's the matter?”
The mother asked back, surprised.
“Is this brat your kid?”
The woman asked angrily, mixing in curses, but the child's mother still replied politely.
“Yes, he is...”
“Tch! Like mother, like son. Look at this child's injury. What are you going to do about it!”
Benjamin, who had been quietly eating next to them, asked back in a calm voice.
“Why did your son come alone, ma'am? Where are the other kids? They cowardly ganged up on me. And do you know why I fought with your son?”
Benjamin spoke in a chilling tone, unlike a child, and when he glanced at the child holding the woman's hand, the child flinched and hid behind the woman.
“What did you say? You fatherless brat!”
“How can you say such a thing!”
This time, the mother flared up in anger.
“Ma'am, I hit that child because he made remarks like yours. How can both children and adults be so ill-mannered?”
Benjamin, on the contrary, subtly provoked the woman. And in his words, for a moment, there was a murderous intent that no child could possibly possess, making the listener flinch.
“What! This kid!”
The woman tried to slap Benjamin, but he easily dodged it, causing her to lose her balance and fall. Then the woman screamed and lunged at the mother, and the restaurant became chaotic, causing vigilantes to appear.
“What in the world is going on! I'll arrest everyone first. Don't you know there's a war going on right now!”
The mother and Benjamin were locked in a detention cell with the woman and her child. But soon, the woman and child were called out. Looking out through the iron bars, a man who seemed to be the woman's husband arrived, exchanged a few words with the vigilantes, and the woman and child were soon released. The hateful child glared at Benjamin, stuck out his tongue, and disappeared.
Evening came, the lights in the public office went out, and only the two of them remained in the cold cell.
Quite some time seemed to have passed, as moonlight streamed in through the small barred window in the wall, and the vigilante on duty appeared to be dozing at his post.
Benjamin, who had grown up alone, usually pretended to be quite strong, unlike a young child, but when he was alone with his mother, he was nothing more than a spoiled child. Confirming that no one else was around and they were alone, Benjamin quietly sobbed on his mother's lap. The mother held young Benjamin in her arms. Perhaps because he resembled his father, he was a strong child. But Benjamin, held in his mother's arms, was just a tender-hearted boy.
“I'm sorry, Benjamin... It's your birthday, of all days...”
The mother spoke pitifully, and the child asked back, crying.
“Sniff, sniff. Mom. Where's Dad? Everyone makes fun of me. That's why I fought. But what the kids say is true, isn't it? Dad isn't here. Did Dad go to war and die?”
The mother, holding young Benjamin, also felt a lump in her throat. Adele, seeing Benjamin whimpering, rolled her dark eyes and looked at him as if something was strange.
“Don't mind what the children say. Your father, you see, is a wonderful person. He's a hero who will end the war and bring peace.”
“Is Dad a soldier?”
The child asked, but the mother shook her head.
“Then is he a general?”
“He's someone even higher than that.”
“Pfft- There's no such thing.”
“When peace comes, you see. This will lead you to your father.”
The mother took off the necklace she was wearing around her neck and placed it in Benjamin's hand. It was a gold artifact with a blue dragon emblem and a crown engraved on it.
“When will Dad come?”
“He'll be here soon.”
“Mom. I'll make sure you live comfortably. I'll earn money. Even though I look like this, I'm strong. I can take on five or six kids by myself.”
At that, the mother shed tears instead of answering.
Seeing that, Benjamin raised his small hand, wiped his mother's tears, and said.
“No. I'm sorry. Don't cry, Mom... I'm sorry I fought.”
The mother wiped away her tears again and said with a smile.
“It's okay. Mom's not crying. I have my dependable Benjamin here. Good children should go to bed early, shouldn't they?”
Holding Benjamin in her arms, the mother began to sing.
Her voice was half-laden with sorrow, sometimes breaking in parts as her throat tightened, but its timbre was beautiful. The mother's singing was more splendid than any gypsy's or street musician's. Moonlight seeped in, illuminating her hat, and her beautiful singing seemed to circle the cell and fly towards the blue moonlight.

Your eyes are the North Star that sailors use as their compass.
With you, I can go anywhere.
Barely turning in this world. You, whom I barely reached.
I swear to God.
Our promise, more solid than a dragon's tooth,
will make the World Tree bloom at the end of the world.
Before long, Benjamin fell asleep, breathing softly, and his mother kissed the child's lips.
“My prince. I cannot hate you. For if I hate you, I will come to hate this child too.”
Tears were still flowing from the eyes of Aysia, Benjamin's mother.

titleEn: August 18, 2009
Please Sell MP3s on Me2day.
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}
In fact, I think Cyworld was the biggest hit in the SNS business model. Gifting a single skin or a single BGM wasn't too much of a burden and felt really good. However, as I use Me2day, I feel a similar desire. (Is it just me?)

I think it would be great if I could listen to good music and read books together with my "michin" (friends on Me2day). East Asians fundamentally enjoy giving and receiving things. While we appreciate the support we get on Twitter or blogs, it's natural that the desire to be someone special to someone else is stronger than the desire to be a hero leading the masses. Especially for women.
(But I'm a man. {{IMG:2}})

In today's busy world, the meaning of SNS seems even more precious. I want to go back to Cyworld, but there's a strong feeling that everyone has lost interest, and it requires too much time investment. Being busy is truly the culprit.

So, what gives that special feeling? Most people would want to leave a great comment, but it's not easy with clumsy writing skills. In that case, the easiest way is to buy something for someone. Especially at an affordable level... That's why Cyworld's skin and BGM gifts were very meaningful. However, these gifts have a drawback. They lose their meaning outside of Cyworld, and they don't really help in remembering someone. While they have meaning within Cyworld or Naver, they don't seem to maximize their value as gifts. Cyworld has over 200 songs, and Naver BGM is approaching 100 songs, but I can't remember the meaning of each individual song.

However, there's something that lasts the longest: music on a local PC. Sometimes, one song is better than a hundred words. How about gifting DRM-free music on Me2day, Cyworld, or Naver blogs? Or perhaps e-books, which are just starting to become active.

The characteristics of the gifts I'm talking about are:
1) An affordable price, under 1,000 won.
2) Permanence.
3) Stimulating emotional sensitivity.

These three points. And I believe that if SNS platforms utilize this, there will be sufficient profit. Me2day is reportedly struggling with its business model despite its explosively growing subscriber base, so I wonder if a model like this would work.
Furthermore, I believe this model can normalize the music and e-book distribution markets. I think content that is not dependent on a specific platform and the resulting revenue model have already begun.

If MP3 gifting becomes possible on Me2day, I'll send a song to my "michin" (friends). {{IMG:3}}

titleEn: Naver Blog is a Turtle. (Blog Feature
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

http://inside.naver.com/freeblog

Everyone knows the fable of the Tortoise and the Hare.
Looking at the recent blog feature improvement project <Third Story>, Naver Blog isn't a noisy hare, but rather a steady tortoise.
Points 1 through 5 were actually areas I had requested improvements for quite a long time ago. {{IMG:2}}

**Blog, Memolog, Photolog? It's complicated. [http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70005567552](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70005567552)
(As of June 28, 2006) Only 8 people saved the post!! {{IMG:3}}
**
**Frankly, these kinds of requests don't pose a big business issue.**
It's not like something dramatically changes, like widgets or OPEN APIs, nor does the UI drastically transform like a remote control.
And in many aspects, moving categories to the top, strengthening search, and enabling post movement are convenient from a content management perspective, but they are not particularly meaningful features for attracting new content.

**But For User!**
However, many blog users are still confused with mini-hompies, and frankly, blogs are still not as user-friendly as mini-hompies, and most people don't want to communicate as much as external bloggers might think. (Of course, this might just be my opinion) Koreans generally have strong ties to their immediate circle, a strong distrust of outsiders, and don't particularly like being at the center of issues, much like the Japanese.
Instead, they show more attachment to [my data], are more afraid and curious about the gaze of someone they know looking at them, and prefer to become celebrities rather than being at the center of social issues.
The reason I also mention social issues and IT on my blog is not to be at the center of something, but rather to aim for a kind of **writing practice and thought practice aspiring to be an expert**.

Anyway, the weakness of blogs that **only strengthen external connections is that they tend to be indifferent to the user patterns of internal users**. Naver Blog, too, as various logs were additionally developed, from a development perspective, they would clearly have been in different DBs or Tables, and given its scale as the largest portal in Korea, which is beyond imagination, the free movement of data between each Table would not be an easy task. **It might even be a task where the cost-effectiveness is low compared to the resource input.**

However, although it took a very long time... (it seems to be delayed by 1 or 2 years on average. But from a developer's perspective, planning, designing, implementing, and testing is by no means a long time.) Seeing that they eventually released the desired features, I feel like I made a good choice using Naver Blog.
While I was satisfied with the recent feature enhancements of Naver Blog, seeing them gradually make improvements that scratch where it itches, it seems they are at least listening to user feedback. **Such a tortoise is at least trustworthy.**

Naver Blog reduces the time spent looking at HTML or CSS, ensures a sufficient influx of users through search, and thankfully, alleviates worries about data loss if the company were to fail.
Considering that Naver also discontinued its homepage service, they might discard it if it's not profitable, but fundamentally, a blog is internal content, an asset, so it's clear they would sell it rather than simply discard it. Indeed, the game of scale still applies here.

If there's a slight drawback, it's that **there are fewer friends and less feedback than on mini-hompies? Most users seem reluctant to expose their trivial daily lives.** That's why Me2day was even started (should I invite Cyworld friends to Me2day..), and currently, I am very satisfied.
Also, the Naver Episode series felt good, but at some point, it changed to the name 'Improvement Project'. It seems there's a lack of consistency in marketing. I also think it would be a bit better if the **promotion of these changes had more consistency.**

It's already hard to utilize space because of widgets, so I hope September comes quickly so I can move the messy categories on the left upwards and pull all the data from review logs.
Now, Naver Blog finally feels like it's finding consistency.
