titleEn: NoSQL Movement: Anti-RDB? Or Distributed
contentEn:
[http://www.idg.co.kr/newscenter/common/newCommonView.do?newsId=57298](http://www.idg.co.kr/newscenter/common/newCommonView.do?newsId=57298)
I came across an interesting article via Opencast, but I simply can't understand the content of the article, even after reading it. Is it true that distributed storage services like Hadoop are being opposed by the NoSQL community, specifically targeting RDBs?

As someone who has used distributed solutions like Coord and Hadoop, this part is hard for me to grasp. From what I've read, the difficulty in mapping RDBs is being pointed out as an RDB problem, and issues like the process of indexing due to SQL language or speed problems seem to be criticized.

If I try to understand this article at my level, and discuss the difference between RDB and distributed storage services, distributed storage virtualizes memory and operates in a pool-based manner. Therefore, it fundamentally operates like memory or large-capacity storage, which would have the advantage of enabling random seeks.
However, databases retrieve data through SQL language via a data modeling process, resulting in a 2D table format.

Thus, RDBs have weak performance in random seeks and are not suitable for querying multi-dimensional information. So, can Hadoop really be an alternative? This part makes me a bit skeptical. In fact, efforts to solve these problems in databases have existed. OODB and ORDB were the alternatives. However, unlike traditional SQL, they required queries specific to their respective databases and had performance issues.

But will Hadoop truly solve all these problems at once, just by allowing large objects to be easily uploaded?

Honestly... I don't think so. While blind faith in distributed solutions also presents technical challenges at present, fundamentally, object fundamentalists claim that a perfect object alone provides great reusability and excellent scalability. Unfortunately, objects are not as great as they are thought to be. This is mostly because the people designing objects are not perfect, and the human brain has varying levels of abstraction; developers and designers processing real-world data often get confused even with just three dimensions. Therefore, when numerous real-world data, which largely remain in 2D, are mapped to objects, the difficulties will still arise if the object design is flawed later on.

Hadoop can also process 2D data. However, if that functionality is merely the goal, couldn't one achieve the same objective as Hadoop simply by using a distributed database?

SQL certainly presents many limitations, but for understanding data with my simple mind and viewing information by printing it, table data is quite convenient.

Fundamentally, databases are for data processing, not for software development, so I wonder if there's really a need to 'fight' with Hadoop. I also wonder if the NoSQL movement is fundamentally about problems arising from using a DB unnecessarily where it shouldn't be used. Or is it a new alternative to OR Mapping?

I'm not sure if my understanding is lacking... or if the translation is wrong. But from what I vaguely understand, it seems to be a different story than an anti-RDB movement, as the article suggests. Of course, Oracle is also well aware of the limitations of RDBs. That's why, starting from 8i, it seems to be called ORDB... And with NHN's Cubrid, for example, the problem is that most developers still find RDBs too difficult to understand, and their performance is below expectations.

So, will ORDBs, distributed solutions, and hybrid services eventually emerge? Or will that just be a distributed DB?
Perhaps... the problem is that I'm neither a DB expert nor a distributed systems expert... so my understanding reaches its limit here.

titleEn: Turnkey Contracts: A Bad Habit Born from Construction
contentEn:
Related URL: [http://blog.naver.com/stein12/30052617074](http://blog.naver.com/stein12/30052617074)

IT fundamentally involves creating intangible products and operates on a project basis. Many of the project management techniques used in IT originated from the construction industry. Indeed, many terms come from construction projects, and these engineering techniques have greatly contributed to increasing IT productivity.

However, IT also suffers from problems that resemble the chronic bad habits of Korean construction companies.

That is the turnkey order. If one were to force a positive aspect of turnkey orders, it would be that it creates a structure where many companies can survive. If a project 'A' generates a profit of 100, 'Gap' (the prime contractor) participates in various bids, gets their capabilities verified, and secures the 100. Then, for the actual development, they entrust it to 'Eul' (the subcontractor) and bid it out as a 50-unit project. That project is then further subdivided, leading to a structure where even more companies participate and share the profits.

The absolute number of companies making a profit is high, and from 'Gap's' perspective, it becomes a better business to secure even one more new project, manage it, and then hand over new bids, rather than spending time on development. Consequently, the actual implementing companies – in construction, the contractors – end up building and developing programs with meager profits.

Therefore, the problem is that as the 'Gap, Eul, Byeong, Jeong' (prime, sub, sub-sub, sub-sub-sub) turnkey structure deepens, project prices are frequently inflated compared to the actual cost of program and construction production. As a result, the practitioners and technicians at the 'Byeong' and 'Jeong' levels want to become 'Gap' or 'Eul' by any means, and 'Gap' and 'Eul' become arrogant within this structure.

Even when the market becomes difficult, it's the 'Byeong' and 'Jeong' companies that fail first, with 'Gap' and 'Eul' failing last, which is also a problem for 'Byeong' and 'Jeong' due to their lack of capital.

Fundamentally, in a capitalist market, such a structure is not much of a problem. This is because companies operate for profit.

However, the story changes when viewed from a national, industrial, or consumer (client) perspective.

The problem of having to purchase goods at a higher price than the actual cost, which for construction companies translates to the issue of public disclosure of pre-sale prices, falls into this category. Furthermore, since the share for implementing companies with actual technical skills decreases, everyone tries to focus only on management, leading to a culture that disparages technicians. For companies like Samsung SDS and LG CNS, their management skills are truly remarkable, but it's difficult to say they possess many core technologies, which is a problem. This ultimately leads to a reduction in the competitiveness of the software and construction industries compared to their international counterparts.

At least in IT, efforts like separate ordering and divided ordering are being made, and since there are many cases where direct competition with overseas companies is necessary, this chronic problem is somewhat recognized within the industry. However, looking at the current construction industry, it seems quite difficult in many respects. They refuse to stop the turnkey ordering model and continue a vicious cycle where the state covers their insolvency, which fundamentally means that these deficiencies are being covered by taxpayer money and the pockets of apartment buyers.

In particular, this leads to an overall increase in real estate prices, effectively blocking opportunities for capital to flow into other industries. It is a unique characteristic of Korea that individual investors with fewer assets have a higher proportion of their wealth in real estate, such as jeonse deposits. The act of repaying loan principals over 20 years also means that the remaining consumer and productive capacity is mortgaged to the real estate market. The real estate dependency of the most productive and consumer-active demographic, those in their 30s, is surprisingly high, and I wonder if this isn't a national loss.

I recall that during the last presidential election, candidate Moon Kook-hyun also estimated the scale of construction corruption (?) to be close to 80 trillion won, arguing that tax cuts and growth were possible through addressing it. While I don't believe the amount is exactly 80 trillion won, and not all of it is due to corruption, I do see it as a somewhat plausible scenario. I also think his proposal for a real-name system for construction companies was one of his brilliant suggestions.

My uncles who work in construction also do turnkey projects and were well aware of these problems. However, no one dares to break this mold. Only the government, which commissions construction and civil engineering projects, can break it. This is because these construction powers have already solidified their foundation in many ways, and I often wonder if the state itself isn't having its policies determined by them.

Along with oil tycoons who often appear as dark forces in dramas, construction companies are frequently cited in Korea for similar reasons, likely due to this image.

Fundamentally, there won't be many 'blue oceans' in any market going forward. All companies will only be able to survive through drastic high-efficiency improvements, and when such companies exist, the Korean economy will survive. Unlike in the past, the government will likely not have much capacity to grant special favors to specific industries. No particular industry can be an exception. If these adjustments are not implemented merely out of desperation for job numbers, isn't it contradictory to be reducing jobs in the public sector and public enterprises?

Job creation, as the current government superficially claims, should indeed come from new businesses and high-efficiency improvements. It is true that fundamentally, implementing high-efficiency improvements using IT, for example, will temporarily lead to a reduction in many jobs. However, if we fear this, it's tantamount to abandoning national competitiveness. Our task is to leverage that competitiveness to compete abroad and create jobs through it.

From that perspective, at a difficult time like now, isn't it even more necessary to contemplate these structural issues? If the emergence of IT governance discussions was due to IT ROI being questioned, then I wonder if construction also needs governance today. Is construction truly carrying out projects based on transparent ROI?

For the software industry to develop, this vicious cycle must certainly be broken first.

As long as the answer to 'What do you do when a problem arises with Gap?' is 'We go to a room salon with Gap and sign the contract,' the Korean industry will not be able to shed its backwardness.

Only then will the notorious overtime decrease, the image of a '3D job' (Dirty, Difficult, Dangerous) be shed, the term 'SI' (System Integration) will no longer be synonymous with 'dead end' in the software industry, and we will be able to compete globally.

titleEn: Media Law Debated Without Its Core Subject
contentEn:
Although it wasn't a matter I was particularly interested in, I've been hearing talk about the media law. Listening to the opinions of both the Democratic Party and the Grand National Party... there are some truly astonishing aspects. Are they really making such claims for the development of media? Isn't their address a bit off? If we're talking about media, it should be a law for content producers, i.e., CPs, and cultural producers. Our country's media can never develop if we only think of the three major broadcasters – KBS, MBC, SBS – or large corporations like Samsung.

This story begins with the biggest problem in Korean media: the lack of diversity. While the spread of CATV and the emergence of channels like tvN and Onmedia have somewhat enriched it, their effect remains minimal, and the capital and market are too narrow to create and sell good content. Ultimately, it should be a law to solve this problem. If it's a law designed to create a favorable situation for certain factions to seize power, then it's failing to escape the shackles of the Cold War era, where culture was sold to buy politics. It seems that in their minds, broadcasting is merely about guidance and propaganda. The current situation of the three major broadcasters is that they are full of journalists who pretend to know a lot about fields they don't understand well. Even if the media law is blocked, this situation will not change.
In conclusion, the media law is necessary. However, it will be necessary to examine each of the so-called "poisonous clauses" to see if they are truly for the media, the public's right to know, and the right to expression.

First, regarding the Democratic Party's opposition to large corporations' participation, I disagree. The participation of large capital in media is absolutely necessary. Do you think the current environment where Korean films can compete with foreign films is due to independent films in Chungmuro? No. While there was certainly the problem of large capital flooding theaters with their own mediocre investment films, it fundamentally expanded the market size and became the foundation for outstanding works like "Old Partner" and "The King and the Clown." This was partly due to complementary measures like the quota system, but the contribution of large corporations to improving the overall quality of Korean cinema and investment culture can never be ignored. Furthermore, I want to ask again, how different are the three major broadcasters from large corporations? In fact, they are not much different from large corporations currently. It is true that they actually have certain biases and argue in their own favor. Most media outlets are not free from this. Neutrality? That doesn't exist in the first place. How can neutrality exist when everyone has a different perspective? The argument that one is righteous and neutral is a relic of the Cold War era. The public good is for the public to decide, not for just three broadcasters.

Second, it's an overblown advertisement that there will be tremendous employment effects, as the Grand National Party claims. Unfortunately, no. Don't make me laugh. In a country with fundamentally only 50 million people, how big do you expect the advertising market to be? Today's broadcast advertising market is already feeling a crisis from the web advertising market. Consequently, when it switches to an all-IP network, the advertising market will be placed on a single infrastructure: the internet network. If the Grand National Party's words are true, the best promising future advertising company would be NHN, not Samsung. However, Korea's advertising market naturally has certain limits as consumers and time are restricted. Furthermore, it's obvious that if the same amount of money were invested in telecommunications or IT instead, there would be more employment effects. In fact, this aspect makes me suspect that broadcasters, feeling a sense of crisis from the internet, are trying to get a foothold in IT.

Since I've criticized both sides once, I'll now talk about what truly needs to be done. The media law should be a law for CPs, accelerate diversity, and adequately consider new media. CP is no longer a specific company as in the past. It could be an individual producing UCC, or a sponsoring company supporting such users. Creating an environment where diverse content can be produced and distributed – that is what the new media law should do.
Therefore, the key areas for discussion should include not only large corporations but also smaller companies' participation in broadcasting, consideration for new media like web TV and UCC, copyright considerations for derivative works, the network for distributing and selling them. And, it should be a system that allows free distribution rather than surveillance. However, neither the Grand National Party nor the Democratic Party is considering these aspects. Why? Because both are busy worrying about their own positions. Naturally, the government and ruling party, who should be paying attention to these areas, deserve more criticism. Do they think they were put there for that? If the media law takes a direction towards surveillance out of concern for negative social impact, media competitiveness will inevitably decline. Let's look at the example of neighboring Japan. That country is a place where rumors are even more rampant than ours. However, because of media diversity, the public is less swayed by rumors, and the market is diverse.

What is the reason why it's easy for a specific faction to seize power today? The problem is that if you just occupy the three major broadcasters, it creates an atmosphere like conquering a castle in Lineage. Large corporate participation is good. But if avenues are opened for broadcasts like OhmyNews or AfreecaTV, their power will be halved anyway, and efforts to secure better content will intensify, leading to more support for content creators.

I earnestly ask. A media law discussed without media producers. Whose media law is it really for? While they are ultimately engaged in a political struggle over just three broadcasters or a few companies, new standards are already being created overseas, and the possibility of new business models emerging from UCC cannot be excluded.
Who are these people who divide this country into two, making you a leftist if you like MBC, or a rightist if you don't? Are you a leftist even if you like MBC's Queen Seondeok? Why can the government arbitrarily fire and appoint broadcast company presidents, and even dismiss reporters and announcers? Seeing these situations, it's truly frustrating. Media that eliminates such diverse voices is nothing more than an advertising page.

I heard a rumor that they're going to show "Daehan News" in movies. Fine. Do it. However, give a 1,000 won discount on tickets to viewers who watch it, and have the government bear the full cost and use it to support independent films. The era of watching advertisements for free is over. No matter how you look at it, that's an advertisement, not a campaign.

titleEn: [Idea] Public Blog Email
contentEn:
**1. Title: Blog Public Mailbox**
- Background: An idea aimed at expanding the scope of email usage by not just a simple convergence of incorporating email into a blog, but by leveraging the blog's comment and reply feedback features and linking it with address book groups.
- Effects: Abolition of storage limits (no 1GB, 6GB limits, permanent like a blog)
  Email activation
  Easy use of webmail by address book groups
  Enhanced email accessibility through blogs
  Easy publication of personal webzines, exploring new services
- First Draft Date: July 24, 2008

**2. Operation Description and UI**
**2.1) Mail Writing Screen**
{{IMG:1}}

- The basic concept is an integrated service of blog and mail.
- In addition to Blog and reviewlog, 'mail' has been added.
- System-generated inboxes / sent mailboxes / bills / trash (missing in image) are set to private.
  (Not visible to other users)
  - In the example above, 'Club' and 'Personal Mail' are mailboxes created by the user, but are set to private (default) as the user does not wish to disclose them to third parties.
  - In the case of 'Data Room' and 'Church Newsletter', they are public as the user wishes to disclose them to others.
  (Similar to blog posts, third-party writing permissions may not be available in mail categories.)
  (Others' posts may be added via replies. This is explained below.)

**2.2) Inbox / Sent Mailbox / Bills (Same as regular mail)**
{{IMG:2}}

**2.3) Reply**
- When a reply is attached to a mail, it appears to the user as a 'reply' within that mail object.
- **Normally, when a reply arrives, it goes into the inbox, but here it accumulates as a reply in the sent mailbox and is displayed as if a reply has been attached. Comment-style replies can also be allowed.**
However, receiving replies in the inbox as before can also be allowed.

{{IMG:3}}
**2.4) Category Group Mail Function**
- Automatic classification for each mailbox can be set by category.
- Additionally, a sending list can be set by category.
{{IMG:4}}
[Setting Sending List by Category]
{{IMG:5}}
[Writing Mail using the Corresponding Category]

**2.5) Writing Public Mail**
- Public mail is disclosed to third parties like a blog post. Therefore, when writing mail in a category set for public mail, a warning should be displayed, or consent for public disclosure must be obtained to prevent user carelessness.
{{IMG:6}}
- If another person writes a reply or comment on a public mail, it remains on that post, making it visible to third parties. Therefore, the recipient must also be informed that it is a 'public mail'.
**2.6) Reply to Public Mail**
{{IMG:7}}
[View of Public Mail Confirmation]

{{IMG:8}}
[ Writing a Reply to Public Mail ]
l When replying to a public mail, it is saved as a reply in the user's private inbox on their own blog, but it appears as a reply in the public mailbox on the blog of the original sender, so the user must be informed that it may be visible to third parties.

**2.7) New User Participation in Public Mail**
{{IMG:9}}
In the case of user Lee367, who is not included in the @ChurchMembers group, if they leave a message expressing their wish to join the mailing list after checking the blog's open mail, they can apply using the comment function, similar to a blog, if the open mail settings allow comments.
Comment and reply writing permissions can be divided into [Not Allowed] [Mutual Friends Only] [Friends Only] [Mail Group Only] [Logged-in Users Only] [Completely Public].

- For 'Completely Public', external users like Hanmail can send replies, but the email field must be mandatory.

**2.8) Public Mail Sent to External Email**
- Users must be informed that public mail can be disclosed externally.
- This must be communicated within the standard email specifications for external emails.
- This utilizes the subject and signature features.
Add a prefix [Public Mail] to the subject.
In the signature section, attach the content: * This is a public mail, and replies will be disclosed in the sender's public mailbox.
* The URL of the sender's public mailbox can also be included.

**2.9) Creating a Guestbook using a Public Mailbox**
If a public mailbox named 'Guestbook' is created, it will appear to external users like a bulletin board or guestbook. This brings about the effect where the sender directly selects the recipient's mailbox, rather than mail being separated into mailboxes based on content. : In the case of a private mailbox, it appears externally the same as an existing private guestbook.
- Differences from a guestbook
: Users must fill in the email field to receive replies.
If the blogger posts a reply in the user's guestbook (mailbox), that reply is sent via email.
Furthermore, if the user replies to this reply again, the reply will be attached to that guestbook (mailbox).

**2.9) Mailbox Recent Reply Feature**
- When implementing the above features, the email retention period will become permanent like posts, compared to the old method. Even very old sent or written emails can receive replies or comments in the public mailbox. Therefore, a 'recent reply' feature, similar to a post's recent reply or comment feature, may be needed.

**2.10) Webzine Subscription Application** - Considering the act of publishing a webzine using a public mailbox linked to an address book, the result is similar to personal publishing like Cyworld's Paper, or a webzine like Usenet. It can be said to be somewhere between Paper and a webzine.
When applying for a subscription, it operates similarly to existing webzine applications, but this process is not automatic registration; instead, the user receives an application comment or reply and adds it to an address book group.
However, if necessary, a method of automatically adding the email entered by the user to the address book, similar to existing webzine subscription features, can also be considered.

**2.9) POP Server Function** – Fundamentally, because it is mail, it can support POP servers. Therefore, it has the extensibility to allow third-party services or other platforms to view or retrieve content from the blog mailbox, and to provide the same service as email in the mobile domain.

**3. Implementation**
- Fundamentally, it is a webmail system overlaid on a bulletin board.
- This is because email has high costs and factors like storage limits.
- Therefore, in the implementation phase, the dependency on mail is reduced by using the mail server as a temporary cache from an external system like a blog's bulletin board, only utilizing the mail server when new input or modifications occur.
**In the case of old emails, they are usually moved to the trash and deleted. However, in this system, they are moved to the bulletin board server, not the trash, without the user's knowledge, but to the user, they appear as existing posts from the beginning, so no difference is felt.**
**If a user sends a reply to an old email on the bulletin board server, a new email is generated using the mail header information (recipient, sender address, etc.) stored in the bulletin board server's DB.**
è Therefore, although the internal email and server are dualized, the user should retain the feeling of using email.
- Furthermore, in the current system, reply information does not exist in traditional mail systems.
Information about replies is merely indicated by a 'Re]' in the subject, and is treated the same as existing mail.
In Google's case,

- **Method to identify reply information:**
: Previously, the only method to identify a reply was through the 'Re]' in the subject.
(In Google's case)
However, with the above idea, even if the subject or content is changed, it must be recognized as a reply. Therefore, when replying, the address or ID of the parent mail post of the public mail sender must be sent along.
To further resolve this, the message ID in the mail header is used. (Therefore, an email message ID is assigned to posts.) It may be necessary to request the sending side to transmit the original message ID as a standard.
If this method is not feasible, hidden HTML tags or user-visible content can be inserted into the body.

1) Webmail part: The section visible as HTML on the blog externally
2) Mail server: The mail server responsible for actual sending and receiving
3) Bulletin board/post server: The server that backs up and maintains data

**4. Increased Importance of Spam Handling**
- As mail exists permanently, if it becomes a target of spam attacks, it incurs very high costs. Therefore, more robust spam countermeasures are necessary.
- In addition to features for catching spam and user settings like traditional email, technology is needed to detect already recorded spam or remove accumulated spam that users haven't checked.
(This may already be utilized in blogs or cafes)

titleEn: Hankyoreh's Absurd Excuse Regarding Na
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}
If it exists merely to criticize, it is not journalism. This holds true regardless of political stance, whether it's Chosun or Hankyoreh. I'm actually curious if Hankyoreh even knows who they were defending this time.
The issue of copyright law that I posted about just yesterday ([http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70051260006](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70051260006)) is also related. It seems that the Korea Music Copyright Association (KOMCA) is involved in sanctioning Naver bloggers (please correct me if I'm wrong).
****
**The article in question:** [http://www.hani.co.kr/arti/culture/culture_general/361887.html](http://www.hani.co.kr/arti/culture/culture_general/361887.html)
**And read this: [Naver Webtoon Artist Kim Gyu-sam's Frank Talk About Naver Webtoons]**
**[http://blog.naver.com/kidrock93/120072359029](http://blog.naver.com/kidrock93/120072359029)**
****
**1. Traditional Media's Unease with New Media**
Traditional offline media, including Chosun Ilbo, JoongAng Ilbo, Dong-A Ilbo, and Hankyoreh, are actually uncomfortable with internet media like Naver and OhmyNews. Furthermore, the recent proliferation of high-quality content through blogs with AdSense, and the emergence of OpenCast, Daum View, and meta-blogging sites, is truly an uncomfortable development.
Moreover, the unique characteristic that paper once held, combined with the improved performance of mobile devices, and the recent re-emergence of e-books as a killer application, means that old media that haven't adapted to the times can't help but feel frustrated, and the development of new media is nothing but inconvenient for them.
New media generally do not control content, users and producers are not separated, evaluation is done by users, authors have significant control over pricing for their earnings, and there is no control over derivative works. Of course, there isn't absolutely no control. Appropriate levels of control are applied when content is deemed anti-social, infringes on personal information, or is harmful to youth. This is not for the sake of control, but because it is illegal. However, these companies fundamentally dislike control. Their business model is not based on profit from content itself, but from the distribution of content.
It's similar to how financial companies don't profit from stock gains when trading stocks, but rather from transaction fees.

A peculiar aspect of this incident is that the App Store, one of these new media platforms, became an issue, and Naver, a dominant portal operator with the characteristics of new media, was targeted. The attackers were traditional media distributors such as newspaper, magazine, and comic associations, and KOMCA.

**2. Has Traditional Media Really Done Well?**
Since the origin of this issue was the comic industry, I will set aside the music industry and talk about the comic industry. In fact, the music industry is similar. Think about who made Jang Ki-ha, from the small agency Bongaka Records, famous. At least the music industry is in a better situation than the comic industry. As someone who has always been very interested in Korean comics, hearing the lip service from traditional distributors really gets my blood boiling. Who killed Korean comics? If you ask that, there are users who circulate scanned copies, our culture that looked down on comics, and various other factors, but above all, I pick magazine publishers as the number one contributor.
Magazine publishers might have made efforts in their own way. But fundamentally, what was the reason for the narrow scope of the market? It was because comics remained just comics. You also failed to expand the amateur market, which you disliked. As Naver webtoon artist Kim Gyu-sam pointed out, their contract methods are almost unfair. If you couldn't apply to a magazine's contest, you couldn't even appear before the public and would disappear. Were there even many magazine publishers? In the past, there were a few like Bomulsom, and recently Young Champ. Did it even cease publication?
That's the reality. What are we supposed to do with a market that doesn't even exist? Let's talk about the comics serialized in Young Champ. Some wonderful domestic artists are visible. But a significant number are works verified in Japan. Also, when school-themed comics were rampant, domestic serialized works were plastered with school themes. I stopped reading comic magazines then. By whose logic are works evaluated and selected? Who was it that evaluated content based on commercialism and imposed one-sided contracts on artists? When rental shops were rampant, what did you do?

**3. Webtoons Emerge as the Only Escape for Cartoonists**
One artist even called webtoons a new trend, and said that vertically arranged webtoons create a different market feel from traditional page-turning comics. In fact, Naver Webtoon also uses a different panel arrangement method from the traditional one, and even features forms with music or animation. The evaluation of Park Moo-*, who is suspected to be the protagonist of the "600,000 won cartoonist" story, was also excellent. (Who exactly created that 600,000 won? Was it Naver?)
And thanks to webtoons, many artists gained fame and debuted professionally, and expensive color graphic novels are selling well. Naver does not restrict graphic novel sales; in fact, it kindly provides links for purchasing books. It's true that many artists are consistently working hard to be ranked highly for this reason.
A similar concept is newspaper comics, which are also essentially free comics given when you buy a newspaper. Why isn't this being contested? Doesn't Hankyoreh also publish comics? According to their argument, newspapers should not publish comics other than political cartoons.

**4. New Media Begins to Develop**
Think about why the App Store became an issue. All software has both free and paid versions. If a paid version has enough value, people pay for it. Free versions are offered because of social contribution, brand recognition, or other business models (like advertising). Comics are no different. They are also a form of media or content, and various business models can emerge. In the past, various models were actually attempted, such as Heo Hye-yoon's Coca-Cola cartoon or Bacchus-man comics.
Furthermore, derivative works hold great significance for comics. This means that amateur works or doujinshi can actually be sold through legitimate means with the artist's consent. Currently, it's completely impossible! Do you think a magazine publisher would allow you to create a doujinshi, get an ISBN, and sell it? The fan characters of Windows ME are already world-famous and, whether MS wanted it or not, have greatly helped improve MS's image. The possibilities are clearly endless.

Also, among the content in the reporter's answer that Kim Gyu-sam deleted, there was the view that **wireless content would not spread because it is expensive.** I don't know why this sounds like licking the boots of telecom companies. Does this mean that newspaper companies, unlike when they were uniformly criticizing the structure of telecom companies and the spread of wireless content, now acknowledge it? Unfortunately, that is completely wrong.
The future platform itself will not allow that. This is because the ones actually making money are not network operators, but content providers. Will AT&T make more money, or will Google make more money? From Google's perspective, wireless networks need to become cheaper. And technology is actually causing network costs to plummet significantly.
Ultimately, no matter when, an era of constant network connection will arrive, and the iPhone was essentially designed for that. Companies like Google, Samsung, and Intel, which could buy out all your companies and telecom companies, are putting it on a serious trajectory, and international technologies are also moving in that direction. That is the reality.
Such predictions have actually existed since the PCS era, and devices like the iPhone could have been made at any time, but they weren't due to market or technological circumstances. However, users now actually hold these phones. It can be said that preparations are complete, and these large vendors have made their judgment on the market.

**5. If the Problem is Simply Free Content, Then Traditional Media, I'll Tell You How to Make Money, Just Get Off the Internet.**
Internet content was created from the beginning with the purpose of participation and sharing. If you don't like that, then don't upload your content to the internet in the first place. Aren't you uploading it and providing it to Naver or Daum because it benefits you? If you're confident enough to stick to your claims, then start imprisoning bloggers for the crime of scraping articles, like some despicable corporations. You all know very well that scraping articles is illegal under current law, don't you? You also know very well that a blog is a one-person **media**, don't you?
If you put "blog" in the search options and type in the title of an article you uploaded, a long list will appear. If you extract settlement money from all of them according to that law, you could earn in one year what you would earn in 10 years. Isn't that attractive? And then just get off the internet and create daily newspapers for yourselves.

**6. What Naver Webtoon is Doing Well**
I've been wanting to write a post about Naver Webtoon recently, and they are truly doing well. In fact, two or three years ago, I used to read a lot of comics on Daum Media. But now, I only read about four comics on Daum Media. In contrast, I read two or three comics on Naver every day.
****
**1) Its position on the main page is clean and prominent.** The size and prominence are already different compared to Daum.
****
**2) Its connection with senior comic artists is outstanding.**
Hwang Mi-na's Botox: [http://comic.naver.com/webtoon/list.nhn?titleId=63129](http://comic.naver.com/webtoon/list.nhn?titleId=63129)

: What impressed me recently is our past artists

Remakes of their works and veteran cartoonists have returned as webtoons.
   Who knew the day would come when we could comment on Hwang Mi-na's works?
   Through 'Meet the Cartoonist', renowned individuals (I mentioned a few, but erased their names, as there are too many who would be greatly offended if even one was left out) and emerging artists meet, directly inspiring the dreams of children who aspire to be cartoonists, and not severing ties with the past. Do people even visit senior cartoonists from the past? Aren't they just pointed at for being outdated?

titleEn: Copyright Law Discussions Flowing in a Strange Direction
contentEn:
Recently, a lot of talk about copyright law has been heard through neighbor's posts and the like. However, as Akasa-nim suggested, I can't shake the feeling that the copyright law discussion is flowing in a strange direction. ([http://nblog.akalog.wo.tc/120072301924](http://nblog.akalog.wo.tc/120072301924))
 
**1. Copyright Law Being Discussed Incorrectly: Is bloggers' UCC illegal? The answer is yes, it is illegal.**
 [http://atombit.net/30051032297](http://atombit.net/30051032297) Bloggers, all get out? Copyright law activated!
{{IMG:1}}

I'm concerned that the repercussions from the post by power blogger Atom Beat are growing. However, upon carefully reading the content, I believe the very direction of the copyright law discussion is mistaken.

There are complaints asking if UCCs made from broadcast content, music, or commercial works as derivative works on blogs are illegal. In fact, they are strictly illegal. While those who only use the internet might not know this, it's common knowledge for people who draw, write, or make music. On Munpia, where I used to be active, there were many such discussions due to the large number of writers. Do homages or parodies fall under copyright? The conclusion was yes, they do. Basically, copyright law is intended to protect the rights of creators, and if strictly applied, its scope of protection is quite broad and comprehensive. In the case of songs, you have to pay a license fee even if you use more than two measures.

I sang a birthday song and uploaded it to UCC. Is it illegal? Yes, it is. The reason why "Happy Birthday to You" is not commonly sung in movies is precisely for this reason. If it's stored for personal use where others cannot see it, it's not illegal. However, since the meaning of UCC itself includes "Contents," it falls within the legal scope.

**Strictly speaking, this post, which is currently being discussed and widely shared, has nothing to do with the current administration or the revised copyright law.** On the contrary, posts that encourage such indiscriminate sharing could turn users who actively spread the same content

**Active Utilization and Understanding of [Subject]**
Recently, Yahoo launched an image search related to CCL. This seems like a very positive development. In fact, even a single image is usually not free from copyright, making it difficult to find images. **Even if 'reposting' (pumping) has become common, attaching a CCL to an image taken from a commercial site and posting it does not mean that CCL applies to that image. 'I put CCL on it, so it's fine!' This kind of thinking is a truly perilous mindset.** **Therefore, using CCL also requires a corresponding level of responsibility and understanding. Furthermore, for information producers, the more content they create using CCL, the freer the activity of derivative works will become. I believe this is the way for Naver bloggers and Cyworld users to shed the stigma of being 'reposters' (pump-loggers) and enrich the internet.**

*   If things continue this way, I wonder if the day will come when CCL is included in elementary school textbooks. In fact, many copyright infringers are minors. I think it's good to definitely inform your sons and daughters about copyright law if you have them these days. If there are any school teachers reading this, please be sure to educate your students.

titleEn: [Idea] Open Comment Notifier Open API Between
contentEn:
After seeing Rainlethe's post [I strongly support the socialization of blogs.([http://www.rainlethe.com/149](http://www.rainlethe.com/149))], I tried to find related files because it was similar to an idea I conceived about a year ago, but it seems I've lost the data somewhere. So I've reorganized it. It doesn't seem much different from back then.

****
**1. Title: Open Comment API between Blogs**
**2. Background: Considering standards and methods for comment notifications between different types of blogs.**
**3. Date: June 19, 2009**
**4. Scenario**
** 1) After logging into the blog, set a comment password and an OpenAPI password.**
   : This password must be different from the login password. This password is used when commenting on other blogs.
   : The OpenAPI password is used when sending a Notify to another blog. (For verifying that you sent it)

** 2) The blog user comments on an external blog.**
   : At this time, the blog has input fields for the blog address and password.
** 3) Assume the external blog supports the Comment Open API.**
   * Comments consist of the blog address (Url) to be notified, comment password (Pwd), title (Title), and content (Content).

**3.1) Actions performed when abc.tistory.com receives a comment**
** 3.1.1) When a comment is posted on [http://abc.tistory.com/1234](http://abc.tistory.com/1234), a comment notification page is created.**

titleEn: [Idea] Korean Input Method Using Drag on Touch Devices (Samsung Moakey Improvement Plan)
contentEn:
**1. Title: Hangeul Input Method Using Drag on Touch Devices (Samsung Moakey Improvement Plan)**
**2. First Written: July 24, 2008**
3. **Related Naver Service**: Embedded Machine Input Method Using a Touch Pen
4. **Existing Service**:
**Samsung's Moakey**
[http://blog.naver.com/yuoo10?Redirect=Log&logNo=100043098413](http://blog.naver.com/yuoo10?Redirect=Log&logNo=100043098413)

**5. Background**
**1)** When inputting vowels, except for ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, two or more strokes are required.
: For vowels like ㅣ, ㅡ, ㅐ, ㅙ, new button images must be combined.
In environments where it's difficult to find keys by touch, such as while traveling on a bus, locating specific keys is extremely challenging. This improvement plan aims to extend drag input to other vowels, inspired by the fact that ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ rarely encounter such problems and allow for fast input.
**2)** The screen is 2.8 inches, but there are too many keys, making it difficult to operate with just fingers.
**3)** For touch devices, reducing misrecognition during movement is more important than the number of key presses. The number of times a key needs to be searched for must be reduced.
**4)** As an alternative, handwriting recognition could be considered, but handwriting input with a large number of classes (2350 characters for Hangeul) has a very high error rate when moving, and requires using both hands with a stylus pen.

**6. Improvement Method**
1) Let's enable input of ㅐ and ㅙ with a single drag.
l ㅣ : ↗↓
l ㅡ : ↙→
**Unlike the existing Moakey, the above cases recognize diagonal directions to input ㅣ and ㅡ instead of ㅜ and ㅏ.**
l ㅐ : →(ㅏ)←(additional vowel command)↗↓(ㅣ)
l ㅙ : ↑(ㅗ)↓(additional vowel command)→(ㅏ) ←(additional vowel command)↗↓(ㅣ)
l ㅑ : →(ㅏ) ←(additional vowel command) →(ㅏ)
- **Additional Vowel Command Stroke**: When the initial drag input for a vowel is entered in the opposite direction, it signifies the input of an additional vowel.
Ex) When inputting [왜]
: ㅇ ↑↓→←↗↓
(After finishing the drag, the moment the pen is lifted, it returns to the consonant input mode.)
ㅇ : Click ㅇ
오 : ㅇ↑
와 : ㅇ ↑↓→
왜 : ↑↓→←↗↓

2) Let's reduce the number of keys and eliminate unnecessary keys when they are not needed for input.
Ex) If you click ㅁ and don't lift the pen, it means it's ready to receive a vowel input, so there's no need to show other consonant keys.
{{IMG:1}}

Currently, vowel input keys like the above only appear when the stylus is lifted.

After improvement
{{IMG:2}}

If you click ㅁ and don't lift the pen, the drag keys are activated. (**The background is darkened and the size is increased to enhance visibility.**)
If you drag to ㅏ
{{IMG:3}}
When moving back for an additional stroke
{{IMG:4}}

Basically, Moakey has too many keys.
* This can be solved by using repeated clicks of consonants on a mobile phone.
At this time, the minimum characters are
ㄱ -> ㅋ -> ㄲ
ㄴ
ㄷ -> ㅌ -> ㄸ
ㅇ -> ㅎ
ㅅ -> ㅆ
ㅈ -> ㅊ -> ㅉ
ㄹ
ㅁ -> ㅂ -> ㅍ

It can be reduced to about 7 characters.
**If ㄴ and ㄹ are included in other characters, it can be reduced further. Using this to enlarge the button size and secure space for dragging would help utilize the input method described above. Currently, with Samsung's Moakey, when inputting '머' using the 'ㅁ' key in the corner, it often hits outside the screen, causing inconvenience.**

Furthermore, the touch method of the screen can enhance user convenience by actually changing the key shape with each press. When ㅇ is clicked and the pen is lifted, the ㅇ key should change to the ㅎ key.
Ex) When inputting '황'
Double click ㅇ key (ㅎ) ↑(ㅗ)↓(additional vowel command)→(ㅏ) ㅇ

ㅇ : ㅇ
ㅎ : ㅇㅇ
호 : ㅇㅇ ↑
화 : ㅇㅇ↑↓→
황 : ㅇㅇ↑↓→ ㅇ

l Using the method above, all Hangeul input can be done with just 5-7 keys, and with minimal key movement, very fast touch typing is possible on an LCD. **(Once accustomed, a drag can effectively be considered a single input.)**

titleEn: [Idea] How to Sell Music on Your
contentEn:
This is an idea I had organized previously, and since there's a related article ([http://bloggertip.com/3546](http://bloggertip.com/3546)), I'm sharing it.
****
**1. Title: Method for Selling Music on Personal Websites**
2. Date of Creation: February 12, 2008
3. Background: There is no method for individual users to legally embed music on their websites. As interest in copyright increases and laws are strengthened, a need for this technology is emerging.

4. Problems: Copyright issues, abuse issues

5. Summary: Describes a method for using music purchased from a portal on a personal website. It is largely divided into background music services and post music embedding services.

6. Implementation Method: A user logged into Naver purchases music from Item Factory using a widget. The URL of the website to be used is registered, and a player widget is selected. JavaScript or Flash source code for use is issued. Alternatively, an open API is provided. When a play request comes from a user, it is checked via the referrer to see if it came from a registered site. The widget operates normally only if the referrer is from a registered site.

l Background Music Registration
1) After logging into Naver, purchase music that can be played externally.
2) Register the URL where the music will be serviced.
3) Select the player skin and playlist.
4) Naver issues music widget embedding source code containing a key paired with the URL.
Ex) <embed src=[http://myhomemusic.naver.com/player.swf?key=45930](http://myhomemusic.naver.com/player.swf?key=45930)></embed>
5) The user embeds the source code on their website.
6) When played, the Naver player verifies if the play is a legitimate call using the referrer and key value, then plays the music.
7) Users can change or manage their background music playlist by logging into Naver.

l Music Control in Bulletin Boards
1) After logging into Naver, purchase music that can be played externally.
2) Register the URL where the music will be serviced.
3) Naver informs the user of the key paired with the URL.
4) Users can use it in the form of a Power Editor control or a Zeroboard XE widget.
5) When first requesting music embedding from Naver, the control or widget asks for the key value.
6) The user enters the key value.
7) The control or widget requests the music list from Naver using that key value.
8) The user selects the music to embed from the music list.
9) The music is embedded in the same way as the blog music embedding service.

l Users who find it difficult to obtain a key value can register their Naver ID and password with Zeroboard XE. Zeroboard XE can then encrypt and remember these credentials, allowing it to function identically through an authentication process with Naver.
- Since Zeroboard XE operates as source code, modules that need to be hidden for security reasons are delivered in Flash format.

l Provision Method
: Using openAPI, after verifying the authentication key value and referrer information, a volatile URL for the music is provided using the MMS protocol. (Easy for developers, high scalability, weak security)
: Using an embed object, directly service within Naver via embed objects like Flash or Silverlight. (In this case, convenient for users, low scalability, high security, easy management, skin provision possible)

titleEn: Evaluating the Features of Samsung's Strategic Z
contentEn:
[http://jet.samsungmobile.com/#/feature](http://jet.samsungmobile.com/#/feature)
It remains to be seen when the actual phone comes out... but if I were to evaluate the phone based on the promotional website, my answer is: **there's nothing new under the sun.**
However, we've already experienced through the iPhone that even subtle differences and marketing prowess can lead to innovation.

First off, the H/W Spec is impressive. **800mhz**
It's about 180 Mhz faster than my M4650, Monahan 642mhz / and the iPhone's ARM11-based 620Mhz.
**Of course, H/W differences don't always translate into noticeable real-world speed.**
The speed will also vary greatly depending on whether this Jet phone uses Win Mobile 7 or Samsung's own embedded OS, and since it shows a lot of 3D usage, it **could also depend on whether a separate DSP chip for 3D processing is built-in.**
**Given that it supports DivX format, I'm inclined to think that a DSP chip for multimedia processing might be built-in.** There would naturally be a DSP chip for the camera, and sound quality and such also depend on the performance of these chips. While I'm enthusiastic about the iPhone, personally, Apple's sound quality is neither particularly good nor particularly bad. Let's not argue about that. Buying good earphones makes more of a difference... haha.

Anyway, the conclusion is that a fast CPU is definitely a strength. To support a **3.1-inch WVGA screen**, that level of performance will be necessary. For full browsing, the iPhone's 480*320 resolution is often frustrating. This kind of resolution, which requires zooming out to 50% and then navigating, has even led to the emergence of strange services like Mobile Naver ([http://m.naver.com/](http://m.naver.com/)). While this form is clearly a transitional service, **honestly, even 800 will still require scrolling around, so it really needs to be 1024**... but cramming 1024 into such a small device might hurt the eyes.
In this regard, it **definitely gets high marks for multimedia and full browsing. It makes me wonder if it's a model that threatens PMPs.**

And if I were to point out unique UI features, honestly, there aren't many. ㅡㅡ;
The cube, touted as its identity, is a technology already seen in SBP mobile3. **While rotating 360 degrees is unique, whether it rotates horizontally or 360 degrees, it's just a flashy UI and not a particularly meaningful technology.** What users truly want (even if they don't quite know it themselves) is to quickly find the screen they need. That's why I wasn't particularly impressed by Apple's flashy UI either.
**Perhaps due to Apple's patents, multi-touch is not supported.** (This is a bit of a pet peeve with Apple; the only UI feature from Apple that truly impressed me was multi-touch. But seeing them hoard technology doesn't sit well with me.)
**Built-in gyro sensor for gesture recognition.** It shows the sound turning off when flipped, and reacts when shaken. Nothing new. These features already existed elsewhere.

**Widget customization** is said to be possible. It likely allows for home screen editing, similar to SBP3 or Omnia. This is much easier than editing XML. While iPhone users don't customize much, these extended editing features are very effective for Koreans who love changing their home screens. Honestly, I dislike having a row of uninspired buttons on the first screen. That's one reason I despise MS Today.

The **multitask manager** stands out, and I'm curious about its performance. It seems to allow n tasks to run and stores each UI's layout as a bitmap, but perfect multitasking is now a fundamental requirement for future phones.

The **web browser** can utilize the screen widely. This was one of the most annoying aspects of the OZ browser, but it seems to support full screen like the iPhone or other browsers. It also seems easy to rotate horizontally. Advertising fast internet browsing... that's just advertising a fast CPU. It's meaningless. Actual web browsing depends on network speed. We need 4G quickly...

**WIFI support!!** While it's a given on the iPhone, it's good news nonetheless. I hope it's supported domestically. And WiBro too, if possible...
It has **built-in GPS.** DM SMS is unique; it seems like a service that can send coordinates via SMS. It looks like a very useful feature. If this were used as a standard, advertisements on websites could simply list an SMS number for a map, and when that SMS is sent, the destination would be automatically entered. It might even become a system where you can send your location to friends... (This is an assumption. It doesn't mean the Jet phone will necessarily do that. ㅡㅅㅡ)

**Online Widgets** - The phrase 'W3C standard online widgets' stands out. It gives Yahoo widgets as an example, implying compatibility with widgets. This is the problem with Apple's App Store, which is walled off from open standards. They only use their own. I suspect Flash widgets and web widgets will be the majority. Ultimately, this brings to mind Google's and MS's prediction that cloud computing will be the trend. In fact, 'widget' and 'gadget' are older terms than 'app'. Apple just used 'app' to try and stand out.

**MS Active Sync** - Links with MS Outlook. Outlook integration, being a de facto market standard, is an irresistible temptation. However, I wish MS would improve their terrible Active Sync. It doesn't sync with multiple PCs, and it's easy to lose data if you're not careful. And ultimately, shouldn't it be moved to a web environment like Google? For me, it's 80% of the reason I can't abandon MS among smartphone features.

**SyncML support** - I wonder if this will solve the above problem. SyncML, an open format for syncing, means that Google Calendar, Cyworld, Naver Calendar, etc., can be supported. In a seamless internet environment, using WiBro and such, it might be possible to remove MS Outlook integration and replace it with this feature.

**Why is it a strategic phone?** Samsung is clearly aiming for an an all-IP-based mobile environment, similar to the iPhone or Google Phone. However, it doesn't seem to have much distinctiveness. The actual distinctiveness and competitiveness might depend on software distribution processes like the App Store, or developer support policies like MS's past CE policy or Google's Android. Samsung might even end up purely as a hardware manufacturer. A better CPU, a better LCD – what runs on top could be Google, MS, or even Apple. In that case, the deciding factors would inevitably be marketing ability, after-sales service, and price competitiveness. I wonder if they can beat Chinese companies then.
**While the Jet is clearly the best phone released so far, there's nothing new about it.** Anyone can copy it. That's a shame. Ultimately, **what can add novelty here is marketing ability**... but that's a difficult topic for me as an engineer, so I'll pass. I hope Korea's excellent marketers will take charge and solve it.
For reference, the Lollipop and Kim Yuna phones don't sell well because of good features. ㅡㅡ;

Finally, I'm curious about the **price**... Looking at the specs, it probably won't be cheap. But if it costs over 500,000 won, I'm not sure if it's worth spending that much. For that money, I'd rather buy an eeepc900a.

**Will touchscreens truly never solve the problem of easy text messaging?** Even Samsung's strategic phone ultimately failed to demonstrate a meaningful text input method. In the end, it's still QWERTY all the way. If the Jet phone had a QWERTY keyboard, I might consider buying it.

titleEn: Naver Blog Skin Template (Photoshop PSD File)
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}
**1. Purpose:**
 1) No title
 2) Text is clearly visible
 3) Covers both 1024 and 1280 resolutions
 4) Create a PSD file where background images can be easily changed
 
2. Download the attached files and extract the split archives.  **(You must download all 4 files.)**
{{IMG:2}}
**** 
- Each layer can be edited. 
**3. Layer Description**
** 1) Content Layer:** You can check how it looks when actually applied. Toggle the eye icon on and off, and turn off the eye icon for this layer when saving the final version.
 (It is connected to the overall box background, so if you move it carelessly, the layout may be misaligned.)
** 2) Overall Background Box Layer:** This layer was created to compensate for the drawback of general skins where content is not easily visible. You can change the color, but it's generally better to keep it white. Often, text becomes invisible because it doesn't match the background of scraped posts. By turning on the content layer and appropriately selecting the Transparent opacity value, you can check how the content will appear.
** 3) Natural Background Cover:** Prevents images from looking too sharply cut off. Adjust it up and down appropriately according to the user's image size.
** 4) Background 1, Background 2:** These are user backgrounds. Find suitable images and use them as backgrounds or edit them. If you bring in a new image, you can insert it here.
** 5) Just Background:** It's just a background. It looks odd without it...
 
** * Usage Order**
0) Just in case, make a copy of this PSD file.
1) Bring a suitable background image from the internet and insert it into Background 1 or 2. Turn off the eye icon for other Background 1, 2 layers.
2) Adjust the natural background cover by moving it up and down. Select the layer, press CTRL+SHIFT, and move the mouse; it will only move up and down, not left and right.
3) Turn on the content layer, check if the background image fits well, and then edit the background layer.
4) If it looks good, turn off the content layer, and save it as JPG by pressing Ctrl+Shift+S (Save As).
 (For Photoshop, you need to compress it to about 8 to keep it under 200kb, which is required for Naver uploads.)
5) In the blog remote control, select 'Title' during background registration and upload the created image.
 - The skin layout is 3 columns on the left, with no title, and all boxes are transparent.
 
ps. I made it in a hurry, so I couldn't use pretty images. It took longer than I expected. I modified the layers in OpenCanvas as much as possible for those who don't have Photoshop.
The blog owner might not answer questions because they're lazy.
